title: Analysis of subcellular spatial proteomics data in R
text:
Overview
These materials focus on subcellular spatial proteomics using mass spectrometry-based correlation profiling experiments.






TipLearning Objectives



You will learn about:

The principles underlying subcellular proteomics using mass spectrometry-based correlation profiling
How to import, process and analyse subcellular proteomics data in R using dedicated Bioconductor packages
Data quality control, dealing with missing values, aggregating feature-level data to protein-level, and converting quantitative MS data into correlation profiles
Assessing subcellular resolution and defining sensible markers that are representative of your dataset
How to perform classification of static protein subcellular localisation using semi-supervised machine learning
Identifying candidate protein differential localisation events when comparing two conditions




Target Audience
Proteomics practitioners or data analysts/bioinformaticians that would like to learn how to use R to analyse subcellular proteomics data from correlation profiling experiments.


Prerequisites

Basic understanding of mass spectometry.

Watch this video for an excellent overview.

A working knowledge of R and the tidyverse.
Familiarity with other Bioconductor data classes, such as those used for RNA-seq analysis, is useful but not required.




Exercises
Exercises in these materials are labelled according to their level of difficulty:







Level
Description




  
Exercises in level 1 are simpler and designed to get you familiar with the concepts and syntax covered in the course.


  
Exercises in level 2 combine different concepts together and apply it to a given task.


  
Exercises in level 3 require going beyond the concepts and syntax introduced to solve new problems.

R package installation
In this workshop we make use of open-source software from the R Bioconductor (Huber et al. 2015) project. The Bioconductor initiative provides R software packages dedicated to the processing of high-throughput complex biological data. Packages are open-source, well-documented and benefit from an active community of developers.
Detailed instructions for the installation of Bioconductor packages are documented on the Bioconductor Installation page. The main packages required for this workshop are installed using the code below. Additional packages required for downstream statistics and interpretation are installed as required.

if (!require("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("BiocManager")
}

BiocManager::install(c(
  library("tidyverse"),
  library("QFeatures"),
  library("MSnbase"),
  library("pRoloc"),
  library("pRolocdata"),
  library("pRolocGUI"),
  library("ggplot2"),
  library("Biostrings"),
  library("gridExtra"),
  library("dbscan"),
  library("clusterProfiler"),
  library("org.Hs.eg.db"),
  library("ggpubr"),
  library("pheatmap"),
  library("arrow")))

After installation, each package must be loaded before it can be used in the R session. This is achieved via the library function. Here we load all packages included in this course.

title: 1  The use-case data
text:
1.1 Subcellular proteomics
The field of subcellular spatial proteomics is centered on the determination of protein localisation within the cell. Importantly, protein localisation is intimately linked to protein function and is vital for research into basic biological mechanisms impacting the health and disease of all organisms (Sigaeva et al. 2026).
Quantitative mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics methods have been developed to study protein localisation at the proteome-wide level and generate subcellular “maps”. Several high throughput MS-based correlation profiling methods have been established and include the Localisation of Organelle Proteins (LOP) family of methods (Sadowski et al. 2006; Geladaki et al. 2019; Christoforou et al. 2016; McCaskie et al. 2025), dynamic organellar maps (DOMs) (Itzhak et al. 2016), protein correlation profiling (PCP) (Foster et al. 2006), sequential detergent-based solubilisation (Martinez-Val et al. 2021), COLA (Mardakheh et al. 2017), Prolocate (Jadot et al. 2017) and SubcellBarCode (Orre et al. 2019). Despite subtle differences in experimental design, as summarised in the figure below, all of these methods generate a similar data matrix (PSM, peptide or protein abundance across fractions) and can be analysed using the same subcellular proteomics software.
Generation of correlation profiling data requires considerable effort, expense and well thought-out experimental designs for successful implementation. Equally, data analysis involves considerable time and investment to produce high quality, robust datasets which enable meaningful biological interpretation and utility to the research community.
Modular experimental design of a mass spectrometry-based correlation profiling experiment. Experiments will differ with respect to: 1) the number of samples (replicates and conditions), 2) the method for gentle cell lysis, 3) the biochemical fractionation approach selected to generate crude separation of organelles, 4) the peptide quantitation method (label-based vs. label-free) and mass spectrometry acquisition method (data-dependent vs. data-independent), and 5) the processing software used to produce a quantitative matrix of PSM, peptides or proteins across biochemical fractions. Despite these differences, all types of correlation profiling-based subcellular proteomics experiments can be analysed using the presented workflow.
In this course material, we provide an updated workflow for the processing and analysis of correlation profiling-based spatial proteomics data, based on our F1000 workflow (Hutchings et al. 2025). We cover the key steps required to extract spatial information from quantitative correlation profiling MS data. The first step requires data importation, processing, and quality control followed by the definition of subcellular markers. We discuss how to curate such markers using approaches including unsupervised clustering and dimensionality reduction. Next, we show how to use subcellular markers to generate spatial proteome maps. This involves the classification of protein localisation through classical or Bayesian semi-supervised machine learning algorithms using the pRoloc package.

title: 1  The use-case data

1.2 Software
In this workflow we use R packages from Bioconductor, namely, the QFeatures package for upstream data processing and the pRoloc for downstream machine learning.








Figure 1.1: Main R Bioconductor packages used in this workflow.











NoteMSnSets versus QFeatures data structures



In our first F1000 workflow for spatial proteomics (Breckels et al. 2018) we used the MSnbase package and the MSnSet infrastructure for storing and manipulating our spatial proteomics data. In this workflow, we have transitioned to working with the QFeatures package for data processing. Whilst MSnbase provides functionality for manipulating and storing quantitative proteomics data, the QFeatures infrastructure makes it possible to store all levels of the data together in one object with explicit links maintained between hierarchical levels. For example, it is possible to store the peptide spectrum matches (PSMs), peptides and proteins (among other types of data) derived from all replicates of an experiment together, in one single data container.

title: 1  The use-case data
section: 1.3 The use-case: Subcellular mapping of U-2 OS cells
text:
1.3 The use-case: Subcellular mapping of U-2 OS cells
As a use-case, we will analyse a label-free DIA subcellular proteomics dataset from a partially differentiated human osteosarcoma (OS) cell line (U-2 OS cells) (McCaskie et al. 2025). U-2 OS cells are one of the earliest described cancer derived cell lines and have been applied across many areas of research. For subcellular proteomics they have been widely used in benchmarking as they provide a robust, flat, epithelial-like morphology and a deeply profiled human proteomic reference map.
Mass spectrometry (MS)-based protein correlation profiling data can be generated using a number of methodologies. These methods can differ with respect to (1) biochemical fractionation, (2) peptide quantitation (label-based or label-free), and (3) mass spectrometry acquisition method (data-dependent acquisition, DDA, or data-independent acquisition, DIA).
Our use-case data (\(\ref{fig-use-case}\)) was generated using the DIA-LOP method from the Lilley lab at the Universisty of Cambridge. DIA-LOP (Data-Independent Acquisition Localization of Organelle Proteins) is a high throughput subcellular proteomics method that offers a faster, label-free, and cost-effective alternative to classic multiplexed LOPIT methods (McCaskie et al. 2025). The pipeline works by gently lysing cells and using differential ultracentrifugation to separate intact organelles into 10 distinct fractions based on density. Instead of using expensive chemical tags e.g. tandem mass tags (TMT), these fractions undergo label-free peptide digestion and are analyzed via advanced DIA mass spectrometry, which systematically fragments all ions to capture low-abundance proteins from very low sample inputs. For each fraction, a total of 750 ng of peptide was analysed using using a timsTOF HT mass spectrometer (Bruker Daltonics, Bremen, Germany) coupled with a nanoElute 2 UHPLC system (Bruker Daltonics).
For the paper, the data was processed using the freely available DIA-NN software (v 1.8.2 beta 27) (Demichev et al. 2019) for peptide and protein identification and quantification, followed by the Bioconductor QFeatures package to aggregate and process precursor-level data into robust protein abundance profiles. Subsequently, the pRoloc package was used for protein subcellular localisation and the generation of subcellular maps, matching the abundance profiles of unknown proteins against known organelle markers to map over 8,000 protein groups across 13 subcellular compartments. The raw MS data is available online through ProteomeXchange via the PRIDE repository under the identifier PXD063082.








Figure 1.2: Overview of the use-case data experimental design. U-2 OS cells were cultured in separate flasks to generate three independent biological replicates, each separated into 10 differential centrifugation (DC) fractions (R1F01–R3F10). (A) Gentle cell lysis using a ball-bearing homogeniser to keep organelles intact. (B) Organelle separation by differential ultracentrifugation, using successive spins at increasing speeds. (C) Mass spectrometry using data-independent acquisition (DIA) on a timsTOF instrument. (D) Correlation profiling-based data analysis: peptide identification with DIA-NN, quality control (QC), and spatial mapping with semi-supervised machine learning classification in pRoloc. Adapted from McCaskie et al. (2025).













































































NoteIdentification search of the raw MS data



Database searching of MS data involves comparing the observed MS spectra to expected MS spectra generated via in silico digestion of a selected protein database. Since the use-case data used human cells, we provided the SwissProt human proteome to DIA-NN as the database for searching. We also provided a database of common contaminants that could be present in our sample due to (i) human contamination (e.g., keratin from nails, hair or skin), or (ii) sample preparation (e.g., enzymes used for protein digestion). These two databases are can be found in the course materials and also here.
The result of such a database search is a list of peptide spectrum matches (PSMs), or precursors, that is a list of matches between observed and expected spectra. Most software will also aggregate the PSM or precursor level data upward and provide output files at all data levels (PSM/precursor, peptide and protein). It is up to the user which output file to use for further analysis.
The starting point for this workshop and data processing workflow in R is an output file from the identification search. Different softwares output different file formats, for example the Proteome Discoverer v3.0 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) outputs a .txt file format, as does MaxQuant, FragPipe, other such as DIA-NN output parquet formats, will will show in the subsequent section how to import such data. Of note, the data was reprocessed using DIA-NN v2.0 (Academia) meaning that the files are no longer the exact ones used by (McCaskie et al. 2025).

title: 1  The use-case data
section: 1.4 Which data level should you start from?
text:
1.4 Which data level should you start from?
Proteomics search and quantification software can report results at several levels: PSMs, precursors (a peptide sequence with its modifications and charge state), modified peptides, peptide sequences, and protein groups. In general, we recommend starting from the lowest level available. This gives you maximum control over data quality filtering, normalisation and aggregation, and makes each step of the analysis easier to understand and report transparently.
What “lowest level” means depends on the acquisition method. For TMT data acquired by DDA, each MS2 spectrum is matched to a peptide, so analysis can start from the PSM level. In DIA, MS2 spectra are chimeric and identification is peptide-centric, so there are no PSMs and the lowest level is the precursor. Some tools for label-free data also only accept peptide-level input, so starting at the lowest level is not always possible.
The data we will use in this workshop is label-free DIA-LOP, so we will start from the precursor level (rather than the PSM-level TMT data typical of DDA LOPIT). The data was reprocessed using DIA-NN v2.0 (Academia) meaning that the files are no longer the exact ones used by (McCaskie et al. 2025).

title: 2  Import and infrastructure
text:
2.1 The data structure
In this course material we provide a start-to-finish workflow for the analysis of subcellular spatial proteomics data derived from an MS-based correlation profiling experiment. Depending on the experimental goal (e.g., generation of subcellular spatial maps versus discovery of differentially localised proteins) and level of data available (e.g., precursor, PSM, peptide or protein), users may only need to follow part of the workflow. For simplicity, we have divided the workflow into three parts:
We begin with demonstrating how to import quantitative MS data into R using the QFeatures infrastructure. We will then discuss the key data cleaning and quality control steps required to ensure that only high quality data is retained. Finally, the quantitative data will be transformed into correlation profiles which hold the spatial information required for protein localisation prediction, as covered in part II of the workflow.
MS-based quantitative proteomics data is typically represented as a matrix in which the rows represent features (PSMs, precursors, peptides or proteins) and the columns contain information about these features, including their quantification measurements across several samples. As we saw before, this type of quantitative proteomics matrix can be generated by using third party softwares to process raw MS data. Moreover, the software usually outputs a quantitative matrix for each data level (e.g., PSM, precursors, peptide, peptide groups, protein groups). In this lesson we will explain how we can make use of R/Bioconductor packages with dedicated functions and data structures to store and manipulate quantitative proteomics data.
We begin with importing the data at the lowest data-level. In this DIA-LOP experiment this is the precursor level. The raw DIA mass spectrometry data was processed using DIA-NN v2.0 (Academic), which outputs a report file in .parquet format. Unlike a simple abundance matrix, this is a long-format table — each row corresponds to a single precursor–sample combination, rather than one row per precursor across all samples simultaneously. The file contains precursor-level identifications and quantities for every sample, along with quality metrics from the DIA-NN search.

title: 2  Import and infrastructure
text:
2.2 Importing the data into R
We start with loading the packages we will be using in this workflow.

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library("tidyverse")
  library("QFeatures")
  library("MSnbase")
  library("pRoloc")
  library("ggplot2")
  library("Biostrings")
  library("gridExtra")
  library("arrow")
  })

The data we need to get started is stored in parquet file format (when data has been processed with DIA-NN>=2.0), opposed to one main report .tsv output file from earlier versions. We begin by using the arrow package to unpack the parquet files using the read_parquet function.

df <- read_parquet("data/report.parquet")

Let’s have a look at the data to check we’ve imported it correctly. We can inspect the dimensions and column names to understand what the data contains.

We can see many columns, each containing information about a given precursor peptide in a given sample. These include the precursor peptide sequence, the protein(s) and protein group (PG) to which it has been mapped, and various quality control parameters. For a full explanation of the DIA-NN output we direct users to the DIA-NN GitHub page.
The key columns we will use in our analysis are:

Precursor.Id: a unique identifier for each precursor — typically the modified peptide sequence and charge state (e.g. "PEPTM[ox]IDEQ..2")
Protein.Group: the canonical protein group identifier used for aggregation to protein level. Proteins that cannot be distinguished from each other based on proteotypic peptides detected in the data are grouped together under one Protein Group
Protein.Ids: the UniProt accession(s) of the protein(s) to which the precursor is assigned
Genes: the gene symbol(s) associated with the identified proteins
Run: the identifier for the sample run — one value per LC-MS sample injection
Precursor.Quantity: the quantified abundance of the precursor in that run
Q.Value: the precursor-level Q-value, representing the estimated false discovery rate (FDR) at the precursor level; lower values indicate more confident identifications
Lib.Q.Value: the library-level Q-value — the confidence that the precursor was matched to the correct entry in the spectral library
Protein.Q.Value: the protein-level Q-value, representing the estimated FDR at the protein level

Information about the precursor Id and its peptide sequence can be found in the Precursor.Id, Stripped.Sequence and Modified.Sequence columns, as shown below.

title: 2  Import and infrastructure
text:
2.3 The structure of a SummarizedExperiment
To simplify the storage of quantitative proteomics data we can store the data as a SummarizedExperiment object (as shown in Figure 2.1). SummarizedExperiment objects can be conceptualised as data containers made up of three different parts:

The assay - a matrix which contains the quantitative data from a proteomics experiment. Each row represents a feature (a precursor, peptide or protein) and each column contains the quantitative data (measurements) from one experimental sample. Hence, the matrix is in a wide format.
The rowData - a table (data frame) which contains all remaining information associated with each feature (i.e. every column from your search output that was not a quantification column). Rows represent features but columns inform about different attributes of the feature (e.g., its sequence, name, modifications).
The colData - a table (data frame) to store sample metadata that would not appear in the output of your search software. This could be, for example, the condition, replicate, or batch each sample belongs to. Again, this information is stored in a matrix-like data structure.

Finally, there is also an additional container called metadata which is a place for users to store experimental metadata, such as which instrument the samples were run on or the date of data acquisition. We will focus on populating and understanding the three main containers above.








Figure 2.1: Diagramatic representation of the structure of a SummarizedExperiment object in R (modified from the SummarizedExperiment package)





Data stored in these three main areas can be easily accessed using the assay(), rowData() and colData() functions, as we will see later.

title: 2  Import and infrastructure
section: 2.4 The structure of a QFeatures object
text:
2.4 The structure of a QFeatures object
Whilst a SummarizedExperiment is able to neatly store quantitative proteomics data at a single data level (i.e., precursor, peptide or protein), a typical data analysis workflow requires us to look across multiple levels. For example, it is common to start an analysis at a lower data level and then aggregate upward towards a final protein-level dataset. Doing this allows for greater flexibility and understanding of the processes required to clean and aggregate the data.
A QFeatures object is essentially a list of SummarizedExperiment objects. However, the main benefit of using a QFeatures object over storing each data level as an independent SummarizedExperiment or in a normal list object is that the QFeatures infrastructure maintains explicit links between the SummarizedExperiments that it stores. This allows for maximum traceability when processing data across multiple levels — for example, tracking which precursors or peptides contribute to each protein (Figure 2.2, modified from the QFeatures vignette with permission).








Figure 2.2: Graphic representation of the explicit links between data levels when stored in a QFeatures object.











NoteQFeatures nomenclature



When talking about a QFeatures object, each dataset (individual SummarizedExperiment) can be referred to as a set (short for dataset). Previously, each dataset was referred to as an experimental assay, and some older resources may still use this term. However, the experimental assay should not be confused with the quantitative matrix section of a SummarizedExperiment, which is called the assay data.


In order to generate the explicit links between data levels, we need to import the lowest desired data level into a QFeatures object and aggregate upwards within the QFeatures infrastructure using the aggregateFeatures function. If two SummarizedExperiments are generated separately and then added into the same QFeatures object, there will not automatically be links between them. In this case, if links are required, we can manually add them using the addAssayLink() function.
The best way to get our head around the QFeatures infrastructure is to import our data into a QFeatures object and start exploring.

It is important that this column is named runCol, as the readQFeaturesFromDIANN function expects this exact column name when importing the DIA-NN results.






NoteThe pipe operator



In this course we will frequently use the pipe operator (|>). The pipe passes the output of one function directly as the input to the next, allowing you to chain together multiple operations in a linear, readable way — rather than nesting function calls or creating many intermediate variables.

Why we use R pipe (|>) rather than the magrittr pipe (%>%)?
Since version 4.1, R has had its own built-in pipe, |>, so we don’t need to load an extra package to chain steps together. Because it’s part of the language, it runs slightly faster and gives clearer error messages when something goes wrong. It’s also what the tidyverse style guide and R for Data Science now recommend. You’ll still see the older magrittr pipe, %>%, in plenty of existing code and online examples. In everyday use the two behave almost identically, so you can read either one. For more information see Hadley Wickham’s Tidyverse at https://www.tidyverse.org.

title: 2  Import and infrastructure
section: 2.7 Converting the data into a QFeatures object
text:
2.7 Converting the data into a QFeatures object
The readQFeaturesFromDIANN takes DIA-NN output as a data.frame and converts it into a multi-set QFeatures object. We pass the runCol column from our data.frame to be the column that readQFeaturesFromDIANN uses to split the data into sets - we will end up with a QFeatures object with one set per unique value of runCol. This is important because some quality control metrics are calculated on a per-run basis, so we need to keep each run separate in order to use these. We also pass Precursor.Id to the fnames argument to tell readQFeaturesFromDIANN how to name the rows.
We also need to tell QFeatures where the quantitation data is located. As previously mentioned you will notice with DIA-NN output there are multiple qunatitative columns e.g. PG.Quantity, PG.Normalised, Precursor.Quantity etc., and these will vary between DIA-NN versions. Make sure to check the column names for the version you are using. As mentioned before, these columns represent different types of quantitation rather than quantitation across different samples.
Using Precursor.Quantity for quantitation Since our analysis started from the precursor level, we will use precursor-level quantitation and aggregate upwards to protein-level. Whilst DIA-NN provides the Precursor.Normalised column containing quantitative data pre-normalised using the MaxLFQ algorithm, this normalisation step makes the assumption that the majority of the proteome does not change between any two samples (Cox et al. 2014). Since biochemical fractions derived from a correlation profiling experiment are expected to be relatively different from each other in terms of their composition, our data does not meet the assumptions required. Hence, we use the Precursor.Quantity column which contains the raw quantitation data.

Creating the data object

qf <- readQFeaturesFromDIANN(assayData = df, 
                             quantCols = "Precursor.Quantity", 
                             runCol = "runCol", 
                             fnames = "Precursor.Id",
                             colData = sample_metadata)


# check
qf

 ...

You will notice that each run (fraction) appears as a separate set within the QFeatures object and we now have 30 sets (individual SummarizedExperiments). Note, that this differs from when we import labelled correlation profiling data when we would have one set containing all of the fractions together and as such the upstream processing is slightly different. Information on the analysis of label-based or correlation profiling data can be found in (Hutchings et al. 2025).

NoteAlternative input methods



There are several ways to import correlation profiling data into a QFeatures object, and the correct way will depend upon the data structure (long vs. wide) as well as the quantitation (label-free vs. label-based) and acquisition (DDA vs. DIA) method.
For example, TMT-based methods (e.g., LOPIT) allow for sample multiplexing meaning that all biochemical fractions from a correlation profiling experiment can be pooled and analysed in a single MS run. Here, the identification of a peptide sequence across multiple fractions is derived from a single MS2 spectrum. Therefore, there is no per-run or per-fraction quality control metrics, only global statistics that apply to that peptide for all fractions. This data can be imported into a QFeatures object in a single set with one row per feature (PSM, peptide or protein) and one quantitative column per fraction. When multiple replicates or conditions have been used, each experiment (one full correlation gradient) can be imported as a separate set. Hence, if you had three replicate LOPIT-DC experiments, you would import the data as three sets within a QFeatures object.
Details about different import options for DDA datasets is outlined in (Hutchings et al. 2025). For label-free DIA datasets, we recommend using the multi-set import approach demonstrated in this workflow, with one set per run.



Discussion
Why does readQFeaturesFromDIANN create one SummarizedExperiment per run, rather than a single combined set across all runs from the outset?







AnswerAnswer






The DIA-NN output contains per-run quality metrics stored in the rowData of each precursor. These are run-specific values and would be ambiguous or impossible to retain if all runs were immediately merged into a single matrix.
By keeping one SummarizedExperiment per run, we can inspect and filter on these per-run metrics before joining the data. We will join the per-run sets into a single combined precursor set per replicate in the next lesson, once filtering is complete.





2.8.1 How many precursors per sample?
Each run will have a different number of precursors identified and quantified. We can explore this by inspecting the number of rows in each per-run set, which corresponds to the number of precursors quantified in that run (here a biochemical fraction from one replicate).

## Create data.frame of information we need

  n_precursors = n_precursors,

  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +

2.8.2 Exploring the row data

However, we want to access this information across all the MS runs. To do this we can use the rbindRowData function.

rdata <- rbindRowData(qf, i = names(qf))

The rbindRowData functions returns a DFrame table that contains the row binded rowData tables from the selected sets. In this context, i is a character(), integer() or logical() object for subsetting sets. Only rowData variables that are common to all sets are kept.
Recall, there is also a slot in the QFeatures object that stores information on the MS samples/runs. This is the colData slot.

In the below code chunk we create a data.frame called cdata containing the sample information and merge this with the rdata so we get group information for each sample. This will help with our data exploration.

# 1. Create a data.frame of the sample information

cdata <- data.frame(colData(qf))

# 2. Merge this with the row data
# Note: Our data is in separate sets, so the sample names are in the 'assay'
# column. We merge with the column data (using the runCol column) to get group
# information for each sample

rdata <- rdata |>
  data.frame() |>
  merge(cdata, by.x = "assay", by.y = "runCol")

Now we have one data.frame with precursor-level and sample-level information we can now visualise quality metrics from DIA-NN.

TipKey Points




DIA-NN outputs a .parquet format report file containing precursor- and protein-level quantification data for each MS sample/run
The readQFeaturesFromDIANN function imports DIA-NN output into a QFeatures object, creating one SummarizedExperiment per sample run
Sample metadata is stored in the colData of the QFeatures object and can be used to annotate samples with experimental group information
The rowData of each per-run SummarizedExperiment contains quality metrics from DIA-NN that can be used to explore data quality and guide downstream filtering decisions

title: 3  Data processing
text:
3.1 Filtering (Part I): Sample specific quality control
Now that we have our precursor-level data stored in a QFeatures object, the next step is to carry out data cleaning — filtering to retain only high-confidence identifications and removing precursors with excessive missing values across samples.
DIA-NN assigns a Q-value to each precursor and protein group identification, representing the local false discovery rate (FDR) at that score threshold — i.e., the expected proportion of identifications at that level that are incorrect. Filtering by Q-value ensures we retain only high-confidence identifications before proceeding to downstream analysis.
DIA-NN outputs several Q-value columns:
The output from DIA-NN contains information about q-values at different data levels. As discussed in the main workflow, FDR should be controlled at the highest data level to minimise the impact of FDR inflation during data aggregation. Here, the highest data level corresponds to protein groups. Therefore, we set a 1% FDR on PG.Q.Value, as well as the global experiment-wide Q.Value.
Since our data was processed with match-between-runs (MBR) enabled, we additionally filter on the library-level Q-values (Lib.Q.Value and Lib.PG.Q.Value). When MBR is used, DIA-NN rescores identifications across runs using an empirical library built in a first pass; the library-level Q-values reflect the confidence of those cross-run matches and are therefore the most stringent and appropriate filter for MBR data. We apply a standard 1% FDR threshold (Q-value ≤ 0.01) to all four columns.
To remove features based on variables within our rowData we make use of the filterFeatures function. This function takes a QFeatures object as its input and filters it against a condition based on the rowData (indicated by the ~ operator). If the condition evaluates to TRUE for a feature, that feature will be kept; features returning FALSE are removed.
The filterFeatures function provides the option to apply a filter either (i) to the whole QFeatures object and all of its SummarizedExperiments, or (ii) to specific SummarizedExperiments within the QFeatures object, by passing the name or index of the desired set to the i argument.
Since we want to apply the Q-value filter across all per-sample SummarizedExperiments simultaneously, we do not pass an i argument — this causes filterFeatures to apply the filter to every set in the QFeatures object.
# qc
qf <- qf |>
  filterFeatures(~ Q.Value < 0.01) |>        # Run-level precursor Q-value
  filterFeatures(~ PG.Q.Value < 0.01)  |>    # Run-level protein group Q-value
  filterFeatures(~ Lib.Q.Value < 0.01)  |>  # Library-level precursor Q-value
  filterFeatures(~ Lib.PG.Q.Value < 0.01)    # Library level protein group (PG) Q-value

section: 3.2 Joining per-run sets into a single precursor set
text:
3.2 Joining per-run sets into a single precursor set
After filtering, our QFeatures object contains one SummarizedExperiment per sample run. To work with the data combined across all samples, we use the joinAssays function. This merges all per-run sets into a single combined set called "precursors", aligning features (precursors) by their Precursor.Id. Where a precursor was not detected in a particular sample, the corresponding entry will be NA.

# Total number of samples
N <- 30

# Number of replicates
R <- 1:3

# make combined precursor SE
qf <- joinAssays(x = qf, 
                 i = seq(N),
                 name = "precursors",
                 fcol = "Precursor.Id")

Removing redundant sets
When we have many fractions (runs) the QF object can get quite large (over 10GB), quite quickly. Therefore, now that we have obtained a single precursor level dataset, we create a new QF object with only the combined dataset. This isn’t strictly necessary for every dataset, but it may be if you have a very large experiment. It also helps to keep the object tidy and focused on the combined set for downstream analysis.
In the code chunk below we create a new QF object with only the final joined precursor level data.

## Identify which sets to remove
sets_to_rm <- which(names(qf) != "precursors")

title: 3  Data processing
section: 3.3 Filtering (Part II) - Whole dataset quality control
text:
3.3 Filtering (Part II) - Whole dataset quality control

3.3.1 Removing contaminant proteins
In any proteomics experiment, some identified peptides will derive from contaminant proteins rather than the sample of biological interest. Common contaminants include proteins introduced during sample preparation — for example, human keratins from skin or hair, bovine serum albumin from cell culture media, and trypsin used for proteolytic digestion. These proteins are not informative for the biological question and should be removed before downstream analysis.
It is standard practice to include a curated contaminants database alongside the primary sequence database during the database search. For this data, we used a modified version of the contaminants fasta from Hao Group’s Protein Contaminant Libraries for DDA and DIA Proteomics (Frankenfield et al. (2022)), where we removed the contaminants from Fetal Bovine Serum, which are not relevant here. The entries in this contaminant database are named with a Cont_ prefix, which is carried through into the Protein.Ids column of the DIA-NN output, making them straightforward to identify computationally. In addition to this external database, we also selected the “Contaminants” option in the DIA-NN GUI. Therefore, DIA-NN also included its own built-in contaminant database, for which all contaminant protein accessions are preceded with cRAP-, again making these easy to find.
In this section we remove:

Precursor peptides corresponding to contaminant proteins
Precursor peptides which lack a master protein accession
Precursor peptides which are not unique to a single protein within a single protein group

We can inspect the rowData to check the contaminants can be identified as expected.

# Extract the rowData
rd <- rowData(qf[['precursors']]) |>
  data.frame()

# Check for proteins with the prefix "Cont_"
table(grepl('Cont_', rd$Protein.Ids))


 FALSE   TRUE 
192762   2262 


We see that we do have contaminants in the dataset. We will now proceed to filtering them out.
As with all data analyses, it is sensible to keep a copy of the data before applying filters, in case we need to refer back to the unfiltered data later. We therefore extract a copy of the dataset using addAssay, giving it a new name that reflects the processing step we are about to apply. We will only apply filters to this new copy, leaving the original set untouched.






NoteAssay links



QFeatures maintains hierarchical links between quantitative levels, allowing easy access to all data levels for individual features of interest. This is fundamental to the QFeatures infrastructure and will be exemplified throughout this course. When using addAssay to add a copy of an existing set, the newly created SummarizedExperiment does not automatically have a link to the set it was copied from. Where a link is required, it can be added explicitly using addAssayLink.



# Add a copy of the existing data 
qf <- addAssay(qf, 
               qf[["precursors"]], 
               name = "precursors_filtered")
plot(qf)







# Add a link between the original raw and filtered
qf <- addAssayLink(qf, 
                   from = "precursors", 
                   to = "precursors_filtered")
plot(qf)








We now use filterFeatures to retain only precursors whose Protein.Ids field contains no Cont_ entry. We specify the i argument to apply the filter only to the "precursors_filtered" set. This retains the original "precursors" set with all precursors for reference, while the new set contains only those precursors that pass the filtering criteria (i.e., are not contaminants).

qf <- qf |>
  filterFeatures(~ !grepl("Cont_", Protein.Ids),
                     i = "precursors_filtered")

'Protein.Ids' found in 2 out of 2 assay(s).

qf

An instance of class QFeatures (type: bulk) with 2 sets:

 [1] precursors: SummarizedExperiment with 195024 rows and 30 columns 
 [2] precursors_filtered: SummarizedExperiment with 192762 rows and 30 columns 


We could also use the same nomenclature to remove precursors whose Protein.Ids field contains cRAP. For now, we leave these in so that we can demonstrate manual removal below.






NoteWhy filter on Protein.Ids and not Protein.Group?




Protein.Ids lists every protein in the FASTA that a precursor’s peptide could have come from.
Protein.Group is the group DIA-NN assigns after protein inference. A peptide shared between a contaminant and a real protein can be assigned to the real protein’s group, so the contaminant accession never appears in Protein.Group.
Filtering on Protein.Ids catches these shared peptides, which stops contaminant signal leaking into your quantification. It is the more conservative choice. The trade-off is losing a few peptides that genuinely belong to non-contaminant proteins, which is usually acceptable.




Filtering out contaminants manually
If you didn’t include a contaminant database in your search, or your contaminant IDs do not have an easily recognisable pattern, you can still remove contaminants afterwards. The example below shows how. We read in a contaminant FASTA file, then identify and remove any proteins in the data whose accessions match an entry in that file.
First let’s load our contaminants FASTA file

# load contaminant FASTA
cont_fasta <- "data/220813_Universal_Protein_Contaminants_HaoGroup.fasta"
conts <- fasta.index(cont_fasta, seqtype = "AA")

# extract contaminant accessions
cont_acc <- str_extract(conts$desc, "(?<=_).*?(?=\\|)")

In the next code chunk we define a function for identifying any rows (precursor peptides) with a Protein.Ids entry that matches any entry in our contaminant fasta file (i.e., in the cont_acc vector we generated above). At the same time, to cover all cases, we search for any rows with a Protein.Ids containing either the Cont or cRAP pattern. The output of this function will be a logical vector with one entry per row - TRUE means that the row has a Protein.Ids value that matches either the imported fasta file accessions or contains Cont or cRAP.

# define function to find contaminants
find_contaminants <- function(se, contaminants) {
  acc_match <- str_detect(
    rowData(se)$Protein.Ids,
    regex(paste0(contaminants, collapse = "|"))
  )
  default_cont <- str_detect(
    rowData(se)$Protein.Ids,
    regex("Cont|cRAP", ignore_case = TRUE)
  )
  acc_match | default_cont
}

Now we run this function on our dataset to identify any contaminant matches

# create a new object called `cont_tf`
cont_tf <- 
  find_contaminants(se = qf[["precursors_filtered"]], 
                    contaminants = cont_acc)

table(cont_tf)

cont_tf
 FALSE   TRUE 
192232    530 








ExerciseExercise 1 - Challenge: Manual filtering of remaining contaminants






Level: 

Create a column called is_contaminant that can be used with the filterFeatures function.
Use the newly created is_contaminant column in the rowData to remove any precursors which match a protein accession in the manually imported contaminant fasta.







AnswerAnswer






Task 1
The filterFeatures function carries out conditional filtering based on columns within the rowData. So, we add a new column to the rowData called is_contaminant which we can now filter on.

rowData(qf[["precursors_filtered"]])$is_contaminant <- cont_tf

Let’s check our is_contaminant column has been successfully created.

# Check it has been created
qf[["precursors_filtered"]] |> 
  rowData() |> 
  as_tibble() |> 
  pull(is_contaminant) |> 
  table()

Let’s look at some of these proteins.

  as_tibble() |> 
  filter(is_contaminant == TRUE) |>
  dplyr::select(Protein.Ids, Protein.Group)

As expected, these are the contaminant proteins from DIA-NNs built-in database that contain cRAP.
Task 2
Now we can easily apply filterFeatures as we have before.

  filterFeatures(~ !is_contaminant, 
                 i = "precursors_filtered")

 [1] precursors: SummarizedExperiment with 195024 rows and 30 columns 
 [2] precursors_filtered: SummarizedExperiment with 192232 rows and 30 columns 













3.3.2 Removal of peptides with no protein assignment
Since the analysis will be carried out at the protein-level, we will need to aggregate precursor peptides into their corresponding proteins. Precursor entries which lack protein assignment cannot be used and must be removed.
Let’s see if we have any such precursors in the dataset.

qf[["precursors_filtered"]] |>
  rowData() |> 
  as_tibble() |> 
  pull(Protein.Ids) |>
  anyNA()

[1] FALSE


This data does not contain any precursor peptides without a protein assignment, so we don’t have to remove any here.


3.3.3 Removal of shared peptides
As well as removing precursors without a protein assignment, we also wish to remove precursor peptides which are assigned to multiple proteins. Although most precursor peptides have a single accession in the Protein.Ids column, there are some precursors for which this column contains multiple accessions separated by a ;. Since the output does not contain a column to specifically tell us how many proteins a peptide is mapped to, we take advantage of the ; and remove all rows (precursors) with a ; in the Protein.Ids column.
Check precursors present in the data before,

qf

An instance of class QFeatures (type: bulk) with 2 sets:

 [1] precursors: SummarizedExperiment with 195024 rows and 30 columns 
 [2] precursors_filtered: SummarizedExperiment with 192232 rows and 30 columns 


Now filter and check number of precursors after,

qf <- qf |>
  filterFeatures(~ !str_detect(Protein.Ids, ";"),
                 i = "precursors_filtered")

'Protein.Ids' found in 2 out of 2 assay(s).

qf

An instance of class QFeatures (type: bulk) with 2 sets:

 [1] precursors: SummarizedExperiment with 195024 rows and 30 columns 
 [2] precursors_filtered: SummarizedExperiment with 184629 rows and 30 columns 








TipKey Points




DIA-NN Q-value columns (Q.Value, PG.Q.Value, Lib.Q.Value, Lib.PG.Q.Value) represent the local FDR for each identification; filtering at ≤ 0.01 retains only identifications at 1% FDR
When match-between-runs is enabled, library-level Q-values (Lib.Q.Value, Lib.PG.Q.Value) are the most appropriate filter as they reflect the confidence of cross-run matches
filterFeatures applies row-level filters based on rowData variables, and can be applied to the whole QFeatures object or to specific sets
Contaminant proteins (e.g., keratins, trypsin, BSA) should be removed before downstream analysis; including a curated contaminant database in the search and filtering on a Cont_ prefix in Protein.Ids is a straightforward way to do this
joinAssays combines per-sample SummarizedExperiment objects into a single combined set, with missing values (NA) where a precursor was not detected in a given sample

title: 4  Missing data
text:
4.1 Missing values (Part I): fractions
Missing values are a common feature of proteomics data. How many there are can vary substantially depending on the experimental design and the acquisition method used. Before filtering, it’s important to understand how many values are missing and how they are distributed across samples and proteins.
When processing correlation profiling data, handling missing values is a crucial first step to ensure reliable downstream analysis. Missing values can arise for a variety of reasons, including low peptide abundance, stochastic detection, or technical issues. Alternatively, missing values can be biologically meaningful with proteins only distributed over a subset of biochemical fractions. To address this, we first filter column-wise, removing samples (fractions) with an excessive proportion of missing data, which helps avoid bias from poorly quantified replicates. Next, we filter row-wise, removing precursor peptides that are missing in too many samples, ensuring that the remaining dataset contains sufficient information for accurate subcellular localisation and machine learning classification. This two-step approach balances data completeness with retention of informative features.
crumbs: {{< iconify fa6-brands github size=lg title='CRIT GitHub' >}}

title: 4  Missing data
text:
4.1.1 Overall presence of missing values
It is important to assess the frequency and distribution of missing values in any dataset before deciding how to handle them. Recall that the quantitative data and, therefore, missing values are stored in the assay slot of our SummarizedExperiment.
The way that proteomic software encode missing values varies, so it is good practice to check for 0, NA and NaN values within the data. Therefore, we start by examining the DIA-NN output to determine how missing values are represented.

## Does the data contain any zeros?
qf[["precursors_filtered"]] |>
  assay() |>
  longForm() |>
  filter(value == 0) |>
  nrow()

[1] 0


The data does not contain any zeros.
If the data did contain zeros we would need to convert them to NA, because this is how QFeatures expects missing data to be denoted. To do so, we would use the zeroIsNA function.

qf <- zeroIsNA(qf, i = "precursors_filtered")

In this case, since we had no zero values, the code above should have made no changes to our data. Let’s see if we have missing values encoded as either NAs or NaNs.

## Does the data contain NAs?
qf[["precursors_filtered"]] |>
  assay() |>
  longForm() |>
  filter(is.na(value) == TRUE) |>
  nrow()

[1] 2838131


Yes, it does. Let’s explore missingness on (1) column-wise and then later, (2) row-wise levels.


4.1.2 Column-wise filtering of fractions/samples
The first step in handling missing values is to filter samples based on their overall completeness. Column-wise filtering identifies and removes samples/fractions that have an excessive proportion of missing values, which could bias downstream analyses. By excluding poorly quantified samples, we ensure that the dataset retains only those samples with sufficient coverage across peptides. This step improves the reliability of subsequent row-wise filtering, clustering, and machine learning classification, while preserving the overall structure and integrity of the dataset.
Since our missing data is denoted as NA values, we can to use the nNA function to explore from the QFeatures infrastructure.

nNA(qf, i = "precursors_filtered")

This function outputs information about missing values at three levels: (1) the overall dataset ($nNA), (2) per row i.e., per precursor ($nNArows), and (3) per column i.e., per sample/fraction ($nNAcols).
We see that we have 2838131 missing values, which represent 0.51 of the entire dataset. Let’s plot the percentage of missing values per quantitative sample (i.e., per biochemical fraction).
Create a data.frame of missing value information at the sample level.

na_cols <- nNA(qf[["precursors_filtered"]])$nNAcols
df <- cbind(na_cols, colData(qf))

We can plot percentage of NAs across fractions.

df |>
  as_tibble() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Fraction), y = pNA * 100)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 75, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~ Replicate, nrow = 1, labeller = label_both) +
  ylim(0, 100) +
  labs(x = "Fraction", y = "Missing values (%)") +
  theme_bw()








Several fractions show more than 75% missing data. Based on the plots above and the output of nNA, these correspond to fraction 10 in replicate 1, fraction 3 in replicate 2, and fraction 2 in replicate 3. Because the high column-wise missingness occurs in different fractions across replicates, this pattern is more consistent with a mass spectrometry–related issue rather than a biological effect. A missingness level of 75% within a single sample is substantial, and exceeds what can be reliably addressed using current data imputation methods.






NoteConsiderations for fraction removal



This DIA-LOP experiment represents a “static” setup, where the goal is to generate a cell-wide protein map for a single condition. In contrast, in a comparative experiment, we compare subcellular fraction profiles across two or more conditions. In that case, removing fractions requires caution, because the shape of the profiles is what informs localisation and protein movement between organelles. Current methods for detecting changes in localization depend on having the same number of fractions across replicates and conditions. Removing a problematic fraction would therefore require removing the corresponding fraction in all samples. In our case, this is not a concern, because we are building a map for a single condition. All fractions and replicates will be concatenated and carry equal weight before machine learning classification.


In the below code chunk we generate boxplots of the intensities across samples.

qf[, , "precursors_filtered"] |>
  longForm(colvars = c("Replicate", "Fraction")) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Fraction), y = log2(value))) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~ Replicate, nrow = 1, labeller = label_both) +
  labs(x = "Fraction", y = "log2 abundance", title = "Pre-normalisation") +
  theme_bw()








Let’s do a current count of how many precursors, peptides and proteins we have in the data before removing fractions.

## Extract the rowData
rd <- rowData(qf[["precursors_filtered"]])

## Count
nrow(rd)                               # precursors

[1] 184629

length(unique(rd$Stripped.Sequence))   # peptides

[1] 151881

length(unique(rd$Protein.Group))       # proteins

[1] 9743








NoteRecap: Protein.Ids or Protein.Group?



Because we kept only proteotypic precursors (those mapping to a single protein), Protein.Ids and Protein.Group now contain the same accession for every precursor, so either column gives the same count. We use Protein.Group from here on because it is the column DIA-NN uses for protein-level quantification, and the one we will aggregate on later.


Fractions with more than 75% missing values are marked for removal.

(fracs_to_rm <- na_cols$name[na_cols$pNA > 0.75])

[1] "R1F10" "R2F03" "R3F02"


We remove these fractions from precursors_filtered and store the result in se.

se <- qf[["precursors_filtered"]]
se <- se[, !colnames(se) %in% fracs_to_rm]
se

We can now add this back to the qf object.

qf <- addAssay(qf, se, name = "precursors_subset")
qf <- addAssayLink(qf, from = "precursors_filtered", to = "precursors_subset")
qf

title: 4  Missing data
text:
4.2 Intensity-based filtering
Non-specific filtering by summing precursor intensities across rows (per replicate) allows us to identify features that contribute very little to the overall signal. Precursors whose total intensity represents less than 10% of the overall dataset provide limited quantitative information and are more likely to be dominated by noise. Removing these low-contributing precursors reduces technical variability, improves the signal-to-noise ratio, and focuses downstream analyses on features that meaningfully reflect protein abundance and subcellular localisation patterns. This approach helps ensure that clustering, profile visualisation, and machine learning classification are driven by reliable and informative signals.
In the below code we sum the intensity across each precursor profile and then examine the distribution.

## Calculate rowSums across profiles
rs <- qf[["precursors_subset"]]  |> 
    assay() |> 
    rowSums(na.rm = TRUE)  

## Add rowSums to rowData
rowData(qf[["precursors_subset"]])$precursor_sum_intensity <- rs

## Get quantiles
rsq <- quantile(rs, probs = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3))

## Plot
rs |>  
  as_tibble() |>

The summed intensity per precursor across all fractions is approximately normally distributed. We see a threshold of 10–30% of the total signal distribution provides a practical balance between sensitivity and robustness. Precursors contributing below this level typically fall at the lower end of the dynamic range, where measurements are more variable and noise-prone. Removing these features improves signal-to-noise ratio and stabilises downstream analyses. Lower thresholds (e.g. 10%) are more permissive, while higher thresholds (e.g. 30%) favour robustness. Users are encouraged to explore different cut-offs and assess their impact, as the optimal threshold will depend on the specific dataset and analytical objectives.

title: 4  Missing data
text:
4.3 Subsetting data into replicates
If you have replicated data it is necessary to subset the data by replicate (i.e., per complete biochemical gradient) prior to calculating row-wise (precursor peptide) missingness. When all replicates are combined, missing values can be obscured or diluted, making it difficult to detect replicate-specific issues. By examining each replicate separately, we can identify systematic problems affecting individual runs—such as fraction-specific MS performance issues—rather than confounding these with biological variation. This replicate-level assessment ensures that decisions about filtering or removal are based on technical data quality within each run, rather than aggregated summaries across the entire dataset.
Information on the replicate structure has already been added to the QFeatures object during data import and is found in the colData slot under Replicate.

qf[["precursors_subset"]] |> 
  colData()

DataFrame with 27 rows and 3 columns
      Replicate  Fraction      runCol
      <integer> <integer> <character>
R1F01         1         1       R1F01
R1F02         1         2       R1F02
R1F03         1         3       R1F03
R1F04         1         4       R1F04
R1F05         1         5       R1F05
...         ...       ...         ...
R3F06         3         6       R3F06
R3F07         3         7       R3F07
R3F08         3         8       R3F08
R3F09         3         9       R3F09
R3F10         3        10       R3F10


We can extract this information and use it to split our data by replicate.

## get replicate data
rep_info <- colData(qf[["precursors_subset"]])$Replicate


## Recall we have 3 replicates
R <- 1:3 

## Create an empty list of length (number replicates, R)
se <- vector("list", length(R))

## Create names for the replicate SEs in QF
rep_id <- paste0("precursors_R", R)

## Subset data into replicates
for (i in R) {
  se[[i]] <- qf[["precursors_subset"]][, rep_info == i]
  qf <- addAssay(qf, y = se[[i]], name = rep_id[i])
  qf <- addAssayLink(qf, from = "precursors_subset", to = rep_id[i])
}

## Separate and add back to QF object

title: 4  Missing data
text:
4.4 Missing values (Part II): precursors
Once column-wise missingness has been assessed, we apply row-wise filtering to remove peptides absent in a high proportion of fractions. Frequently missing peptides provide limited information for subcellular localisation and may introduce noise into clustering and machine learning analyses. However, filtering must be applied carefully, as overly stringent thresholds can remove genuine biological signal, particularly for proteins that are strongly enriched in a single compartment and therefore naturally sparse across the fractionation profile.
This is especially relevant for label-free experimental designs. Although DIA generally provides more consistent measurements across runs, low-abundance or highly compartment-specific proteins may fluctuate around the detection threshold. As a result, biologically meaningful, singly localised proteins can appear partially missing rather than truly absent. Strict row-wise filtering may therefore bias the dataset towards highly abundant or broadly distributed proteins.
The appropriate missing value threshold depends on the specific dataset. Users are encouraged to explore different levels of allowable missingness and assess their impact on downstream analyses. Ultimately, the number of missing values permitted per replicate should be considered relative to the total number of fractions in the experiment. Let’s do some exploration.






ExerciseExercise 1 - Challenge: Exploring the effects of missing value thresholds






Level: 
For replicate 1, create a plot to visualise the number of unique precursors, peptides and proteins that would remain in the data if we allowed a maximum of 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9 missing values.


Hint

Use columns in the QFeatures rowData to count unique precursors, Stripped.Sequence, and Protein.Group, like we did above.







AnswerAnswer






One (of many different) answers. We first extract the data we need.

## Extract missing data per row
na_rows <- nNA(qf, i = "precursors_R1")$nNArows |>
  as_tibble()

## Extract rowData
rd <- rowData(qf[["precursors_R1"]]) |>
  as_tibble()

## Merge
cbind(rd, na_rows)

## Define thresholds to test
thresholds <- seq(0, 9, 1)

## Count precursors, peptides and proteins with each threshold
counts <- tibble()
for (t in thresholds) {
  
  keep <- na_rows$nNA <= t
  
  counts_t <- tibble(Threshold = t, 
                     Precursors = sum(keep),
                     Peptides = n_distinct(rd$Modified.Sequence[keep]),
                     Proteins = n_distinct(rd$Protein.Group[keep]))
  
  counts <- rbind(counts, counts_t)
}

Now we can generate the plot.

## Plot
counts |>
  pivot_longer(-Threshold, names_to = "level", values_to = "n") |>
  mutate(level = factor(level, levels = c("Precursors", "Peptides", "Proteins"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Threshold, y = n, fill = level)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), vjust = -0.3, size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~level, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 9, 1)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
















In this specific example, we choose to allow up to 7 out of 9 missing values (i.e., require presence in at least two fractions) to retain sharply enriched profiles. To remove rows, here precursors, that do not meet our missing value threshold, we apply the filterNA function within the QFeatures infrastructure and pass the maximum number of missing values that we consider acceptable to the pNA argument. We apply this to each of our indiviudal replicates.

## Remove precursors with > x% MVs
qf <- filterNA(qf,
               pNA = 7/9,
               i = rep_id)
qf

In the below code chunk we calculate the current number of proteins per replicate.

## Calculate number of proteins per replicate
sapply(rep_id, function(z) {
  qf[[z]]  |> 
  rowData() |>
  as_tibble() |>
    pull(Protein.Group) |>
    n_distinct()})

precursors_R1 precursors_R2 precursors_R3 
         9185          8995          8955 


We can use nNA() to look at the overall amount of missing data in each replicate.

na_reps <- nNA(qf, i = rep_id)$nNA
as.data.frame(na_reps)

          assay    nNA       pNA
1 precursors_R1 376979 0.2912328
2 precursors_R2 490460 0.3819184
3 precursors_R3 441926 0.3590495


Recall, the nNA column gives the number of missing values in each set, and pNA gives this as a proportion of all values in the set.
Replicate 1 is the most complete, with 29% of values missing, compared with 38% for replicate 2 and 36% for replicate 3. Replicates 1 and 2 contain a similar number of precursors, so the higher missingness in replicate 2 suggests lower detection across its fractions, rather than simply fewer precursors. Overall, the level of missing data is moderate and broadly similar across the three replicates, and no single replicate stands out as a concern.
Missingness is also lower here than in the per-fraction values we saw earlier. This is expected, because we have now split the data by replicate and removed the fractions with the most missing values.
Not all of these missing values reflect a failure to detect a precursor. Proteins are distributed unevenly across fractions, so a precursor may be genuinely low or absent in some of them. These values are therefore largely missing not at random, which is important to bear in mind when we decide how to handle missing data later on.






NoteAn additional note on label-based vs. label-free missing values



Our previous workflow ((Hutchings and Breckels 2025)) focused on a use-case with DDA TMT-based peptide quantitation. When using a DDA TMT approach, TMT co-isolation interference often results in very low abundance values where there should really be a missing value. As a result, despite the potential for MNAR values due to biochemical fractionation, TMT correlation profiling based experiments tend to have a low proportion of missing data. This means that the datasets require minimal filtering and imputation. By contrast, label-free datasets have a much high proportion of missingness. This is the case for several reasons. Firstly, label-free samples are each run independently on the MS rather than being multiplexed as is done for label-based methods. For DDA label-free experiments this means that different peptides are measured across different samples, thus leading to lots of missing values. This effect is seen in all DDA label-free proteomics experiments but is even more dramatic for correlation profiling data as most approaches rely on selecting the top N most abundant precursor peptides for analysis, but the most abundance peptides are expected to be different across fractions of the biochemical gradient. In DIA label-free correlation profiling experiments, as we show in this course, missingness is not due to the stochastic selection of precursors ions but rather due to the fact that missing values present as truly missing, with no co-isolation interference to buffer the effect of biochemical fractionation. As a result of greater missingness, users should spend more time testing combinations of filtering and imputation for label-free correlation profiling experiment data.

title: 4  Missing data
text:
4.5 Imputation
As we have seen, the data still contain missing (NA) values. This is expected, because our row-wise filtering only removed precursors quantified in fewer than two of the nine fractions per replicate (i.e. more than seven missing values). How many missing values remain, and how they are distributed across the gradient, depends on the experimental design and the acquisition method. For example, label-free (LFQ) methods typically produce more missing values than label-based approaches such as TMT. Among label-free methods, DDA datasets usually contain more missing values than DIA datasets.
Imputation was discussed in our previous workflow (Hutchings et al. 2023). Rather than recommending a single approach, we encourage users to decide for themselves whether, and how, to deal with missing values in their own data. A key question is whether values are missing for biological or technical reasons.
In several label-based datasets we found very few missing values, and those that did occur tended to be at the ends of the gradient. This suggests they are missing for biological reasons: the protein is genuinely low or absent in those fractions. Removing these precursors would therefore risk losing biologically meaningful information. Similarly, in label-free DIA-LOP data we found that much of the missingness was shared between matching fractions across replicates, again pointing to biological rather than technical causes.
Missing values can be imputed with the impute() function in QFeatures. Several imputation methods are available, and they can be combined into a mixed strategy, for example using one method for values thought to be missing for biological reasons and another for values missing at random.

## Which methods are available for imputation within the impute() function?
MsCoreUtils::imputeMethods()

 [1] "bpca"    "knn"     "QRILC"   "MLE"     "MLE2"    "MinDet"  "MinProb"

4.5.1 Recording missing values before imputation
Once we impute, we can no longer tell which values were measured and which were filled in. Before imputing, we therefore record the number of missing values for each precursor in a new rowData column called nNA. This column is carried over to the imputed and normalised sets, and we will summarise it to the protein level after aggregation.

The table shows how many precursors have 0, 1, 2, … missing values across the fractions of the first replicate.


4.5.2 Mixed imputation
In this next section of the course we show how to implement a mixed imputation approach using the impute() function in QFeatures. Mixed imputation is useful when the data contain a mixture of values missing at random (MAR) and missing not at random (MNAR). Deciding which missing values belong to each category is extremely challenging. As an example, it seems reasonable to assume that proteins with narrow abundance distributions across the gradient will have more missing values per precursor, because they are genuinely absent from many fractions. This is the case for mitochondrial proteins in this dataset. These are biologically meaningful MNAR values. By contrast, values missing for technical reasons (MAR) should be spread evenly across the dataset and occur at low frequency for any given precursor. We therefore treat precursors with two or fewer missing values as MAR, and those with more than two as MNAR. This strategy is for demonstration only, and users should test different approaches on their own data.
We first create a logical vector with one value per precursor, indicating whether its missing values should be treated as MAR (TRUE) or MNAR (FALSE). We add this, along with the number of missing values per precursor, to the rowData of each replicate.

for (i in rep_id) {
  ## Define MAR if <= 2 missing values, otherwise MNAR
  tf <- rowData(qf[[i]])$nNA <= 2
  
  ## Append this information to the dataset
  rowData(qf[[i]])$randna <- tf
}

NoteDo I have to impute?



Not always. Robust summarisation during aggregation (e.g. MsCoreUtils::robustSummary in aggregateFeatures()) can estimate protein-level values from incomplete precursor data. In practice, however, it does not always cope with highly sparse data or proteins with many precursors. Many classifiers used for spatial proteomics, such as those in pRoloc, also require a complete data matrix. The alternative, removing incomplete profiles, risks losing the sparse, sharply enriched profiles of singly localised proteins.








TipKey Points




Missing values are common in proteomics data. Always check how they are encoded (zeros or NA) and assess how many there are, and where, before filtering or imputing.
Column-wise filtering removes fractions with excessive missingness (here > 75%). If high missingness occurs in different fractions across replicates, a technical rather than biological cause is likely.
In comparative/dynamic experiments, removing a fraction means removing the same fraction from every replicate and condition, so that profiles stay comparable.
Intensity-based filtering removes precursors at the low end of the dynamic range, where measurements are noisier. The threshold is a trade-off between sensitivity and robustness and should be explored for each dataset.
Row-wise missingness should be assessed per replicate (complete gradient), so that replicate-specific problems are not hidden by combining the data.
Row-wise thresholds must be set relative to the number of fractions. Overly strict filtering removes sharply enriched, singly localised proteins and biases the data towards abundant, broadly distributed proteins.
In subcellular proteomics, many missing values are biological (MNAR): the protein is genuinely low or absent in some fractions. These should not be treated in the same way as technical, random (MAR) missingness.
Mixed imputation with impute(method = "mixed") applies different methods to MAR and MNAR values. How values are assigned to each category is a modelling choice and should be tested on your own data.

title: 5  Data transformation and aggregation
text:
5.1 Normalisation
In our previous expression proteomics workflow we described the processing steps required to prepare quantitative proteomics data for differential abundance analysis (Hutchings et al. 2023). Such preparation involved log2 transformation of the peptide-level quantitation data before aggregating to the protein level and normalising. These steps differ from those required when processing subcellular spatial proteomics data.
Quantitative proteomics data often undergoes logarithmic transformation prior to statistical analysis. The reason for this is that the majority of statistical tests require the data to display a normal distribution. Whilst raw quantitative MS-based proteomics data is dramatically skewed towards 0, the log2 transformed data is approximately normal. In this subcellular spatial proteomics workflow, however, the goal is not to prepare our data for downstream statistical differential abundance analysis. Instead, we are preparing the data for a machine learning classifier for which the input is protein correlation profiles across a biochemical gradient. The machine learning algorithm which we will use does not make the assumption that our data has a normal distribution, therefore we do not need to perform logarithmic transformation. In fact, logarithmic transformation would reduce the subcellular resolution by flattening our abundance distribution profiles.
The second data processing step which differs between expression and spatial proteomics analysis is that of normalisation. In most proteomics experiments the goal of normalisation is to remove any technological variation and account for experimental error. As a result, normalised data should contain near-identical samples in which the majority of variation is of biological importance. In spatial proteomics normalisation plays a different role because we are interested in the shape of protein abundance profiles rather than the magnitude of the intensity in each channel. Hence, the aim of normalisation here is to scale all of our quantitation data into the same space (within the range of 0 and 1) whilst maintaining the shape of our abundance profiles. If we did not do this, proteins with the same distribution across the gradient but different abundances would display very different profiles.
Based on De Duve’s principle (Duve 1964) we know that proteins which are co-localised within the cell will exhibit similar abundance distribution profiles across a fractionation gradient. This means that we we can infer the location of proteins by matching their abundance profiles to profiles of well-known organelle residents, termed “markers”. In order to get information about the abundance distribution of each protein across the fractionation gradient we need to carry out row sum normalisation. To do this we make use of the normalize function within the QFeatures infrastructure.
# Define number of replicates
R <- 1:3
## Define names for indexing imputed datasets
imp_names <- paste0("imp_precursors_R", R)

## Define new names for normalised datasets
norm_names <- paste0("norm_precursors_R", R)

qf <- normalize(qf, 
                i = imp_names,
                name = norm_names,
                method = "sum")

qf

Through the process of row sum normalisation we have now converted our raw quantitative values into a correlation profile or protein profile across the fractionation gradient. The abundance values represent the proportion of total quantification for each precursor that comes from each fraction, with each row sum being equal to 1. This scales all data into the same space so that we can use the shape rather than the intensity of profiles for downstream machine learning.
plot(qf)
Let’s take a look at what normalisation has done to the data, starting with replicate 1.
## Evaluate the effect of data normalisation on rep1

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

## Plot pre-normalised data
qf[["imp_precursors_R1"]] |>
  assay() |>
  longForm() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = colname, y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "", y = "Raw abundance", title = "Pre-normalisation") +
  theme_bw()







## Plot post-normalised data
qf[["norm_precursors_R1"]] |>
  assay() |>
  longForm() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = colname, y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "", y = "Normalised abundance", title = "Post-normalisation") +
  theme_bw()
We can see from these plots that the raw precursor abundance values are spread across a wide dynamic range, spanning 7 orders of magnitude. This is very normal for cellular proteomics data. If we were to use the pre-normalised data, the profile of a high abundance protein would be numerically very different to that of a low abundance protein, even if they fractionate in the same pattern across our biochemical gradient. Once we normalise our precursors, all have an abundance between 0 and 1. We can now see some shape to the profiles.
Unlike in total proteome experiments where normalisation aims to remove variation, we do not expect the boxplots of normalised correlation profiles to be perfectly aligned. For each fraction, many proteins have low to 0 abundance. These are proteins that belong to organelles that primarily sediment elsewhere in the gradient. However, each fraction also has a long tail towards 1, indicating a subset of proteins that did predominantly pellet in this fraction. A box plot with shape and structure like this is a first indication that our experiment may have worked - we would not want a flat profile of boxplots.

title: 5  Data transformation and aggregation
text:
NoteAt what stage should I normalise to generate profiles?




Before or after imputation? (Depends on extent of data missingness)
Some experimental designs yield a relatively low proportion of missing values, for example label-based methods that use TMT such as LOPIT. As a result, after an initial filtering step, there are very few values to impute. Applying a baseline k-NN imputation to such data can be more successful when the data are in a similar space after normalisation, as discussed in Hutchings et al. (2025). We note that by applying imputation after normalisation, the final imputed profiles will no longer sum to exactly 1. However, since such designs have such low missingness, the sum should not greatly exceed 1. By contrast, where datasets have a greater proportion of missing data to impute, as is the case for this example where we have a DIA LFQ design row sum normalisation of a limited number of fractions would generate a short profile summed to one and subsequent imputation could result in a correlation profile with an undesirably high sum value. Here it is necessary to impute prior to normalisation to ensure the generation of sensible correlation profiles in the same final space (between 0 and 1).


Before or after aggregation? (In practice, it makes little difference)
In this workflow we normalise each precursor profile to sum to 1 before aggregating to protein level. Precursors from the same protein can differ in raw intensity by orders of magnitude, mainly because they ionise differently, not because of the biology. If we aggregated raw intensities, a single very intense precursor could largely determine the protein’s profile.
For localisation, what matters is the shape of the profile across fractions, and each precursor is an independent measurement of that shape. Normalising first puts all precursors on the same scale, so each contributes equally to the protein profile. Aggregating with a median then gives a consensus profile that is robust to the occasional precursor with an unusual profile.
The trade-off is that low-intensity, noisier precursors are given the same weight as high-intensity ones. Our earlier intensity-based filtering helps by removing the weakest precursors. Because the median of profiles that each sum to 1 does not itself sum exactly to 1, we normalise once more after aggregation.
In practice, we find the order makes little difference to the resolution of the final spatial map. Either approach is reasonable, as long as the final protein profiles are normalised before downstream analysis.
