title: 5  Data transformation and aggregation
text:
5.2 Aggregation
Now that we have our final precursor-level dataset we can aggregate this upward to the protein level. The aim of this step is to combine data from all component precursors into a single protein-level entry. This entry will have one master protein accession and one quantitative value per biochemical fraction per sample.
Within the QFeatures infrastructure aggregation is carried out using the aggregateFeatures function. This function provides users with several options on how to aggregate multiple quantitation values into a single value. The methods differ with respect to how they deal with missing data as well as whether they require log2 or raw quantitation data as their input.
In our sister workflow Hutchings et al. (2023) we aggregate using robustSummary, a state-of-the-art aggregation method which is notably robust to outliers and missing values (Sticker et al. 2020; Goeminne et al. 2016). However, our data is not currently suitable for robustSummary aggregation as this method requires log2 transformed data. Whilst it would be relatively simple to log2 transform our quantitative data using the logTransform function within the QFeatures infrastructure, we would need to reverse this transformation by taking the exponential of the resulting protein data, which is not so simple. Instead we will aggregate precursors straight to protein level using colMedians method from the matrixStats package. We specify this method using the fun = argument, as well as telling the function which rowData column we wish to use for aggregation.
Here, we demonstrate one-step aggregation, from precursors directly to protein. This means aggregating all precursors with the same value of "Protein.Group". For an example of two-step aggregation, from precursor to peptide followed by peptide to protein, users are directed to Hutchings et al. (2023).

agg_names <- paste0("proteins_R", R)

qf <- QFeatures::aggregateFeatures(qf,
                                   i = norm_names,
                                   fcol = "Protein.Group", 
                                   name = agg_names,
                                   fun = matrixStats::colMedians)


  |                                                                            
  |                                                                      |   0%
  |                                                                            
  |=======================                                               |  33%
  |                                                                            
  |===============================================                       |  67%
  |                                                                            
  |======================================================================| 100%

## Verify
qf

An instance of class QFeatures (type: bulk) with 15 sets:

 [1] precursors: SummarizedExperiment with 195024 rows and 30 columns 
 [2] precursors_filtered: SummarizedExperiment with 184629 rows and 30 columns 
 [3] precursors_subset: SummarizedExperiment with 166166 rows and 27 columns 
 ...

 [14] proteins_R2: SummarizedExperiment with 8995 rows and 9 columns 
 [15] proteins_R3: SummarizedExperiment with 8955 rows and 9 columns 


We have now populated the QFeatures object with protein-level data containing the row normalised protein correlation profiles. From looking at the summary in experiments(qf) we have around 9000 proteins in each replicate experiment. These protein correlation profiles contain spatial information and are the input to downstream machine learning classifers.

plot(qf)














ExerciseExercise 1 - Challenge: Using the .n column from aggregateFeatures






Level: 

Look at the ??aggregateFeatures help documentation. What is the .n column? What does the column mean for our data specifically?
Plot a histogram to explore the .n column in replicate 1 of our aggregated protein-level data.







AnswerAnswer






Task 1
One advantage of using the aggregateFeatures function is that it automatically adds a column to the aggregated data to indicate how many lower-level features (here precursors) were aggregated into each higher-level feature (here protein groups). This column is called .n. Of note, this column is created every time you use the aggregateFeatures function, and always has the same name. Hence, if you did a two-step aggregation from precursors to peptides to proteins, the .n column in the peptide-level data would indicate how many precursors per peptide and in the protein-level data would be how many peptides per protein.
Task 2
Let’s plot a histogram of the precursor support per protein group in our dataset. Again, we demonstrate with replicate 1 but advise users to plot for all replicates of all conditions.

qf[["proteins_R1"]] |>
  rowData() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = `.n`)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  labs(x = "Precursor support", y = "Number of proteins") +
  theme_bw()

`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.









This initial histogram shows us that most proteins have < 100 precursors supporting them, which is not surprising. It’s hard to see how low with the current binning. Let’s create bins for 1-20 and then merge all others into a > 20 category.

qf[["proteins_R1"]] |>
  rowData() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(n_binned = factor(
    if_else(.n > 20, ">20", as.character(.n)),
    levels = c(as.character(1:20), ">20"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n_binned)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Precursor support", y = "Number of proteins") +
  theme_bw()

















5.2.1 Re-normalisation
Before aggregation, each precursor profile summed to 1. However, the median of several profiles that each sum to 1 does not itself sum exactly to 1. Let’s check the row sums of our protein-level data.

qf[["proteins_R1"]] |>
  assay() |>
  rowSums() |>
  summary()

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
 0.3724  0.9302  0.9665  0.9533  0.9990  1.1904 


The row sums are close to 1, but not exactly 1. To make sure every protein profile is on exactly the same scale before machine learning, we apply row-sum normalisation once more, this time at the protein level.

prot_norm_names <- paste0("proteins_norm_R", R)

qf <- normalize(qf,
                i = agg_names,
                name = prot_norm_names,
                method = "sum")

qf

Every protein profile should now sum to exactly 1.

qf[["proteins_norm_R1"]] |>
  assay() |>
  rowSums() |>

title: 5  Data transformation and aggregation
text:
5.3 Concatenating datasets for machine learning
Previous subcellular proteomics experiments utilising protein correlation profiles have benefited from the combining of datasets (Barylyuk et al. 2020; Christoforou et al. 2016; Moloney et al. 2023), that is the concatenation of replicates or experiments that utilise different gradients (Trotter et al. 2010). Since the use-case experiment included three biological replicates each with 9 biochemical fractions we can concatenate these data into a single dataset with 27 columns. In order to do this, the column names must be different in each replicate. By looking at the colnames of each experimental set per condition we verify we indeed have unique names.

colnames(qf[["proteins_R1"]])

[1] "R1F01" "R1F02" "R1F03" "R1F04" "R1F05" "R1F06" "R1F07" "R1F08" "R1F09"

colnames(qf[["proteins_R2"]])

[1] "R2F01" "R2F02" "R2F04" "R2F05" "R2F06" "R2F07" "R2F08" "R2F09" "R2F10"

colnames(qf[["proteins_R3"]])

[1] "R3F01" "R3F03" "R3F04" "R3F05" "R3F06" "R3F07" "R3F08" "R3F09" "R3F10"


If the colnames were not unique to each replicate we would have to use the renameColname function, specifying which experimental set we wish to change the column names of (i = argument) and then providing a vector of new column names (value = argument).
We can use joinAssays to concatenate the fractions across replicates to improve the discrimination between organelle signatures.

agg_names <- c("proteins_norm_R1", 
               "proteins_norm_R2", 
               "proteins_norm_R3")

qf <- joinAssays(qf, 
                 i = agg_names, 
                 name = "proteins_joined")
## Verify
qf

An instance of class QFeatures (type: bulk) with 19 sets:

 [1] precursors: SummarizedExperiment with 195024 rows and 30 columns 
 [2] precursors_filtered: SummarizedExperiment with 184629 rows and 30 columns 
 [3] precursors_subset: SummarizedExperiment with 166166 rows and 27 columns 
 ...
 [17] proteins_norm_R2: SummarizedExperiment with 8995 rows and 9 columns 
 [18] proteins_norm_R3: SummarizedExperiment with 8955 rows and 9 columns 
 [19] proteins_joined: SummarizedExperiment with 9326 rows and 27 columns 


Finally, we filter to only keep proteins that are found in all replicates. This is necessary because the machine learning algorithms in pRoloc do not accept missingness.

qf <- filterNA(qf, i = "proteins_joined")

## Verify
qf

An instance of class QFeatures (type: bulk) with 19 sets:

 [1] precursors: SummarizedExperiment with 195024 rows and 30 columns 
 [2] precursors_filtered: SummarizedExperiment with 184629 rows and 30 columns

 ...

 [19] proteins_joined: SummarizedExperiment with 8736 rows and 27 columns 


We see our final protein level data contain 8736 proteins.

plot(qf)









5.3.1 Concatenation gives equal weight to all replicates
By concatenating the datasets we give each biological replicate an equal weight for the downstream machine learning classification. This means that any variability between experiments will be accounted for. For example, if a protein has an abundance distribution profile similar to that of nuclear protein markers in one of the three replicates, but is more similar to cytoplasmic markers in the remaining two replicates, this will be reflected by the fact that the protein will either be classified with a lower confidence or not classified at all. If each replicate was analysed separately, the protein may receive conflicting classifications in each replicate which would require a user-defined resolution.
Another potential advantage of concatenating datasets is the inclusion of data derived from different gradient variations (Barylyuk et al. 2020; Trotter et al. 2010). Although many subcellular compartments are well resolved using a single gradient, some compartments remain more challenging to resolve due to their similarities or connections with other compartments. For example, compartments within the endomembrane system can generate similar fractionation profiles. Where no single gradient will provide optimal separation of all organelles of interest, it is possible to design different gradients which provide optimal separation different organelles. These data can then be concatenated to generated a combined dataset with greater final resolution of all desired compartments.
Overall, data concatenation has been shown to have benefits for downstream machine learning in many cases. Ultimately, however, the decision to concatenate replicates will depend on the goal of the experiment and type of data analysis required to answer the experimental question. In particular, where the experimental aim is to identify differential localisation between conditions it is recommended to repeat the same biochemical gradient across all three replicates to avoid complicating downstream analysis.


5.3.2 Keeping track of peptide support and missing values
Before we move on, we record two pieces of information about the quality of each protein profile, so that we can use them later when interpreting our spatial maps:

Peptide support: the number of precursors used to calculate each protein profile. Proteins quantified from only one or two precursors tend to have noisier profiles. aggregateFeatures recorded this in a rowData column called .n.
Missing values: how much of each profile was imputed. In the previous lesson we recorded the number of missing values per precursor, before imputation, in a rowData column called nNA. Proteins whose precursors had many missing values rely more heavily on imputation and should be interpreted with more caution.

Neither of these makes it through to the joined set. aggregateFeatures does not carry nNA up to the protein level, and joinAssays only keeps rowData columns that are identical in every set, which .n is not.

## .n is in the protein-level set of each replicate...
rowData(qf[["proteins_R1"]])$.n |>
  summary()

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   1.00    5.00   10.00   15.66   20.00  474.00 

## ...but not in the joined set
".n" %in% colnames(rowData(qf[["proteins_joined"]]))

[1] FALSE


We have written a small function, addProfileQC(), that summarises these to the protein level for each replicate and adds them to the joined set. For each protein it calculates the proportion of its precursor values that were missing before imputation, and then adds the following columns to the joined set:

n_rep1, n_rep2, n_rep3: number of precursors in each replicate
n_min, n_mean: minimum and mean across replicates
missing_rep1, missing_rep2, missing_rep3: proportion of values missing before imputation in each replicate
missing_max, missing_mean: maximum and mean across replicates

We report the minimum peptide support and maximum missingness because a protein profile is only as good as its weakest replicate.


Show the addProfileQC() function
## addProfileQC()
##
## Records two indicators of protein profile quality in a QFeatures object
## and carries them through to the joined (concatenated) set:
##
##   - peptide support: the `.n` column added by aggregateFeatures()
##   - missingness: the proportion of precursor values that were missing
##     before imputation, calculated from the per-precursor `nNA` column
##
## Both are lost by joinAssays(), because they differ between replicates.
##
## Arguments
##   qf          a QFeatures object
##   prec_sets   named character vector of precursor-level sets that carry `nNA`
##   prot_sets   named character vector of protein-level sets that carry `.n`
##               (same names and order as prec_sets, e.g. rep1, rep2, rep3)
##   joined_set  name of the joined protein-level set
##   group_col   rowData column linking precursors to proteins
##
## Adds to each protein-level set:
##   prop_missing
## Adds to the joined set:
##   n_<rep>, n_min, n_mean, missing_<rep>, missing_max, missing_mean
##
## Returns the updated QFeatures object.

addProfileQC <- function(qf,
                         prec_sets,
                         prot_sets,
                         joined_set = "proteins_joined",
                         group_col = "Protein.Group") {

  stopifnot(identical(names(prec_sets), names(prot_sets)))
  reps <- names(prot_sets)
  joined_ids <- rownames(qf[[joined_set]])

  for (r in reps) {
    prec <- prec_sets[[r]]
    prot <- prot_sets[[r]]
    rd <- rowData(qf[[prec]])

    ## Proportion of missing values per protein:
    ## total missing values / (number of precursors x number of fractions)
    tot_na <- tapply(rd$nNA, rd[[group_col]], sum)
    tot_values <- tapply(rd$nNA, rd[[group_col]], length) * ncol(qf[[prec]])
    prop <- tot_na / tot_values

    ## Add to the protein-level set of this replicate
    rowData(qf[[prot]])$prop_missing <-
      as.numeric(prop[rownames(qf[[prot]])])
  }

  ## Extract a rowData column from each replicate, matched to the joined set
  per_rep <- function(col, prefix) {
    m <- sapply(prot_sets, function(s) {
      rd <- rowData(qf[[s]])
      rd[[col]][match(joined_ids, rownames(rd))]
    })
    m <- matrix(m, ncol = length(prot_sets))
    colnames(m) <- paste0(prefix, reps)
    m
  }

  n_mat <- per_rep(".n", "n_")
  miss_mat <- per_rep("prop_missing", "missing_")

  ## Per-replicate values plus summaries across replicates
  qc_df <- DataFrame(n_mat,
                     n_min = apply(n_mat, 1, min),
                     n_mean = rowMeans(n_mat),
                     miss_mat,
                     missing_max = apply(miss_mat, 1, max),
                     missing_mean = rowMeans(miss_mat))

  rowData(qf[[joined_set]]) <- cbind(rowData(qf[[joined_set]]), qc_df)

  qf
}



qf <- addProfileQC(qf,
                   prec_sets = c(rep1 = "norm_precursors_R1",
                                 rep2 = "norm_precursors_R2",
                                 rep3 = "norm_precursors_R3"),
                   prot_sets = c(rep1 = "proteins_R1",
                                 rep2 = "proteins_R2",
                                 rep3 = "proteins_R3"),
                   joined_set = "proteins_joined")

## Verify
rowData(qf[["proteins_joined"]]) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  dplyr::select(starts_with("n_"), starts_with("missing_")) |>
  head()

TipKey Points




Spatial proteomics data are prepared for machine learning on profile shape, not for statistical tests, so log transformation is not needed and would flatten the profiles.
Row-sum normalisation turns raw intensities into profiles that sum to 1. This puts all features on the same scale while preserving the shape of their distribution across the gradient.
For sparse label-free data, impute before normalising, so that profiles are complete before they are scaled.
Aggregation combines precursors into one profile per protein group. The aggregation method must match the data: robustSummary needs log-transformed input, whereas colMedians can be used on normalised profiles directly.
Whether you normalise before or after aggregation makes little practical difference, as long as the final protein profiles are normalised.
aggregateFeatures() and joinAssays() only keep rowData columns that are the same for every feature being combined, so per-replicate quality information, such as the number of precursors (.n) and the proportion of missing values, must be summarised and added back to the joined set.
Concatenating replicates with joinAssays() gives each replicate equal weight in classification, so inconsistent proteins are classified with lower confidence rather than given conflicting labels.
Concatenation can also combine different gradients to improve resolution. For differential localisation between conditions, however, the same gradient should be used across all replicates.

title: 6  Assessment of resolution
text:
6.1 Generating a subcellular spatial map
Now that we have generated our final dataset containing protein correlation profiles, we can use this data to generate spatial maps. Specifically, in part 2 of this course we will discuss how to determine the steady-state localisation of proteins utilising classical or Bayesian supervised machine learning algorithms. To do so we will focus on the concatenated U-2 OS DIA-LOP dataset and show how to generate a static spatial map from this data. We will also look at each replicate individually, to check that they show the same structure before we rely on the combined data.
All protein correlation profiling methods, including LOP, PCP, DOMs and others, are based on the fractionation patterns of different organelles across a biochemical gradient. Patterns of proteins which co-fractionate together are indicative of proteins which co-localise together within the cell (De Duve and Beaufay 1981). The computational analysis of such methodologies requires us to (1) identify distinct patterns of protein co-fractionation, and (2) associate each identified fractionation pattern with marker proteins known to reside in a particular subcellular compartment. Hence, we predict protein localisation by comparing the correlation profiles of query proteins to those of marker proteins with a known subcellular localisation.
We will first discuss the definition of marker proteins, that is proteins which are known to consistently localise to a subcellular niche in a given cell type and under given conditions. The correlation profiles of the selected marker proteins will then be used to train a supervised machine learning classifier. The output of this algorithm will be a predicted subcellular localisation for each of our proteins. Finally, we show how to visualise the predicted protein localisations to generate a spatial map of the cell.

title: 6  Assessment of resolution
text:
6.2 Conversion to MSnSet
This section of the workflow requires specialised functions for data visualisation and machine learning. Such functions exist within the pRoloc package (Gatto et al. 2014). In order to use the functions within pRoloc we need our data to be stored in an MSnSet rather than a QFeatures object. Although there is currently no function available to directly convert a QFeatures object into an MSnSetList, we can use the as function to coerce each experimental set (or SummarizedExperiment) of our QFeatures object into an MSnSet.

## Coerce each experimental set of interest into an MSnSet
msn <- as(object = qf[["proteins_joined"]], Class = "MSnSet")

## Verify
msn

MSnSet (storageMode: lockedEnvironment)
assayData: 8736 features, 27 samples 
  element names: exprs 
protocolData: none

  sampleNames: R1F01 R1F02 ... R3F10 (27 total)
  varLabels: Replicate Fraction runCol
  varMetadata: labelDescription
featureData
  featureNames: A0A096LP01 A0A0B4J2F0 ... Q9Y6Y8 (8736 total)
  fvarLabels: Channel Decoy ... missing_mean (23 total)
  fvarMetadata: labelDescription
experimentData: use 'experimentData(object)'
Annotation:  
- - - Processing information - - -
 MSnbase version: 2.39.5 


As a reminder for readers, the structure of an MSnSet object is very similar to that of a SummarizedExperiment, or QFeatures experimental set. The relationship between these QFeatures and MSnSet functions is summarised below.



Equivalent accessors/slot names between MSnbase and QFeatures


Description
MSnbase function

Extract quantitative data

rowDataNames

The columns we added to the rowData of the joined set at the end of part 1 are carried over into the fData of our MSnSet. These are the number of precursors per protein in each replicate (n_rep1, n_rep2, n_rep3) with their minimum and mean (n_min, n_mean), and the proportion of missing values per protein in each replicate (missing_rep1, missing_rep2, missing_rep3) with their maximum and mean (missing_max, missing_mean).

## Columns carried over from the QFeatures object
fData(msn) |>
  names()

 [1] "Channel"            "Decoy"              "Proteotypic"       
 [4] "Protein.Ids"        "Protein.Group"      "Protein.Names"     
 [7] "Genes"              "PG.TopN"            "Genes.TopN"        
[10] "Translated.Q.Value" "Channel.Q.Value"    "Lib.PG.Q.Value"    
[13] "is_contaminant"     "n_rep1"             "n_rep2"            
[16] "n_rep3"             "n_min"              "n_mean"            
[19] "missing_rep1"       "missing_rep2"       "missing_rep3"      
[22] "missing_max"        "missing_mean"      



Peptide-level subcellular spatial mapping
The majority of correlation profiling experiments aim to generate one or more protein-level cell maps. Therefore, previous data analysis workflows, including our first F1000 workflow for spatial proteomics (Breckels et al. 2018), started with the protein-level data output from a database search. However, it is also possible to generate cell maps at the peptide or even PSM/precursor level. In particular, peptide-level spatial maps have the potential to provide information about the differential localisation of proteoforms by revealing cases where peptides corresponding to the same master protein accession behave differently. For instance, the modified and unmodified versions of peptide sequences can be mapped separately rather than being aggregating into a single protein-level entry. Further, peptide-level maps can be used for quality control to investigate how consistent the profiles and predicted localisations of peptides are for proteins with limited peptide support.
One of the advantages of processing the data from the lowest possible level (PSM/precursor-level) within the QFeatures infrastructure is the ability to store and access all of these data levels in a single object. In part 1 of this workflow we aggregated our PSM data directly to protein by using the aggregateFeatures function to group precursors based on their protein accession. To get peptide-level information, we could have included an additional intermediate aggregation step, as demonstrated in Hutchings et al. (2023). Here, we would first aggregate all precursors into peptides by passing either Sequence (ignore modifications) or Modified.Sequence (include modifications) to the fcol argument in aggregateFeatures, and then all peptides into proteins by passing Protein.Group. The peptide-level data could then be extracted into an MSnSet in the same way as demonstrated above. All functions used throughout the rest of the workflow could be equally applied to an MSnSet containing peptide-level data, although some functions may require longer to run given that the peptide-level data is larger than the corresponding protein-level dataset.
To generate peptide-level spatial maps using this workflow:

Aggregate from PSMs/precursors to peptides within the QFeatures infrastructure
Extract peptide-level experimental set from QFeatures into an MSnSet
Continue to use the rest of the workflow in the same way as demonstrated for protein-level data

An example workflow for peptide-level mapping is provided in the Appendix, which is available from Zenodo under the identifier doi:10.5281/zenodo.15100485.

title: 6  Assessment of resolution
text:
6.3 Initial assessment of data resolution
Prior to the annotation of marker proteins, it is first necessary to assess the resolution of the data. The aim of this assessment is to verify that subcellular niches have been successfully separated along the biochemical fractionation gradient and that there are distinct patterns of co-fractionation present in the data.

6.3.1 Visualisation using dimensionality reduction
One way in which the initial assessment of resolution can be made is by using dimensionality reduction methods to summarise and visualise the dataset. Rather than looking directly at protein correlation profiles, here comprised of 27 dimensions (the fractions of all three replicates), we simplify the data and visualise it in a two dimensional space. In this case, proteins which are localised to the same subcellular niche should have similar correlation profiles and cluster together within a two dimensional space. For a more in-depth discussion regarding the interpretation of dimensionality reduction plots for correlation profiling data users are directed to Gatto et al. (2019).
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and t-distributed Stochastic Neighbour Embedding (t-SNE) are two dimensionality reduction methods which are commonly used for the visualisation of spatial proteomics data. The plot2D and plot3D functions within pRoloc can be used to generate and visualise PCA and t-SNE data, along with other approaches to dimensionality reduction (all methods are listed in plot2Dmethods). We pass our msn object to plot2D and specify "PCA" or "t-SNE" as our method. We also specify fcol = NULL to ignore any feature data and prevent the colouring of features (proteins) based on any annotation. Finally, when using any method which requires random number generation, we include a set.seed function to ensure reproducibility. Without setting a seed we would get a different t-SNE plot each time the code is executed.

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

## Visualise unlabelled data using PCA and t-SNE
msn  |> 
  plot2D(fcol = NULL, col = "black", method = "PCA", main = "PCA")

set.seed(399)
msn |>
  plot2D(fcol = NULL, col = "black", method = "t-SNE", main = "t-SNE")

Loading required namespace: Rtsne









By visualising the data without any annotation we can see evidence for the presence of clusters within our dataset. This is our first indication that the experiment has been successful and that different subcellular compartments have been separated along the fractionation gradient. At this point users are looking for the data to have shape and structure. If dimensionality reduction results in a mass of features in the middle of the plot with minimal shape or clusters, this indicates that (1) data pre-processing was not performed correctly e.g., a log2 transformation was applied, or (2) the experiment itself lacks resolution, potentially due to over-lysis of cells resulting in loss of subcellular structures prior to biochemical fractionation.






NoteAn additional note on dimensionality reduction



Dimensionality reduction methods are excellent visualisation tools for subcellular proteomics data. However, users should be careful when interpreting such figures since they only represent a simplified snapshot of the data. PCA, for example, uses a linear data transformation which means that distance can be directly interpreted (proteins closer together have more similar fractionation profiles). However, only two or three principal components can be visualised in a given plot meaning that clusters resolved in alternative principal components (i.e., dimensions) cannot be seen. The t-SNE and Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for Dimension Reduction (UMAP) methods, on the other hand, require non-linear transformation of the data which prevents interpretation of distance and can result in clustering artefacts (Wattenberg et al. 2016) but tends to show more of the overall variation. Only visualisation of the protein correlation profiles themselves can provide a true picture of the data.




6.3.2 Do the replicates agree?
Before relying on the combined data, it is worth checking that each replicate shows the same overall structure. We coerce the normalised protein-level set of each replicate, before joining, into its own MSnSet and plot each one.

## Normalised protein-level sets for each replicate, before joining
rep_sets <- c(rep1 = "proteins_norm_R1",
              rep2 = "proteins_norm_R2",
              rep3 = "proteins_norm_R3")

## One MSnSet per replicate
msn_reps <- lapply(rep_sets, function(s) as(qf[[s]], "MSnSet"))


par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
for (r in names(msn_reps)) {
  plot2D(msn_reps[[r]], fcol = NULL, col = "black",
         main = paste("PCA:", r))
}








Each replicate has its own PCA, so the plots may be rotated or mirrored relative to each other. What matters is that the same clusters and overall shape appear in each replicate. If one replicate showed much less structure, this could indicate a problem with that fractionation and would be worth investigating before combining the data.
In this course we classify proteins using the combined data rather than each replicate separately. As discussed in the aggregation lesson, combining the replicates increases resolution, since each protein is described by its profiles in all three replicates, and avoids having to reconcile three separate sets of predictions, for example by a majority vote. It also reduces the influence of any one replicate on the result.


6.3.3 Visualisation using heatmaps
In addition to dimensionality reduction, heatmaps are also a popular tool for visualising patterns and relationships in large datasets. To gain a snapshot of proteins behaviour across different fractions and replicates we can use the pheatmap function from the pheatmap package to generate a clustered heatmap of the normalised protein correlation profiles. The input to pheatmap is the matrix of correlation profiles stored in the exprs slot of the MSnSet. By default a hierarchical clustering is performed on the correlation profiles and the heatmap is ordered according to this clustering.
Since we wish to visualise the correlation profile of each protein in an intuitive order (that is the order of the biochemical fractionation gradient), we tell pheatmap not to cluster based on columns (quantitative channels) by setting cluster_cols to FALSE. This will retain the column order we have in our MSnSet rather than clustering similar columns together. In order to get some idea of which proteins (rows of the MSnSet) exhibit similar normalised abundance distributions and, therefore, could reside in the same subcellular compartment, we set cluster_rows to TRUE. This means that proteins (rows) with similar correlation profiles will be grouped together.

## Plot heatmap of protein correlation profiles - row clustering only
pheatmap(mat = exprs(msn),
        cluster_rows = TRUE,
        cluster_cols = FALSE,
        show_rownames = FALSE)











We can quickly see patterns of similarity emerging for proteins across fractions, and also across replicates, indicated by coloured blocks. The colours reflect the normalised relative abundance for each protein in each fraction and replicate; blue indicating a low recorded normalised abundance and yellow, orange and red indicating a high normalised abundance value for a given protein. Protein (row) names are omitted for clarity. Blocks with different colours across columns are indicative of structured correlation profiles. A block of proteins that all peak in the same fractions, with a pattern not shared by other blocks, gives us confidence that these profiles will be resolved from others in the dataset and that this set of proteins could represent a subcellular niche. Depending on the experimental design we expect to see a similar trend between replicates in where proteins peak in abundance across the same fractions.

title: 6  Assessment of resolution
text:
6.4 Unsupervised learning

6.4.1 Hierarchical clustering with hclust
Although visualisation tools can help us see structure and indicate that some subcellular compartments have been resolved, the plots we have looked at so far cannot tell us which compartments are resolved. Unsupervised learning via clustering analysis can be used to gain insight into which subcellular niches we have the ability to resolve in our data. At a basic level, clustering methods simply seek to find structure in an unlabelled dataset via grouping data points whose members are similar in some way. This step is particularly useful for those studying the spatial proteome of non-model organisms or aiming to discover new subcellular structures. Several unsupervised machine learning algorithms such as hierarchical clustering and k-means, are available in pRoloc via the MLInterfaces package, as outlined in the vignette Using pRoloc for spatial proteomics data analysis.
In the section above we carried out hierarchical clustering and visualisation using the pheatmap function. This allowed us to cluster rows and see groups of rows (proteins) with similar abundance profiles (correlation profiles). We can take this a step further by annotating the discovered clusters on our data using dimensionality reduction.
First, we regenerate the same heatmap as above with some additional annotations to make the individual clusters easier to see. Here, we choose to do the hierarchical clustering separately from the plotting so that we have all of the data we need in an accessible object. The same hierarchical clustering carried out within the pheatmap function can also be completed using the hclust function from the stats package. We first pass the quantitative exprs data of our msn to the dist function to generate a distance matrix, and then pass this distance matrix to hclust. We will store the results in an object called hc. Next, we use the cutree function to specify how many clusters we wish to split the data into. The most appropriate number will vary depending on the data size and resolution, so users should test a few options. Here, we demonstrate using 12 clusters since most high-quality correlation profiling experiments resolve 10-15 subcellular compartments.

## Carry out hierarchical clustering with hclust
hc <- msn |>
  exprs() |>
  dist() |>
  hclust()

## Specify number of clusters (k) and extract proteins in each cluster
k <- 12
cl <- cutree(hc, k)

Now that we have a named vector containing all of our proteins with an associated hierarchical cluster number, we can regenerate our heatmap and annotate this information. To do so, we generate a data.frame with a column called Cluster containing the cluster number and make sure that the rownames match the featureNames of our msn object. We also define our own colours to match the default colours used by plot2D such that our clusters have the same colour annotations in our heatmap and dimensionality reduction visualisation. Finally, we use the pheatmap function as above but pass our row annotation data.frame to annotation_row and our pre-defined colours to annotation_colors.

## Create a dataframe containing cluster annotations
cl_annot <- data.frame("Cluster" = factor(cl))

## Define colours (to be same as PCA below = default plot2D)
my_cols <- list("Cluster" = getStockcol()[1:k] |> set_names(1:k))

## Plot heatmap with rows annotated by cluster number
pheatmap(mat = exprs(msn), 
         cluster_rows = TRUE,
         cluster_cols = FALSE,
         show_rownames = FALSE,
         cutree_rows = k, 
         annotation_row = cl_annot,
         annotation_colors = my_cols)








To plot these hierarchical clusters on a dimensionality reduction map, we first add the cluster information to the fData of our MSnSet. We can then use the plot2D function to generate PCA plots with the discovered clusters annotated. As above, we pass our msn object and specify the dimensionality reduction method to use. We also tell the function which column of our fData to be used for colouring the points - here we use the newly created hc column.

## Add hierarchical cluster information to MSnSet fData
fData(msn)$hc <- cl

## Visualise hierarchical clusters on PCA
msn |>
  plot2D(fcol = "hc", method = "PCA", main = "Hierarchical clustering results on PCA")

## Add legend
msn |>
  addLegend(fcol = "hc", cex = 0.7)










6.4.2 Hierarchical clustering with HDBSCAN
Hierarchical DBSCAN (HDBSCAN) is another form of clustering which can be executed in R using the dbscan package (Hahsler et al. 2019). This algorithm has been used to successfully uncover and validate clusters in subcellular spatial proteomics data generated from Toxoplasma gondii (Barylyuk et al. 2020) and African trypanosomes (Moloney et al. 2023). Extensive documentation on the use of HDBSCAN and related algorithms can be found at https://hdbscan.readthedocs.io/en/latest/basic_hdbscan.html. The main benefit of the hdbscan function is its simplicity. Users are only required to optimise a single parameter; the minimum number of points to comprise a cluster, termed minPts. The optimal value for this parameter will depend upon the structure and resolution of the data, so some initial exploration is required. Given that a subcellular compartment will need to comprise at least 10-15 marker proteins for use in machine learning (discussed later in this workflow), we recommend testing values between 10 and 20 for minPts, as demonstrated below.

## Test a cluster size between 10 and 20 proteins per cluster
min_N <- c(10:20)
cluster_N <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = length(min_N))

## Run HDBSCAN -- this takes a few minutes to run
for (i in seq_along(min_N)) {
  result <- msn |>
    exprs() |>
    hdbscan(minPts = min_N[i])
  cluster_N[i] <- max(result$cluster)
}

## Structure results into a data.frame
hdb_opt <- data.frame(min_N, cluster_N)

## Plot minimum cluster size against resulting number of clusters
hdb_opt |>
  ggplot(aes(x = min_N, y = cluster_N)) + 
  geom_col() + 
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Min proteins per cluster", 
       y = "Number of clusters")

For this data the unsupervised algorithm has identified only a small number of clusters within our correlation profiling data. Whilst it may be worth exploring the results of clustering with various minPts, we will here demonstrate how to look at the results derived from a minPts value of 10. We first run the HDBSCAN algorithm with our selected minPts and append these results to the fData of our msn object to look at the results.

## Run HDBSCAN using optimal minimum cluster size - here 10
hdb_results <- msn |>
  exprs() |>
  hdbscan(minPts = 10)

## Add the results of HDBSCAN to our MSnSet
fData(msn)$hdb_cluster_id <- hdb_results$cluster
fData(msn)$hdb_cluster_prob <- hdb_results$membership_prob

## Check how many proteins are in each cluster 
msn |>
  fData() |>
  pull(hdb_cluster_id) |>
  table()


   0    1    2    3    4    5    6 
4409   53   18 2895  592   60  709 


As we can see, hdbscan has allocated the proteins to 1 of the 6 clusters it has found in the data. This information is found in hdb_results$cluster and we have added it to our MSnSet and it is can be accessed via fData(msn)$hdb_cluster_id. If we check the column names of the fData we can verify the results have been stored in the MSnSet.

## Check columns in fData
msn |> 
  fvarLabels()  # does the same as names() for fData

 [1] "Channel"            "Decoy"              "Proteotypic"       
 [4] "Protein.Ids"        "Protein.Group"      "Protein.Names"     
 [7] "Genes"              "PG.TopN"            "Genes.TopN"        
[10] "Translated.Q.Value" "Channel.Q.Value"    "Lib.PG.Q.Value"    
[13] "is_contaminant"     "n_rep1"             "n_rep2"            
[16] "n_rep3"             "n_min"              "n_mean"            
[19] "missing_rep1"       "missing_rep2"       "missing_rep3"      
[22] "missing_max"        "missing_mean"       "hc"                
[25] "hdb_cluster_id"     "hdb_cluster_prob"  


Notice that some proteins are allocated to cluster “0”. The “0” category denotes proteins which did not fit into any of the discovered clusters.
We can use the plot2D function to generate PCA and t-SNE plots with the discovered clusters annotated. As before, we pass our msn object and specify the dimensionality reduction method we wish to use. We also tell the function which column of our fData to be used for colouring the points - here we use the newly created hdb_cluster_id column. Finally, we pass the argument unknown = "0" so that the large cluster of uncertain proteins remains unlabelled.

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

## Visualise HDBSCAN unsupervised clustering using PCA
msn |>
  plot2D(fcol = "hdb_cluster_id", method = "PCA", unknown = "0",
         main = "HDBSCAN results on PCA")

## Visualise HDBSCAN unsupervised clustering using t-SNE
set.seed(399)
msn |>
  plot2D(fcol = "hdb_cluster_id", method = "t-SNE", unknown = "0",
         main = "HDBSCAN results on t-SNE")

## Add legend
msn |> 
  addLegend(fcol = "hdb_cluster_id", unknown = "0", cex = .7)










6.4.3 Validation of clusters
Visualisation confirms that the clustering looks real and sensible. Therefore, we will use gene ontology (GO) enrichment analyses to determine which subcellular niches each of the discovered clusters represent. Many packages exist to facilitate GO enrichment analysis in R, including topGO (Alexa 2022), GOfuncR (Grote 2022), and clusterProfiler (Wu et al. 2021). Here we will use enrichGO function in the clusterProfiler package. The aim of this gene ontology enrichment analysis is to determine whether the proteins assigned to a given cluster are enriched for any cellular component (CC) GO terms. That is, we ask whether the proteins in a cluster are annotated with a CC GO term more than expected by chance based on the entire dataset.
To use the enrichGO function we will pass a vector containing the protein accessions of interest, here those within a given HDBSCAN cluster. We also need to provide a background, or ‘universe’, which is a vector containing the accessions of all proteins within our spatial map. Other arguments include the keyType to tell the function that we are using UniProt accessions, OrgDb to pass a database object for the species of interest (here org.Hs.eg.db for human samples), and ont to indicate that we wish to consider only GO categories annotated as cellular component (CC). For users studying other model organisms, the org.Hs.eg.db object can be swapped out for a database corresponding to the species of interest e.g., org.Mm.eg.db for mouse. Users mapping the spatial proteome of a non-model organism may need to manually assess the proteins comprising each cluster to determine their identities.
Below we demonstrate how to carry out GO enrichment on cluster number 6.

## Extract protein accessions in the cluster
protein_id <- msn |>
  fData() |>
  filter(hdb_cluster_id == 6) |>
  pull(Protein.Group)

## Extract all protein accessions in the data
background_proteins <- msn |>
  fData() |>
  pull(Protein.Group)

## Carry out GO enrichment searching for CC terms
cluster_6_go <- enrichGO(gene = protein_id,
                         universe = background_proteins,
                         OrgDb = org.Hs.eg.db,
                         keyType = "UNIPROT",
                         ont = "CC",
                         pAdjustMethod = "BH",
                         readable = TRUE,
                         pvalueCutoff = 0.01,
                         qvalueCutoff = 0.01)


## View the first few enriched terms
cluster_6_go |> 
  slot("result") |> 
  pull(Description) |> 
  head()

[1] "mitochondrial inner membrane"            
[2] "mitochondrial matrix"                    
[3] "organelle inner membrane"                
[4] "mitochondrial protein-containing complex"
[5] "respiratory chain complex"               
[6] "organellar ribosome"                     


We can plot the results using the barplot function. We pass the argument showCategory = 10 to tell enrichGO to only plot the first 10 enriched terms. Other plotting functions are available in the enrichGO package. We refer users to the online book for the package which can be found at https://yulab-smu.top/biomedical-knowledge-mining-book/.

## Plot results
barplot(cluster_6_go, showCategory = 10) +
  ggtitle("Enriched terms in Cluster 6")








The results of GO enrichment indicate that cluster 6 represents proteins associated with the mitochondrion. This provides an additional unbiased level of evidence that the mitochondrion is sufficiently resolved in our dataset to be included as a compartment in the downstream analyses.
To simplify the investigation of all discovered clusters, the code below can be used to generate a list of the enriched CC GO terms for each cluster.

## Extract the number of clusters we have found
n <- hdb_results[["cluster"]] |>
  max()
  
## Define protein background
background_proteins <- msn |>
  fData() |>
  pull(Protein.Group)


## Initialise a container for the GO output
go_result <- vector("list", n)

## For loop over each cluster number carrying out GO enrichment
for (i in 1:n) {
  ## Step (1) - extract protein IDs in the cluster
  protein_id <- msn |>
    fData() |>
    filter(hdb_cluster_id == i) |>
    pull(Protein.Group)
  
  ## Step (2) - run enrichGO
  go_result[[i]] <- enrichGO(gene = protein_id,
                             universe = background_proteins,
                             OrgDb = org.Hs.eg.db,
                             keyType = "UNIPROT",
                             ont = "CC",
                             pAdjustMethod = "BH",
                             readable = TRUE,
                             pvalueCutoff = 0.01,
                             qvalueCutoff = 0.01)
}

To get an overview of the enrichment results, we plot a selection of significantly enriched GO cellular component terms for each cluster. All terms passed a p-value and q-value threshold of 0.01, and we show five terms from each cluster’s list. Each row is a GO term and each column a cluster. A dot means that term is significantly enriched in that cluster. A term can appear in more than one cluster, so the plot shows both what each cluster is enriched for and where clusters overlap.

## Combine GO outputs into data frames
go_result <- lapply(go_result, as.data.frame)

## Combine all results into one table, with a Cluster column
plot_df <- bind_rows(go_result, .id = "Cluster") |>
  mutate(Cluster = paste("Cluster", Cluster)) |>
  arrange(Cluster, p.adjust) |>
  mutate(Description = factor(Description, levels = rev(unique(Description))))

## Filter for top 5 terms per cluster
top_terms <- plot_df |>
  group_by(Cluster) |>
  slice_min(p.adjust, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  pull(Description) |>
  unique()

## Plot
plot_df |>
  filter(Description %in% top_terms) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Cluster, y = Description)) +
  geom_point(size = 5, colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Enriched GO cellular component terms per cluster",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_bw() 








The plot shows that most clusters correspond to a recognisable subcellular compartment:

Clusters 1 and 2 are enriched for chromatin and chromosome terms, such as heterochromatin, kinetochore and condensed chromosome, so they likely represent chromatin-associated nuclear proteins. They share many terms, which suggests the clustering has split one broad nuclear or chromatin compartment into two. These clusters may reflect real biological differences, or they may be technical: the clustering may have resolved two sub-populations of proteins that we would consider part of the same niche.
Cluster 3 is enriched for terms related to RNA processing and the ribosome: the spliceosome, preribosome and cytosolic ribosome. It also shares some chromosome terms with clusters 1 and 2. This cluster is likely a mixture of nuclear and cytosolic ribonucleoprotein complexes, which often co-fractionate in correlation profiling experiments.
Cluster 4 is enriched for endoplasmic reticulum, cell surface and extracellular matrix terms. Proteins of the secretory pathway and the plasma membrane often have similar fractionation profiles, so they can be hard to separate.
Cluster 5 is enriched for lysosome and Golgi terms. It shares terms such as primary lysosome and azurophil granule with cluster 4.
Cluster 6 is clearly mitochondrial, with terms such as mitochondrial inner membrane, mitochondrial matrix and respiratory chain complex.

When interpreting this plot, keep in mind that GO terms are hierarchical. Many enriched terms are closely related (for example, “condensed chromosome” and “condensed chromosome, centromeric region”), so a cluster can have many significant terms that all describe the same compartment. Showing a few terms per cluster makes the main pattern easier to see. These terms are a selection rather than the most significant ones, so the full list of enriched terms should be checked before drawing conclusions.
Overall, GO enrichment gives us confidence that the unsupervised clusters reflect real subcellular structure in the data. It also helps us decide which compartments are well resolved, and therefore which subcellular classes to include when defining markers. A cluster that maps cleanly to a single compartment, such as cluster 6, is a good candidate for marker selection. Clusters that are mixed or share many terms, such as clusters 1–3 and 4–5, may need to be combined into broader classes or examined more closely before markers are assigned.






TipKey Points




Functions in pRoloc require data in an MSnSet. Protein-level sets in a QFeatures object can be coerced with as(..., "MSnSet"), where assay, rowData and colData become exprs, fData and pData.
Before defining markers, check that the data has resolution: distinct patterns of co-fractionation that separate subcellular niches.
PCA, t-SNE and heatmaps of unlabelled data give a quick first look. Clear shape and clusters indicate good resolution, whereas a single central mass of proteins suggests a processing error (e.g. log transformation) or a failed fractionation.
Plotting each replicate separately checks that they show the same structure before relying on the combined data.
Dimensionality reduction is a simplified view of the data. PCA shows only a few components, and distances in t-SNE and UMAP cannot be interpreted directly. Always set a seed for methods that use random numbers.
Unsupervised clustering with hclust or hdbscan finds groups of proteins with similar profiles without using any prior annotation. Parameters such as the number of clusters (k) or minPts should be explored, not fixed.
GO cellular component enrichment against a background of all proteins in the data links clusters to subcellular compartments. Clusters that map cleanly to one compartment indicate a well-resolved niche. Mixed or overlapping clusters indicate compartments that may need to be combined or examined more closely before markers are defined.

title: 7  Data annotation
text:
7.1 Defining markers for machine learning
In the context of spatial proteomics data analysis, a marker is a protein known to reside in a single subcellular niche within a given system and under given conditions. In other words, markers are proteins which we can confidently assign to a known single localisation based on prior knowledge. In the context of protein localisation prediction, marker proteins constitute the labelled training data provided to the classification algorithm. Defining marker proteins can be challenging and time consuming, but it is critical to obtain a list of markers which are representative of the experiment and dataset of interest.
It is worth stressing at the outset that there is no single correct marker list. Marker curation is not a mechanical step with a fixed answer, but a series of informed decisions that depend on the biology of the system and the structure of the data. Which compartments are resolved, which proteins reliably represent them, and how much variation to tolerate within a compartment will all differ between organisms, cell types, experimental conditions and fractionation methods. A marker list that works well for one dataset may be a poor fit for another, even from the same organism. Two analysts working on the same data may also reasonably arrive at slightly different marker lists, and both may be valid, provided each decision is grounded in prior knowledge and supported by the data.
The definition of subcellular markers can be broadly divided into five steps, with steps 3, 4 and 5 representing an iterative process, as outlined below.
A graphical representation of the process of marker curation. Markers are proteins which are known to localise to a single subcellular compartment in the given cell type and condition of interest. The selection of confident markers is critical for successful prediction of protein localisation and differential localisation. (!) After using curated markers for protein localisation classification, users might still need to do some final curation e.g., if localisation prediction results do not look sensible (over- or under-classification of a particular organelle). However, users should be cautious when repeatedly refining markers lists as to ensure that the final markers remain representative of the literature and data structure.
Having visualised the data to validate the presence of clusters and explored which subcellular organelles may be resolved in the dataset, we can now start with an initial marker list. For model organisms, pre-existing marker lists can often be derived from published subcellular proteomics datasets. For simplicity, the pRoloc package stores a number of curated marker sets as well as published marker sets, as discussed below. However, for non-model organisms with limited pre-existing subcellular proteomics data it may be necessary to manually curate an initial marker list. In such cases we would advise users to apply unsupervised clustering to their data in order to guide marker discovery.

title: 7  Data annotation
text:
7.2 Marker lists from pRolocmarkers
The pRoloc package contains marker protein lists for a number of organisms, including curated organism reference sets and published marker lists. To see which marker sets are available we can use the pRolocmarkers function. Type ?pRolocmarkers for more details.

## View available marker sets within pRoloc
pRolocmarkers()

 Ids: TriTrypDB gene identifier, 891 markers


We can see a number of lists, each labelled with species, ID type (UniProt protein accessions, species-specific gene IDs etc.) and the number of markers. The name of the marker set is indicated inside of square brackets. Reference marker sets for model organisms are named after their species: atha for the Arabidopsis thaliana reference set, dmel for Drosophila melanogaster, hsap for Homo sapiens, mmus for Mus musculus, and ggal for Gallus gallus. Marker sets extracted directly from publications are named using the nomenclature species_author e.g., hsap_christopher for the marker list used in Christopher et al. (2025).
To use one of the marker lists stored in pRolocmarkers, users should first extract the marker list into a named character vector by using the pRolocmarkers function and passing the name of the desired marker list.

## Example extract markers from pRolocmarkers
human_mrk <- pRolocmarkers("hsap")

These markers can then be used to annotate the data via the addMarkers function, as demonstrated below.

title: 7  Data annotation
text:
7.3 Adding user-defined marker lists
It is possible to import and apply a user-defined marker list. The markers should be imported as either (i) a named vector where subcellular marker annotations are entries and feature accessions are the corresponding names, or (ii) from a .csv file with two columns, one for the subcellular marker annotation and another for the corresponding feature name. Of note, the feature names used in the marker list must be of the same format as those in the featureNames of the MSnSet to be annotated. In the use-case the format is UniProt protein accessions but featureNames could also be gene names or organisms-specific identifiers.
We show how to load from a .csv file in the below code chunk and add annotation to the proteins in the data based on the marker list we have provided. A new column will be added to the data, which we will call “markers_initial”. This is done by passing the argument mcol = "markers_initial". For users who have extracted markers from pRolocmarkers, the code below should be edited to pass the extracted named character object (e.g., human_mrk generated above) to the markers argument.

## Add markers to the MSnSet
msn <- addMarkers(object = msn,
                  markers = "data/dialop_markers.csv",
                  mcol = "markers_initial") # Name for newly created fData col

Markers in data: 1725 out of 8736

Upon successfully annotating the markers, a table is printed to the screen summarising the number of markers that have been added to the data. We see a new column has been added to the fData of our MSnSet to annotate these proteins in our dataset, called “markers_initial”.

## Print the column names of the fData
msn |>
  fvarLabels()

If you wish to remove the markers from your data you can assign NULL to the output i.e., one would type fData(msn)[, "markers_initial"] <- NULL to remove the marker list. See the help documentation of addMarkers by typing ?addMarkers for more details.






NoteAn additional note on minimum number of markers per compartment



Determining the optimal number of markers to include in the training data can be challenging. The inclusion of more training data (markers) is usually thought to increase the generalisability of a model, although this is only true if these markers represent the full diversity of data and do not lead to model over-fitting. While there are no fixed rules on the minimum number of training examples needed to learn a classifier, we suggest (1) having a sufficient number of markers per class to run cross-validation e.g. 10-15 for a 5-fold cross validation, (2) more markers than quantitation features e.g. for correlation profiling experiment with 10 abundance channels, > 10. Some classifiers also require the number of examples per class to be balanced. Unfortunately, the number of proteins known to reside in a subcellular niche can vary greatly, and some niches simply have too few proteins to add more markers. For example, the peroxisome is a relatively small organelle with few available marker proteins. This means that for experiments with many fractions and multiple replicates it may not be possible to have the number of peroxisomal markers exceed the number of quantitative channels. Nevertheless, users should be aware of these general guidelines and try to meet them where possible.

title: 7  Data annotation
text:
7.4 Evaluating markers
After annotating the markers we again use dimensionality reduction within the plot2D function as a visualisation tool. This time we pass fcol = "markers_initial" to colour our proteins based on the markers_initial column within our fData. As outlined above, we expect markers to cluster together on these 2D plots.

par(mfrow = c(2, 1))

plot2D(msn, method = "PCA", fcol = "markers_initial",
       main = "Initial marker resolution PCA")
addLegend(msn, where = "bottomright", fcol = "markers_initial", cex = .7)

set.seed(399)

plot2D(msn, method = "t-SNE", fcol = "markers_initial",
       main = "Initial marker resolution t-SNE")

Loading required namespace: Rtsne

addLegend(msn, where = "bottomright", fcol = "markers_initial", cex = .7)








As expected, the majority of markers cluster together with other proteins from the same subcellular compartment. However, we can see some protein markers which do not cluster as tightly with the rest of their compartment. Additionally, whilst the t-SNE plot shows all clusters to be relatively well separated, the PCA plot displays an overlap between the nucleus (dark purple) and ribosomal subunits (light pink and light orange). This is because the plot2D function uses PC1 and PC2 by default which limits visualisation to compartments resolved in these first two dimensions. We can pass a vector of alternative PC dimensions to the dims argument within plot2D to explore resolution in these lower PCs. Below we show that the ribosome compartments, nucleus, Golgi and lysosome are better differentiated when visualised with other PCs.

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

## Visualise PC1 and PC2 - the PCs which explain the most variance in our data
plot2D(msn, method = "PCA", fcol = "markers_initial",
       main = "Marker resolution in PC1 and PC2")
addLegend(msn, where = "bottomright", fcol = "markers_initial",
          cex = .7, ncol = 2)


## Visualise PC2 and PC3
plot2D(msn, method = "PCA", fcol = "markers_initial",
       dims = c(2, 3), main = "Marker resolution in PC2 and PC3")

## Visualise PC1 and PC3
plot2D(msn, method = "PCA", fcol = "markers_initial",
       dims = c(1, 3), main = "Marker resolution in PC1 and PC3")

## Visualise PC3 and PC4
plot2D(msn, method = "PCA", fcol = "markers_initial",
       dims = c(3, 4), main = "Marker resolution in PC3 and PC4")








Importantly, although dimensionality reduction provides a convenient visualisation tool, neither the PCA nor the t-SNE co-ordinates represent the data input for downstream supervised machine learning classification algorithms. The training data for classification are the marker protein correlation profiles. Therefore, it is critical to look directly at these profiles as well as the 2D maps.
The plotDist function within pRoloc generates a line plot showing the protein distribution profiles. We pass our msn object and subset the proteins annotated as "Mitochondrion" in the markers_initial column of the fData.
Check the marker names in the data

## Check marker classes
getMarkerClasses(msn, fcol = "markers_initial")

 [1] "Actin Cytoskeleton" "Chromatin"          "Cytosol"           
 [4] "Endosome"           "ER"                 "Golgi"             
 [7] "Lysosome"           "Mitochondrion"      "Nucleus"           
[10] "Peroxisome"         "PM"                 "Proteasome"        
[13] "Ribosome 40S"       "Ribosome 60S"      



## Get indices of mitochondrial proteins
mt <- fData(msn)$markers_initial == "Mitochondrion"

## Plot the distributions of mitochondrial markers
plotDist(object = msn[mt, ], pcol = "#A65628", las = 2)
title("Mitochondrial markers")

A for loop can be used to plot the distribution of each marker class, as outlined in the code chunk below. The getMarkerClasses function can be used to return a vector of all subcellular marker compartments in a given MSnSet.

## Define marker compartments
marker_organelles <- getMarkerClasses(msn, fcol = "markers_initial")

## Define colours
my_cols <- getStockcol()

## Plot marker distribution profile per compartment
par(mfrow = c(4, 4))
for (i in 1:length(marker_organelles)) {
  marker_indices <- fData(msn)$markers_initial == marker_organelles[i]
  plotDist(msn[marker_indices, ],
           pcol = my_cols[i],
           xlab = "Fraction",
           ylab = "Intensity")
  title(marker_organelles[i])
}








Plotting the concatenated profiles is useful as it allows us to assess the suitability of markers across all three replicates at once. Importantly, a protein can only be considered to be a marker if it behaves as such across all replicates. Overall, this marker set is a good fit to the data. Nevertheless, there are a few markers that could be removed.






NoteAn additional note on outlier marker removal



Decisions regarding what constitutes an “outlier marker” can be challenging. In most correlation profiling experiments the marker profiles will contain a certain degree of noise, and this is to be expected. Further, the degree of noise will differ across subcellular compartments depending upon how well they behave during the biochemical fractionation process. For instance, in the use-case data the proteasomal markers have a very tight profile with minimal noise whilst the nuclear markers have a wider profile indicating more variation in the behaviour of these proteins during fractionation. Whilst it would be possible to extract a subset of nuclear markers to generate a much tighter set of profiles (which would translate to a tighter cluster when visualised via dimensionality reduction), this would be an inaccurate representation of the data. Indeed, over-curation of markers to generate unrealistically tight clusters can lead to over-fitting of downstream protein localisation classification models. In other words, the nuclear markers would no longer be a true representation of the nucleus and the model may fail to recognise which of our unknown proteins should be classified as nuclear. The goal of marker curation is to select a set of markers which accurately represent the dataset being analysed. Moreover, some machine learning models are more robust to outliers than others.

title: 7  Data annotation
text:
7.5 Quantifying resolution using QSep
In addition to identifying outlying markers in each of the annotated compartments, users should also consider whether all of the initial compartments have sufficient resolution to be included in downstream classification. From the marker plots generated above, the initial compartments in our marker set do seem to be reasonably well resolved, perhaps with the exception of the actin cytoskeleton. However, we can take a more quantitative approach to exploring resolution by using the QSep function within pRoloc. QSep is a method for quantifying the separation of clusters in subcellular spatial proteomics datasets (Gatto et al. 2019).
We can carry out QSep analysis using the QSep function on the markers annotated on our MSnSet.

## Carry out QSep
qsep_res <- QSep(object = msn, fcol = "markers_initial")

## Verify
qsep_res

Object of class 'QSep'.
 Data: msn 
 With 14 sub-cellular clusters.


The QSep function returns a specialised object of class QSep. Within this object we can access matrices containing two types of QSep score: (1) the original and (2) normalised QSep scores. Original QSep scores are calculated as the average Euclidean distance between two clusters and thus directly quantify how far apart the clusters are when visualised via PCA. These scores are calculated using one of the clusters as a reference cluster. Since the distance between two clusters is the same regardless of which is the reference, the original QSep scores will be a symmetrical matrix. We can access this matrix by executing qsep_res@x.

For both raw and normalised QSep scores, a higher score indicates better resolution between clusters.
We can also visualise the results of QSep in multiple ways. Firstly, the plot function within the pRoloc package can be used to generate a boxplot of the QSep scores for each included compartment. The norm argument takes a logical input to indicate whether to use normalised or raw QSep scores.

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

## Plot a boxplot of raw QSep scores
plot(x = qsep_res, norm = FALSE)
title("Raw QSep scores for initial markers")

## Plot a boxplot of normalised QSep scores
plot(x = qsep_res, norm = TRUE)
title("Normalised QSep scores for initial markers")








From these boxplots we are able to see which of our subcellular compartments have higher overall normalised QSep scores, thus indicating that they are well resolved. In the use-case data, chromatin, mitochondrion, and lysosome are our three most well-resolved compartments.
Secondly, to take a closer look at the pairwise QSep scores we can use the levelPlot function, again with the norm argument to specify which type of score we are interested in.

## Plot a level plot of raw QSep values between each compartment
levelPlot(object = qsep_res, norm = FALSE,
          main = "Raw QSep values for initial markers")









## Plot a level plot of normalised QSep values between each compartment
levelPlot(object = qsep_res, norm = TRUE,
          main = "Normalised QSep values for initial markers")








Looking at the pairwise QSep scores is particularly useful in identifying which subcellular compartments are the least resolved from each other. In the use-case data the ribosomes have the lowest pairwise resolution, some of this may be down to the annotation of individual subunits and class labelling. When resolution between two subcellular compartments is low (i.e., their pairwise QSep scores are low) there is a higher chance of proteins being misclassified between these compartments during downstream machine learning. Indeed, a subcellular compartment could have a high average QSep score, but the ability to correctly classify proteins to that compartment is determined almost entirely by its lowest pairwise QSep score. For compartments where all calculated QSep scores are low, users may consider whether it is appropriate to include the compartment at all or combine them with other classes under one umbrella term, for example here we could combine the 40S and 60S subunits into one term “Ribosome”. We would also likely remove “Actin cytoskeleton” as it has consistently low resolution against all other compartments. By contrast, for compartments with high overall scores but one or two low pairwise QSep scores it may be worth combining the compartments with lower resolution. After making any changes, QSep scores can be recalculated on the updated annotated MSnSet to determine whether resolution has been improved.
QSep scores are a quantitative measure of cluster (subcellular compartment) separation. Higher QSep scores indicate that clusters are more well resolved from each other. However, users should not aim for unreasonably high QSep scores. As discussed above in “An additional note on outlier marker removal”, over-curation can generate unrealistically tight protein clusters which are no longer representative of the dataset. These clusters would have relatively higher QSep scores, since they are tighter and further separated from other compartments, but could still lead to over-fitting during protein localisation classification.

title: 7  Data annotation
text:
7.6 Interactive data visualisation
Visual exploration of correlation profiling datasets is a key aspect of the data analysis. As outlined above, the visualisation of marker protein distribution profiles as well as the annotation of these proteins on 2D maps facilitates the marker curation process required prior to protein localisation classification. To make this process of visual data exploration easier and reduce the need for excess plotting, the pRolocVis function from the pRolocGUI package can be used. We simply pass our MSnSet object to the pRolocVis function, specify a method of dimensionality reduction and a column from our fData which we wish to visualise, here the markers_initial column.

## Open pRolocGUI
pRolocVis(object = msn,
          method = "PCA",
          fcol = "markers_initial")






Screenshot of the pRolocVis GUI application.




Using this interactive visualisation tool enables us to easily identify which proteins the outlier points and profiles correspond to.





Example steps for identifying outlier with pRolocVis.




In the example above we identify a clear endosomal outlier. We see Q7LBR1 is annotated as endosomal (orange) and does not cluster with the other endosomal markers. We can use the pRolocVis app to identify this protein and also check its correlation profile. We indeed see its profile does not fit the average profile of the endosomal markers. For this reason we note this protein as not a good candidate for an endosomal marker in this dataset.






ExerciseExercise 1 - Challenge: Identifying the actin markers






Task 1 Use getMarkers to find out how many actin cytoskeleton markers there are in this marker list.
Task 2 Use the pRolocVis app from the pRolocGUI package to examine the profiles of the actin markers, or the plotDist function. Do you think they should be included as a marker class for downstream machine learning analysis?
Task 3 Extract the UniProt accession numbers of the actin cytoskeleton markers and store them in your R notebook or character vector.






AnswerAnswer






Task 1
The getMarkers function prints a summary table of the number of markers per class in the dataset. The column “markers_initial” contains the current markers we are working with.

getMarkers(msn, fcol = "markers_initial")

organelleMarkers
Actin Cytoskeleton          Chromatin            Cytosol           Endosome 
                30                 69                366                 34 
                ER              Golgi           Lysosome      Mitochondrion 
               231                 38                 36                346 
           Nucleus         Peroxisome                 PM         Proteasome 
               402                 17                 82                 28 
      Ribosome 40S       Ribosome 60S            unknown 
                14                 32               7011 


Task 2
Using the plotDist function.

## Subset actin cytoskeleton markers
actin <- fData(msn)$markers_initial == "Actin Cytoskeleton"

## Plot the distributions of actin cytoskeleton markers
plotDist(object = msn[actin, ], pcol = "red", las = 2)
title("Actin cytoskeleton markers")








You could have also used the pRolocVis function and selected the “Profiles” tab to examine the actin markers.
Task 3 There are several ways to do this, one way -

ind <- which(fData(msn)$markers_initial == "Actin Cytoskeleton")
actin_names <- featureNames(msn)[ind]
actin_names

 [1] "O15143" "O15144" "O15145" "O15511" "O75369" "P06753" "P09493" "P12814"
 [9] "P13796" "P23528" "P28289" "P47755" "P47756" "P52907" "P59998" "P61158"
[17] "P61160" "P63261" "Q01518" "Q14847" "Q16658" "Q562R1" "Q92747" "Q9BPX5"
[25] "Q9BR76" "Q9NYL9" "Q9NZ32" "Q9UJW0" "Q9Y281" "Q9Y4G6"
















ImportantMarker curation requires judgement



In the next section we refine our marker list, and in doing so we make a series of choices: which outliers to remove, which compartments to keep and which classes to combine or drop. None of these choices are black and white, and there are several sensible ways to approach each one. For example, you might:

keep a noisy compartment because it is biologically important, or remove it because it is poorly resolved
combine closely related compartments into one broader class, or keep them separate to gain finer detail at the cost of more misclassification
remove an outlying marker, or keep it because it reflects genuine variation within that compartment

The right choice depends on the organism, cell type, experimental conditions and the question you want to answer. What matters is that each decision is deliberate, justified by prior knowledge and the data, and recorded so that it can be reported and reproduced.
This care is worth taking because markers are the training data for every downstream step. A supervised classifier can only learn the compartments, and the boundaries between them, that the markers define. Any errors or biases in the marker list are carried directly into the predicted localisations, and from there into differential localisation analysis.
