title: 7  Data annotation
text:
7.7 Refining marker lists
Having made an assessment of the suitability of our initial marker list, we can now update our marker list accordingly. There are three different aspects to consider here:

Removal of outlier markers
Combining compartments which lack sufficient resolution
Expansion or removal of marker compartments which have an insufficient number of proteins to use as training data for classification

With respect to removing the annotation for individual outlier proteins, we previously visualised the correlation profiles of each marker compartment and used pRolocGUI to interactively identify which proteins the outlier profiles belong to. As we wish to keep track of marker annotation throughout our analysis we create a new column for our final marker list that we will use for analysis. We will call this “markers”. This is the default value of the fcol argument in pRoloc for many of pRoloc’s functions. This means we can omit fcol in many arguments.
Let’s first create this new list,

fData(msn)$markers <- fData(msn)$markers_initial

Check it’s been created,

msn |>
  fvarLabels()

 [1] "Channel"            "Decoy"              "Proteotypic"       
 [4] "Protein.Ids"        "Protein.Group"      "Protein.Names"     
 [7] "Genes"              "PG.TopN"            "Genes.TopN"        
[10] "Translated.Q.Value" "Channel.Q.Value"    "Lib.PG.Q.Value"    
[13] "is_contaminant"     "n_rep1"             "n_rep2"            
[16] "n_rep3"             "n_min"              "n_mean"            
[19] "missing_rep1"       "missing_rep2"       "missing_rep3"      
[22] "missing_max"        "missing_mean"       "hc"                
[25] "hdb_cluster_id"     "hdb_cluster_prob"   "markers_initial"   
[28] "markers"           


In the below code we remove the annotation for the following outlying proteins in our new markers column,

“Q7LBR1” is labelled as endosome but sits away from the rest of the endosomal markers.
“Q8NBJ9”, “Q9NUN5” are annotated to the lysosome but do not cluster with the other lysosomal markers.






Screenshots of the pRolocVis app with endosomal and lysosomal markers highlighted.




In the below code chunk we define the markers to be renamed.

## Define marker accessions identified as outliers
outlier_acc <- c("Q7LBR1", "Q8NBJ9", "Q9NUN5")

## Convert 'marker' column to unknown
to_rm <- which(fData(msn)$Protein.Group %in% outlier_acc)
fData(msn)$markers[to_rm] <- "unknown"

We can validate the removal of these 3 proteins by looking at a table of the markers using the getMarkers function. We see that previously we had 7011 “unknown” (unannotated) proteins, and now we have 7014.

## Compare marker numbers in initial and updated annotation columns
getMarkers(msn, fcol = "markers_initial")

organelleMarkers
Actin Cytoskeleton          Chromatin            Cytosol           Endosome 
                30                 69                366                 34 
                ER              Golgi           Lysosome      Mitochondrion 
               231                 38                 36                346 
           Nucleus         Peroxisome                 PM         Proteasome 
               402                 17                 82                 28 
      Ribosome 40S       Ribosome 60S            unknown 
                14                 32               7011 

getMarkers(msn, fcol = "markers")

organelleMarkers
Actin Cytoskeleton          Chromatin            Cytosol           Endosome 
                30                 69                366                 33 
                ER              Golgi           Lysosome      Mitochondrion 
               231                 38                 34                346 
           Nucleus         Peroxisome                 PM         Proteasome 
               402                 17                 82                 28 
      Ribosome 40S       Ribosome 60S            unknown 
                14                 32               7014 


Next, we consider whether to remove any compartment annotation and leave these proteins as “unknown” or “unlabelled”. Visualisation of PCA and t-SNE plots and QSep analysis showed good overall resolution of the marker classes, with median normalised between-cluster distances of about 2–5 for all compartments. Mitochondrion and chromatin were the best-resolved classes, with the largest raw distances to other compartments (median about 1.15–1.2) and high normalised scores (median about 4–5). The mitochondrial markers also formed the tightest cluster (within-cluster distance about 0.15). In contrast, the actin cytoskeleton class was poorly defined. It had one of the most diffuse marker clusters (within-cluster distance about 0.48, second only to Chromatin) and, together with endosome, the shortest median distance to other compartments (about 0.7). Because its markers are both dispersed and close to the other compartments, the class does not form a distinct cluster and is likely to cause unreliable classifications. We therefore decide to remove it from the marker set.
This is a judgement call rather than the only correct answer. A researcher whose question centres on the actin cytoskeleton might reasonably choose to keep the class, accepting that classifications to it will be less certain and interpreting them with appropriate caution. In such a scenario, it could also be worth searching the literature for additional Actin cytoskeleton marker proteins to see whether resolution could be improved.
Should users wish to remove the annotation for an entire compartment, the fDataToUnknown function provides an easy way to achieve this. We pass our MSnSet, the "markers" column and then use the from and to arguments to change our annotations from a given organelle to "unknown" (the default), or another annotation if desired, as shown below.

## Change actin to "unknown" in the column "markers"
msn <- fDataToUnknown(object = msn, fcol = "markers",
                      from = "Actin Cytoskeleton", to = "unknown")

## We see the actin annotation has been removed and relabelled as "unknown"
getMarkers(msn)

organelleMarkers
    Chromatin       Cytosol      Endosome            ER         Golgi 
           69           366            33           231            38 
     Lysosome Mitochondrion       Nucleus    Peroxisome            PM 
           34           346           402            17            82 
   Proteasome  Ribosome 40S  Ribosome 60S       unknown 
           28            14            32          7044 


Similarly, this function can also be used to change the names of compartments, replacing “unknown” in the above code chunk to the desired compartment name.
Finally, if users find that their initial or curated marker lists include compartments of interest which appear to be sufficiently resolved but have too few marker proteins (see the note “An additional note on minimum number of markers”) it may be necessary to find some additional marker proteins within the dataset. This could be informed by the results of unsupervised clustering, as demonstrated in the last lesson. Alternatively, users could consider looking at different marker sets to see whether there are any other well-established marker proteins for their compartment of interest.
After updating the marker list, users are advised to re-plot the marker profiles and annotated dimensionality reduction plots to display the final markers. This can be achieved using the same code as above, so for the simplicity of this workflow we will not repeat the plotting here.






ExerciseExercise 2 - Challenge: Re-assess the curated markers






Marker curation is iterative, so after refining the marker list we should check whether our changes have improved the fit of the markers to the data.
Task 1 Re-run QSep using the curated markers column and store the result in a new object called qsep_final.
Task 2 Plot the normalised QSep scores for the initial and the curated markers side by side, both as boxplots and as level plots. Has the separation of the compartments improved? Which compartments are now the least well resolved from each other?
Task 3 Re-plot the curated markers on PCA and t-SNE plots, and plot the marker profiles for each compartment with plotDist. Do the markers now fit the data well?
Task 4 Based on what you see, would you make any further changes to the marker list? Discuss your reasoning with your neighbour. Remember that there is no single correct answer.






AnswerAnswer






Task 1

## Re-run QSep on the curated markers
qsep_final <- QSep(object = msn, fcol = "markers")
qsep_final

Object of class 'QSep'.
 Data: msn 
 With 13 sub-cellular clusters.


Task 2

## Compare normalised QSep scores before and after curation
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
 
plot(x = qsep_res, norm = TRUE)
title("Initial markers")
 
plot(x = qsep_final, norm = TRUE)
title("Curated markers")









## Pairwise normalised QSep scores for the curated markers
levelPlot(object = qsep_res, norm = TRUE,
          main = "Normalised QSep values for the inital markers")









## Pairwise normalised QSep scores for the curated markers
levelPlot(object = qsep_final, norm = TRUE,
          main = "Normalised QSep values for curated markers")








Removing the actin cytoskeleton class and the outlying endosomal and lysosomal markers should give similar, or slightly higher, QSep scores for the remaining compartments. Because normalised scores depend on how tight each reference cluster is, removing a few outliers from a compartment can increase the scores of that compartment. The ribosomal subunits are likely to remain the least well separated pair.

## Lysosome average QSep values initial markers
qsep_res@xnorm["Lysosome", ] |> 
  median()

[1] 3.543174

## Lysosome average QSep values after curation of markers
qsep_final@xnorm["Lysosome", ] |> 
  median()

[1] 4.077058


Task 3

## PCA and t-SNE of the curated markers
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
 
plot2D(msn, method = "PCA", fcol = "markers",
       main = "Curated markers PCA")
addLegend(msn, where = "bottomright", fcol = "markers", cex = .7)
 
set.seed(399)
plot2D(msn, method = "t-SNE", fcol = "markers",
       main = "Curated markers t-SNE")









## Marker profiles for each curated compartment
marker_organelles <- getMarkerClasses(msn, fcol = "markers")
my_cols <- getStockcol()
 
par(mfrow = c(4, 4))
for (i in seq_along(marker_organelles)) {
  marker_indices <- fData(msn)$markers == marker_organelles[i]
  plotDist(msn[marker_indices, ],
           pcol = my_cols[i],
           xlab = "Fraction",
           ylab = "Intensity")
  title(marker_organelles[i])
}








Task 4
There is no single correct answer. Some reasonable options are:

Leave the 40S and 60S ribosomal subunits as separate classes if you are interested in distinguishing them, accepting that some proteins may be misclassified between them.
Combine them into a single “Ribosome” class to improve resolution, at the cost of finer detail. This can be done with fDataToUnknown, using the class names returned by getMarkerClasses(msn), for example:


## Replace the class names below with those in your data
msn_test <- fDataToUnknown(msn, fcol = "markers",
                           from = "40S Ribosome", to = "Ribosome")
msn_test <- fDataToUnknown(msn, fcol = "markers",
                           from = "60S Ribosome", to = "Ribosome")


Keep the marker list as it is. If the markers fit the data well and the compartments are reasonably resolved, further curation risks over-fitting.

Whatever you decide, re-run QSep and re-plot the markers after each change, and keep a record of what you changed and why.














TipKey Points




A marker is a protein known to reside in a single subcellular niche in the system and conditions being studied. Markers are the labelled training data for supervised machine learning, so their quality directly affects the localisation predictions.
There is no universal marker list. Curation involves judgement calls that depend on the organism, cell type, conditions and data quality. Decisions should be justified, documented and revisited as needed, because the markers determine what downstream machine learning can learn.
Marker curation is iterative: select the compartments resolved in the data, start from an existing marker list (e.g. from pRolocmarkers() or a publication), evaluate it against the data, refine it and reclassify.
Aim for enough markers per class to support cross-validation (around 10–15) and, where possible, more markers than quantitative channels. Some small organelles, such as the peroxisome, may not reach this.
PCA shows only two components at a time, so check several components (dims) before concluding that compartments overlap. Dimensionality reduction is only a visualisation: classifiers are trained on the marker correlation profiles, so always inspect these with plotDist().
QSep() quantifies how well compartments are separated. Normalised scores account for how tight each cluster is. A compartment is only as well resolved as its lowest pairwise score, so poorly separated compartments may need to be combined (e.g. 40S and 60S ribosome into “Ribosome”) or removed.
Remove clear outlier markers, but avoid over-curation: some noise is expected, and unrealistically tight marker sets give inflated QSep scores and can lead to over-fitting of the classifier.







Christopher, Josie A., Lisa M. Breckels, Oliver M. Crook, Mercedes Vazquez-Chantada, Derek Barratt, and Kathryn S. Lilley. 2025. “Global Proteomics Indicates Subcellular-Specific Anti-Ferroptotic Responses to Ionizing Radiation.” Molecular and Cellular Proteomics 24 (1): 100888. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mcpro.2024.100888.


Gatto, Laurent, Lisa M. Breckels, and Kathryn S. Lilley. 2019. “Assessing Sub-Cellular Resolution in Spatial Proteomics Experiments.” Current Opinion in Chemical Biology 48 (February): 123–49. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cbpa.2018.11.015.

title: 8  Protein localisation prediction
text:
8.1 Introduction
In the previous lesson we curated a set of markers that are reliable and representative of the structure of our U-2 OS data, and stored them in the markers column of our msn object. We can now use these markers to predict the localisation of the remaining proteins (currently annotated as “unknown”) using supervised machine learning. Whilst unsupervised methods such as hierarchical clustering and HDBSCAN are able to discover tight clusters of proteins with similar behaviours, these algorithms tend to struggle when it comes to identifying compartment borders. There are a number of supervised and semi-supervised machine learning algorithms available within the pRoloc infrastructure and these differ with respect to their data output, interpretability, and computational demand. Ultimately, the choice of algorithm is up to the user and we would recommend trying multiple models to determine which works best on a given set of data and biological question of interest.
The pRoloc package provides a wide range of machine learning methods for predicting protein localisation, described in its dedicated vignette “Machine learning techniques available in pRoloc”. We have also published three workflows showing how to apply these methods to correlation profiling data: one using classical machine learning (Breckels et al. 2018), one using Bayesian machine learning (Crook et al. 2019), and one covering both (Hutchings et al. 2025). In this course we focus on two complementary approaches. We start with a Support Vector Machine (SVM), a widely used classical classifier, and then move on to a Bayesian approach based on t-augmented Gaussian mixture (TAGM) models. Rather than giving only a single best guess, TAGM also estimates how confident we can be in each prediction and allows for proteins that do not fit any of the known compartments. We focus on how to apply these methods and interpret their results rather than on the details of the algorithms. Participants who want to learn more about TAGM are referred to Crook et al. (2018) and Crook et al. (2019).
Remember that a supervised classifier can only assign proteins to the compartments represented in the training data. Any compartment we removed from the marker list in the previous lesson, such as the actin cytoskeleton, cannot be predicted.

title: 8  Protein localisation prediction
section: 8.2 Classification using a Support Vector Machine
text:
8.2 Classification using a Support Vector Machine
Support Vector Machines (SVMs) have been widely used for protein subcellular localisation prediction (Itzhak et al. 2016; Orre et al. 2019; Christoforou et al. 2016; Geladaki et al. 2019; Mulvey et al. 2017; Schessner et al. 2023). To understand how an SVM works, imagine each protein as a point in space, with one axis per fraction (here, 27 axes). Marker proteins from different compartments sit in different regions of this space. An SVM learns boundaries (hyperplanes) that separate these regions, placing each boundary as far as possible from the markers on either side. Unknown proteins are then classified according to which side of the boundaries they fall on. For more details about SVM algorithms readers are directed to Noble (2006).
Real compartments rarely have straight-line boundaries, so the SVM uses a kernel that allows the boundaries to curve. Two parameters control this, and we will optimise both below:

sigma controls how flexible (curved) the boundaries can be.
cost controls how strictly the boundaries must separate the markers. A high cost penalises misclassified markers heavily, while a low cost tolerates some in exchange for simpler boundaries.

For each protein, the SVM also returns a score reflecting how far it lies from a boundary: proteins deep within a compartment’s region get high scores, whereas proteins near a boundary get low scores. The score is a measure of confidence, but it is not a probability.






NoteThe four steps of SVM classification in pRoloc




Optimise the SVM parameters sigma and cost using the markers (svmOptimisation)
Check the results of the optimisation (getF1Scores, levelPlot) and extract the best parameters (getParams)
Classify all proteins using these parameters (svmClassification)
Threshold the predictions so that only confident assignments are kept (orgQuants, getPredictions)




8.2.1 Optimising SVM parameters
As is the case with most supervised learning models, before we can perform any classification the model parameters need to be optimised. We adopt a classical view of training the model parameters and split the data into training and testing sets. By default in pRoloc all methods allocate 80% of the labelled data (marker proteins) for training and optimisation via cross-validation of the free parameters, namely sigma and cost. The remaining 20% labelled data acts as the test set to which the optimised parameters are applied in order to calculate F1 scores. Briefly, an F1 score can be used as a measure of model accuracy as it combines measurements of both precision and recall. A higher F1 score indicates a better quality classifier.
In pRoloc the SVM optimisation process is facilitated by the svmOptimisation function. We pass our MSnSet object (here, msn) to the svmOptimisation function and tell it the name of the fData column where our markers are held (here "markers"). We use the times argument to specify how many iterations of cross-validation to complete and the xval argument to set the value of n in n-fold cross validation. Here, we will use the default 5-fold cross-validation (xval = 5) with 10 iterations (times = 10). We would typically set times = 100, but we use 10 here to keep the run time manageable; 100 iterations can take an hour or more on a laptop. Since our training data contains asymmetric class sizes (subcellular compartments with variable numbers of marker proteins), we also set class weights using the class.weights argument to avoid biasing our localisation towards compartments with a greater number of marker proteins (Huang and Du 2005). Hence, we weight each subcellular compartment by the inverse of the number of marker proteins it has. Finally, to ensure reproducibility of our results we set a seed using the seed argument.

## Get the number of markers per class
marker_tbl <- table(getMarkers(msn, verbose = FALSE))

## Set class weights as inverse of class frequencies
weights <- 1 / marker_tbl[names(marker_tbl) != "unknown"]
weights


    Chromatin       Cytosol      Endosome            ER         Golgi 
  0.014492754   0.002732240   0.030303030   0.004329004   0.026315789 
     Lysosome Mitochondrion       Nucleus    Peroxisome            PM 
  0.029411765   0.002890173   0.002487562   0.058823529   0.012195122 
   Proteasome  Ribosome 40S  Ribosome 60S 
  0.035714286   0.071428571   0.031250000 



## SVM parameter optimisation (using times = 10 for demonstration, usually 100)
svm_params <- svmOptimisation(object = msn,
                              fcol = "markers",
                              times = 10,
                              xval = 5,
                              class.weights = weights,
                              seed = 399)

The output of this code is an object of class GenRegRes, a dedicated data container used to store the results of machine learning optimisation (see Breckels et al. (2018) for more details). Printing it gives a short summary of the optimisation.

svm_params

Object of class "GenRegRes"
Algorithm: svm 
Hyper-parameters:
 cost: 0.0625 0.125 0.25 0.5 1 2 4 8 16
 sigma: 0.001 0.01 0.1 1 10 100
Design:
 Replication: 10 x 5-fold X-validation
 Partitioning: 0.2/0.8 (test/train)
Results
 macro F1:
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
 0.8227  0.8385  0.8586  0.8572  0.8757  0.8840 
 best sigma: 0.1   
 best cost: 16   




8.2.2 Checking the optimisation results

Best parameters in each iteration with getF1Scores
To see which pair of parameters resulted in the highest F1 score in each iteration we can use the getF1Scores function. This gives a matrix with one row per iteration.

## Best F1 score, and the parameters that gave it, in each iteration
getF1Scores(object = svm_params)

             F1 sigma cost
 [1,] 0.8226757   0.1   16
 [2,] 0.8773922   0.1   16
 [3,] 0.8347168   0.1   16
 [4,] 0.8497589   0.1   16
 [5,] 0.8704653   0.1   16
 [6,] 0.8324702   0.1   16
 [7,] 0.8839693   0.1   16
 [8,] 0.8560528   0.1   16
 [9,] 0.8833327   0.1   16
[10,] 0.8611609   0.1   16


How do we interpret this output?

Each row is one iteration of cross-validation. In each iteration, a different random 20% of the markers was held back as a test set, every combination of sigma and cost was tested, and the best-performing combination was recorded.
The best parameters are consistent across iterations. Here, sigma = 0.1 and cost = 16 give the highest F1 score in 10 of the 10 iterations. When the same combination wins in most or all iterations, the choice of parameters is stable and does not depend on how the markers happened to be split into training and test sets.
The F1 scores are high. They range from 0.82 to 0.88, with a mean of 0.86. The F1 score measures how well the model, trained on one part of the markers, predicts the markers it has not seen, balancing precision and recall. A score of 1 would be perfect, so our classifier correctly predicts most held-out markers. This is also a good sign that our curated markers separate the compartments well.
Some variation between iterations is expected. The small spread in F1 scores reflects which markers end up in each test set, and is not a cause for concern.



All parameter combinations with levelPlot
The getF1Scores function only tells us which combination of parameters performed best in each iteration. It does not tell us how the other combinations performed, or whether the best combination is clearly better than its neighbours. For this, we can use the levelPlot function, which shows the F1 score for every combination of sigma and cost tested during optimisation as a heatmap.

## Plot the average F1 score for every combination of sigma and cost
levelPlot(svm_params)








Each cell of the heatmap is one combination of sigma and cost, and its colour shows the F1 score for that combination averaged over the iterations. When reading this plot, we look for three things:

Where the highest F1 scores are. This shows us which region of parameter space gives the best classifier, and should agree with the results of getF1Scores.
Whether the best region is broad or narrow. A broad region of similarly high F1 scores means the classifier is not very sensitive to the exact parameter values, which is reassuring. A single isolated cell with a high score is less trustworthy, as it may reflect chance.
Whether the best values lie at the edge of the grid. If the highest F1 scores are found at the smallest or largest value of sigma or cost tested, a value outside this range might perform even better. In that case, it is worth re-running svmOptimisation with a wider range of values, passed to its sigma and cost arguments.

By default, levelPlot summarises the F1 scores across iterations using the mean. We can change this with the fun argument. For example, using the standard deviation shows how much the performance of each combination varied between iterations.






ExerciseExercise 1 - Challenge: How stable is the parameter search?






Level: 
Use levelPlot with fun = median and then fun = sd. Does the median give the same best region as the mean? Which combinations of sigma and cost give the most variable performance between iterations?






AnswerAnswer







## Median F1 score across iterations
levelPlot(svm_params, fun = median)







## Standard deviation of F1 scores across iterations
levelPlot(svm_params, fun = sd)








The median should highlight the same best region as the mean, because the same parameters performed best in most or all iterations. The standard deviation plot shows which combinations performed inconsistently between iterations. Ideally, the best combination should have both a high average F1 score and a low standard deviation.














NoteOther functions for exploring the optimisation



pRoloc has further functions for exploring a GenRegRes object. For example, f1Count(svm_params, t = 0.8) counts how many times each combination of sigma and cost gave an F1 score above a threshold t, and the full F1 matrix for each iteration can be accessed with svm_params@f1Matrices. With only 10 iterations these add little to getF1Scores and levelPlot, but they become more informative when svmOptimisation is run with the recommended 100 or more iterations.




Extracting the best parameters with getParams
When one combination of sigma and cost performs best in most iterations, the choice is clear. When several combinations perform similarly, the getParams function chooses the best parameters for us. We use it here to confirm the parameters that will be used for classification.

## Return optimal parameters
getParams(object = svm_params)

sigma  cost 
  0.1  16.0 





8.2.3 Protein localisation prediction with SVMs
Now that we are happy with our parameters, we can apply the SVM model to our data using the svmClassification function. Rather than typing the values of sigma and cost by hand, we pass the whole svm_params object to the assessRes argument, and the best parameters (those returned by getParams) are extracted automatically. We again provide our weights to class.weights.

## Carry out SVM classification using optimised parameters
msn <- svmClassification(object = msn,
                         fcol = "markers",
                         assessRes = svm_params,
                         class.weights = weights)

[1] "markers"


After carrying out the SVM classification, we now have two new columns added to the fData of our MSnSet.

## Check the new columns in fData
fvarLabels(msn)

 [1] "Channel"            "Decoy"              "Proteotypic"       
 [4] "Protein.Ids"        "Protein.Group"      "Protein.Names"     
 [7] "Genes"              "PG.TopN"            "Genes.TopN"        
[10] "Translated.Q.Value" "Channel.Q.Value"    "Lib.PG.Q.Value"    
[13] "is_contaminant"     "n_rep1"             "n_rep2"            
[16] "n_rep3"             "n_min"              "n_mean"            
[19] "missing_rep1"       "missing_rep2"       "missing_rep3"      
[22] "missing_max"        "missing_mean"       "hc"                
[25] "hdb_cluster_id"     "hdb_cluster_prob"   "markers_initial"   
[28] "markers"            "svm"                "svm.scores"        


The first of these is the svm column which contains the classification result i.e., the localisation prediction for each protein.

## Look at svm classification column
msn |>
  fData() |>
  pull(svm) |>
  table()


    Chromatin       Cytosol      Endosome            ER         Golgi 
          462          2339           349          1045           128 
     Lysosome Mitochondrion       Nucleus    Peroxisome            PM 
           92           767          2614            38           559 
   Proteasome  Ribosome 40S  Ribosome 60S 
          143            37           163 


The second new column is svm.scores, which contains the SVM score for each protein, as described above.

## Look at svm.scores column
msn |>
  fData() |>
  pull(svm.scores) |>
  summary()

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
 0.1561  0.5469  0.8715  0.7590  0.9881  1.0000 




8.2.4 Thresholding protein localisation classification using an SVM
As we saw above, all proteins have been classified to one of the subcellular compartments included in our training data. However, when applying a supervised machine learning algorithm it is standard practice to set a specific confidence threshold at which we accept new assignments. Any protein with a confidence below this threshold will receive the final classification of "unknown". The way in which confidence is defined differs between classification algorithms. In the case of SVMs, we rely on the SVM score to set our thresholds.
Let’s plot a boxplot of the SVM scores of proteins allocated to each subcellular compartment. We first use the unknownMSnSet function to return an MSnSet with the marker proteins removed. Markers are assigned to their own class with a score of 1, so they cannot tell us anything about the confidence of new predictions.

## Remove markers
msn_preds <- unknownMSnSet(object = msn)

## Use the same colours as plot2D for each compartment
org_cols <- getStockcol()[seq_along(getMarkerClasses(msn))]
names(org_cols) <- getMarkerClasses(msn)

## Visualise svm scores per organelle
msn_preds |>
  fData() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = svm, y = svm.scores, fill = svm)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.size = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = org_cols) +
  labs(x = "SVM classification", y = "SVM score") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        legend.position = "none")








We can see that each compartment displays a different distribution of SVM scores and, therefore, applying a global score threshold would not be appropriate here. Instead, there are several ways in which users can apply compartment-specific thresholding. One common approach is to manually set a compartment-specific FDR to allow up to 5% false discoveries, for example. This would involve putting the proteins localised to each compartment in descending order by their SVM score before going down the list to find the SVM score at which 5% of proteins are incorrectly classified based on reliable subcellular databases and prior knowledge from the literature. Unfortunately, such an approach can never be completely objective and is limited to organisms with well annotated subcellular proteomes. An alternative method would be to threshold each compartment at a set percentile of its SVM scores. Here, we will demonstrate the latter approach using the orgQuants and getPredictions functions within pRoloc.
The orgQuants function takes an MSnSet containing classification results as its input. We pass the column in our fData where the classification assignments are stored (here "svm"), the score column ("svm.scores") and the marker column ("markers"). Finally, we use the t argument to specify our threshold quantile. The quantile threshold is ultimately up to the user and will depend on (1) how exploratory the analysis aims to be, and (2) the data quality and resolution. In reality, we recommend testing multiple thresholds. Here, we demonstrate the use of a 0.75 quantile threshold, which keeps the 25% of proteins with the highest scores in each compartment.

## Get organelle-specific quantile SVM scores
score_thresholds <- orgQuants(object = msn,
                              fcol = "svm",
                              scol = "svm.scores",
                              mcol = "markers",
                              t = 0.75)

    Chromatin       Cytosol      Endosome            ER         Golgi 
    0.9047297     0.9664284     0.7789853     0.9032660     0.8151856 
     Lysosome Mitochondrion       Nucleus    Peroxisome            PM 
    0.8190059     0.9866420     0.9526143     0.5257223     0.8253324 
   Proteasome  Ribosome 40S  Ribosome 60S 
    0.6695862     0.4592555     0.6904836 


We can now use these quantile-based score thresholds in the getPredictions function.

## Use organelle-specific quantiles to get thresholded localisation predictions
msn <- getPredictions(object = msn,
                      fcol = "svm",
                      scol = "svm.scores",
                      mcol = "markers",
                      t = score_thresholds)

ans
    Chromatin       Cytosol      Endosome            ER         Golgi 
          168           860           112           435            61 
     Lysosome Mitochondrion       Nucleus    Peroxisome            PM 
           49           452           955            23           202 
   Proteasome  Ribosome 40S  Ribosome 60S       unknown 
           57            20            65          5277 


After thresholding we have a new column in our fData called svm.pred. This column contains the localisation allocations after thresholding. We also get a summary output when we applied the getPredictions function showing us the number of proteins classified to each subcellular compartment as well as the 5277 proteins which remain "unknown".

## Check fData for new svm.pred column
fvarLabels(msn)

 [1] "Channel"            "Decoy"              "Proteotypic"       
 [4] "Protein.Ids"        "Protein.Group"      "Protein.Names"     
 [7] "Genes"              "PG.TopN"            "Genes.TopN"        
[10] "Translated.Q.Value" "Channel.Q.Value"    "Lib.PG.Q.Value"    
[13] "is_contaminant"     "n_rep1"             "n_rep2"            
[16] "n_rep3"             "n_min"              "n_mean"            
[19] "missing_rep1"       "missing_rep2"       "missing_rep3"      
[22] "missing_max"        "missing_mean"       "hc"                
[25] "hdb_cluster_id"     "hdb_cluster_prob"   "markers_initial"   
[28] "markers"            "svm"                "svm.scores"        
[31] "svm.pred"          








NoteWhy would proteins not meet the classification threshold and remain unknown?



After thresholding our SVM classifications we have 5277 proteins which were not assigned to one of the subcellular compartments and instead remain as "unknown". There are a number of reasons for which proteins may remain unknown after classification. Firstly, the subcellular structure and compartmentalisation of a cell is extremely complex and cannot be completely represented by our labelled training data (markers). For instance, some subcellular structures may have too few well-established marker proteins to be included in classification. This could be due to lack of prior knowledge or absence of a unique protein profile, as seen with P-bodies and stress granules, niches which are defined by many of the same proteins. Secondly, a large proportion of the proteome is known to reside in multiple subcellular niches within a given cell at a given time (Thul et al. 2017). The abundance profiles of these multi-localised proteins can represent a mixture of their localisations and, therefore, no longer match the marker profiles of any given compartment. Further, since correlation profiling experiments utilise bulk proteomics, the observed protein abundance profiles represent an average of the population. Proteins which differ in subcellular localisation across a heterogeneous starting population (e.g., due to differences in cell cycle status) could also display mixed localisation profiles and ultimately remain classified as "unknown".

title: 8  Protein localisation prediction
text:
8.3 Classification using TAGM-MAP
As an alternative to protein localisation classification using a classical SVM approach, users can also make use of newer Bayesian models available within pRoloc. The main advantages of applying a Bayesian framework are that (1) protein localisation predictions come with probabilities, which are on the same scale for every compartment and are, in principle, easier to interpret than SVM scores, and (2) the model includes an outlier component, so proteins that do not fit any of the known compartments can be identified explicitly rather than being forced into one. As we will see, however, these probabilities are only as good as the model that produces them, and they need to be interpreted with care.
Both Bayesian classifiers available within pRoloc are based on a t-augmented Gaussian mixture (TAGM) model, as outlined in Crook et al. (2018). In this course we use the first implementation of this model, TAGM-MAP, which uses maximum a posteriori estimates of the model parameters. The second implementation, TAGM-MCMC, is not covered here (see Crook et al. (2019) for a worked example). Unlike TAGM-MCMC, TAGM-MAP does not sample the entire posterior distribution but instead uses an extended version of the expectation maximisation (EM) algorithm for inference. In terms of user experience, this means that TAGM-MAP is faster and requires less computational power. However, it also means that TAGM-MAP finds a single best set of model parameters and does not account for uncertainty in them. We will return to the consequences of this when we compare the SVM and TAGM-MAP results.






NoteBayesian methods, posteriors and the EM algorithm in brief




Bayesian methods combine what we already believe (the prior) with what we observe in the data (the likelihood) to give an updated belief, the posterior. Here, the posterior tells us how probable it is that a protein belongs to each compartment, given its profile and the markers.
TAGM (t-augmented Gaussian mixture) describes each compartment as a cloud of points with a centre and a spread (a Gaussian distribution), fitted to the markers. An extra, very broad component (a t-distribution) captures outliers: proteins that do not fit any compartment well.
MAP (maximum a posteriori) means finding the single most probable set of model parameters, i.e. the best centre and spread for each compartment.
The EM algorithm (expectation maximisation) is how TAGM-MAP finds these parameters. It alternates between two steps: (E) given the current compartment shapes, estimate how likely each protein is to belong to each compartment, and (M) given these estimates, update the compartment shapes. It repeats until the results stop changing, which is why we check convergence.
TAGM-MCMC (Markov-chain Monte Carlo), which we do not cover here, does not stop at a single best set of parameters. Instead, it samples many plausible sets, which gives a fuller picture of uncertainty but takes much longer.




8.3.1 Optimising TAGM-MAP model parameters
The first step in using TAGM-MAP is executing the tagmMapTrain function. We run the algorithm for 100 iterations (the default, numIter = 100). We set a seed to ensure reproducibility and pass our marker annotated MSnSet to the function.

## Optimise the tagm-map model
set.seed(2)
map_params <- tagmMapTrain(msn, numIter = 100)

The output of the tagmMapTrain function is an object of class MAPParams which contains the optimised model parameters. Importantly, before applying these parameters we need to check that the model has converged. The TAGM-MAP expectation maximisation (EM) algorithm iterates between an expectation and maximisation step until the log-posterior is stable. To check that the model successfully reached this status, we use the logPosteriors function to extract the log-posteriors at each iteration and pass this to the plot function.

## Plot to visualise convergence
map_params |>
  logPosteriors() |>
  plot(type = "b", col = "blue", cex = 0.3,
       ylab = "log-posterior",
       xlab = "Iteration")








We can see that the value of the log-posterior increased until it stopped changing, thus indicating that the TAGM-MAP model has converged. This means that it is suitable to continue with our optimised parameters. For further details of the algorithm we refer readers to Crook et al. (2019).


8.3.2 Protein localisation prediction with TAGM-MAP
Next, we apply the optimised TAGM-MAP parameters to carry out protein localisation classification via the tagmMapPredict function. We pass our MSnSet object and the object storing our parameters, here called map_params.

## Predict protein localisation using converged parameters
msn <- tagmMapPredict(object = msn, params = map_params)

The tagmMapPredict function adds three new columns to the fData of our MSnSet:

tagm.map.allocation: the most probable compartment for each protein. Like the svm column, every protein is assigned to a compartment at this stage, before any thresholding.
tagm.map.probability: the probability that the protein belongs to its allocated compartment, given the model. Values close to 1 indicate a confident allocation.
tagm.map.outlier: the probability that the protein is an outlier, i.e. that it does not belong to any of the compartments defined by our markers. Values close to 1 indicate a protein that fits poorly with all compartments.


## Check which columns we have in the fData
msn |>
  fvarLabels()

 [1] "Channel"              "Decoy"                "Proteotypic"         
 [4] "Protein.Ids"          "Protein.Group"        "Protein.Names"       
 [7] "Genes"                "PG.TopN"              "Genes.TopN"          
[10] "Translated.Q.Value"   "Channel.Q.Value"      "Lib.PG.Q.Value"      
[13] "is_contaminant"       "n_rep1"               "n_rep2"              
[16] "n_rep3"               "n_min"                "n_mean"              
[19] "missing_rep1"         "missing_rep2"         "missing_rep3"        
[22] "missing_max"          "missing_mean"         "hc"                  
[25] "hdb_cluster_id"       "hdb_cluster_prob"     "markers_initial"     
[28] "markers"              "svm"                  "svm.scores"          
[31] "svm.pred"             "tagm.map.allocation"  "tagm.map.probability"
[34] "tagm.map.outlier"    


Let’s take a look at the initial classification results.

## Check overall classifications prior to thresholding
msn |>
  fData() |>
  pull(tagm.map.allocation) |>
  table()


    Chromatin       Cytosol      Endosome            ER         Golgi 
          571          1896           186          1501            81 
     Lysosome Mitochondrion       Nucleus    Peroxisome            PM 
           44           721          2991            18           594 
   Proteasome  Ribosome 40S  Ribosome 60S 
           66            17            50 


We can also look at the range of probabilities given for organelle classifications and outlier detection.

## Check range of probabilities for compartment localisations
msn |>
  fData() |>
  pull(tagm.map.probability) |>
  summary()

     Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean   3rd Qu.      Max. 
0.0000000 0.0000058 0.9989217 0.6352027 1.0000000 1.0000000 

## Check range of probabilities for outliers
msn |>
  fData() |>
  pull(tagm.map.outlier) |>
  summary()

     Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean   3rd Qu.      Max. 
0.0000000 0.0000000 0.0003424 0.3631731 0.9999942 1.0000000 


Notice how extreme the localisation probabilities are: the median is 0.9989 and the upper quartile is 1. Compare this with the SVM scores above, which are spread much more evenly between 0 and 1 (lower quartile 0.55, median 0.87). We will come back to this when we compare the two classifiers.


8.3.3 Thresholding protein localisation classification using TAGM-MAP
As was the case when applying an SVM model, we still need to apply thresholding to the initial classification results to ensure confidence in our results. Again, proteins which do not meet our defined threshold will receive the final classification of "unknown". Thresholding of TAGM-MAP outputs can be achieved by combining the probability of a predicted compartment classification being correct with the probability that a protein belongs to an outlier component. In the code chunk below we create a new column in the fData of our MSnSet called overall_prob. This value is calculated as the probability of the compartment classification multiplied by one minus the probability that a protein is an outlier. Hence, a larger overall_prob indicates a higher confidence in our classification.
Because these are probabilities, they are on the same scale for every compartment, so we can use a single threshold for all compartments rather than the organelle-specific thresholds we needed for the SVM. We use the getPredictions function to update our classification predictions based on our score column (scol) overall_prob with a threshold (t) of 0.999.

## Store classification and outlier probabilities
tagm_prob <- fData(msn)[, "tagm.map.probability"]
tagm_out <- 1 - fData(msn)[, "tagm.map.outlier"]

## Create new column containing overall probability
fData(msn)[, "overall_prob"] <- tagm_prob * tagm_out

## Set prediction thresholds on overall probability
msn <- getPredictions(msn,
                      fcol = "tagm.map.allocation",
                      scol = "overall_prob",
                      t = .999)

ans
    Chromatin       Cytosol      Endosome            ER         Golgi 
          417           642            47          1252            54 
     Lysosome Mitochondrion       Nucleus    Peroxisome            PM 
           36           717           806            17           158 
   Proteasome  Ribosome 40S  Ribosome 60S       unknown 
           32            14            34          4510 


As above, the getPredictions function has printed a summary of the thresholded classification results, which are stored in a new column called tagm.map.allocation.pred.

title: 8  Protein localisation prediction
text:
8.4 Generating a subcellular spatial map
Regardless of the algorithm used, the result of classification is a list of proteins and their predicted subcellular localisations. As was the case for markers, these results can be visualised using dimensionality reduction methods via the plot2D function to create a “subcellular spatial map” of the data. It is also important to remember to plot the protein correlation profiles alongside maps of the data to aid interpretation and verify resolution.
This time, we pass our MSnSet and specify the fcol as the column containing our thresholded localisation results. It is up to the user which dimensionality reduction method is applied. To see the full list of visualisation methods available for use with plot2D see plot2Dmethods, which are also listed in the plot2D documentation (see ?plot2D for details).

plot2Dmethods

 [1] "PCA"    "MDS"    "kpca"   "lda"    "t-SNE"  "UMAP"   "nipals" "hexbin"
 [9] "none"   "scree" 


First, as a reminder, we plot our markers using the default plot2D settings, which produce a PCA plot of the markers column.

## Plot the markers
msn |>
  plot2D(main = "PCA: markers")
msn |>
  addLegend(where = "topright", cex = .6)








Next, we plot the thresholded results of both classifiers side by side by passing fcol = "svm.pred" and fcol = "tagm.map.allocation.pred".

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

## Plot the thresholded SVM results
msn |>
  plot2D(fcol = "svm.pred", main = "PCA: classification using SVM")

## Plot the thresholded TAGM-MAP results
msn |>
  plot2D(fcol = "tagm.map.allocation.pred",
         main = "PCA: classification using TAGM-MAP")
msn |>
  addLegend(fcol = "tagm.map.allocation.pred", where = "topright", cex = .6)

title: 8  Protein localisation prediction
section: 8.5 Comparing the SVM and TAGM-MAP results
text:
8.5 Comparing the SVM and TAGM-MAP results
At first glance the two spatial maps look similar: the same compartments are found in the same regions of the PCA plot. However, looking more closely, the TAGM-MAP map has many more coloured (classified) proteins and fewer grey ("unknown") proteins, and some compartments extend much further into the regions between clusters. Let’s look at this in more detail.

8.5.1 How many proteins are assigned to each compartment?

## Number of proteins per compartment for each classifier
table(compartment = c(fData(msn)$svm.pred, fData(msn)$tagm.map.allocation.pred),
      classifier  = rep(c("SVM", "TAGM_MAP"), each = nrow(fData(msn)))) |>
  as.data.frame.matrix()

               SVM TAGM_MAP
Chromatin      168      417
Cytosol        860      642
Endosome       112       47
ER             435     1252
Golgi           61       54
Lysosome        49       36
Mitochondrion  452      717
Nucleus        955      806
Peroxisome      23       17
PM             202      158
Proteasome      57       32
Ribosome 40S    20       14
Ribosome 60S    65       34
unknown       5277     4510


TAGM-MAP leaves fewer proteins as "unknown" (4510 compared with 5277 for the SVM), and assigns many more proteins to some compartments. The difference is largest for the ER (1252 proteins with TAGM-MAP compared with 435 with the SVM) and chromatin (417 compared with 168). On the PCA plot, these extra assignments extend into the regions between compartments, where we would expect proteins to be less confidently localised.


8.5.2 Why does TAGM-MAP assign more proteins?
The answer lies in the distribution of the scores and probabilities used for thresholding. Let’s plot them for all proteins that are not markers.

## Remove markers
msn_preds <- unknownMSnSet(object = msn)

## Scores and probabilities used for thresholding, in long format
scores_df <- data.frame(
  value = c(fData(msn_preds)$svm.scores, fData(msn_preds)$overall_prob),
  classifier = rep(c("SVM score", "TAGM-MAP overall probability"),
                   each = nrow(msn_preds)))

## Plot their distributions
ggplot(scores_df, aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ classifier, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Score / probability", y = "Number of proteins") +
  theme_bw()








The SVM scores are spread across the whole range from 0 to 1, so a threshold can separate confident from less confident assignments. The TAGM-MAP probabilities, by contrast, are almost all either very close to 0 or very close to 1. With so few proteins in between, a threshold of 0.999 removes very few proteins, and proteins lying between compartments are classified with a probability of 1.






NoteWhy are the TAGM-MAP probabilities so extreme?



Probabilities are only as good as the model that produces them. There are several reasons why TAGM-MAP tends to be overconfident:

TAGM-MAP finds a single best set of parameters. It estimates the centre and spread of each compartment once, and treats these estimates as exact. It ignores any uncertainty in them, which makes the resulting probabilities more extreme than they should be. TAGM-MCMC (not covered here, see Crook et al. (2019)) averages over this uncertainty and generally produces more informative probabilities.
Many dimensions sharpen small differences. Our data has 27 quantitative channels (three concatenated replicates). With this many dimensions, a small difference in how well a protein fits two compartments becomes a very large difference in likelihood, pushing the probability towards 0 or 1.
Broad compartments absorb proteins between clusters. A compartment with a large spread, such as the ER here, can fit proteins lying between clusters well enough to claim them with high probability.
The outlier component may be too small. The expected proportion of outliers is set by a prior (see the u and v arguments in ?tagmMapTrain). If our data contains more proteins that do not fit any compartment than the prior allows for, they are pushed into a compartment instead.





8.5.3 Do the two classifiers agree?
Finally, we can check how often the two classifiers agree. We cross-tabulate the thresholded predictions and calculate the proportion of proteins classified by both methods that are assigned to the same compartment.

## Cross-tabulate the thresholded predictions of the two classifiers
agree_tbl <- table(SVM = fData(msn_preds)$svm.pred,
                   TAGM_MAP = fData(msn_preds)$tagm.map.allocation.pred)
agree_tbl

               TAGM_MAP
SVM             Chromatin Cytosol Endosome   ER Golgi Lysosome Mitochondrion

## Proteins classified (not "unknown") by both classifiers
both <- fData(msn_preds)$svm.pred != "unknown" &
  fData(msn_preds)$tagm.map.allocation.pred != "unknown"

## Proportion of these assigned to the same compartment
agree_prop <- mean(fData(msn_preds)$svm.pred[both] ==
                     fData(msn_preds)$tagm.map.allocation.pred[both])
agree_prop

[1] 0.9033333


Of the 900 proteins classified by both methods, 90.3% are assigned to the same compartment. A further 1634 proteins are left as "unknown" by the SVM but assigned to a compartment by TAGM-MAP. Proteins predicted to the same compartment by two quite different methods are good candidates for a confident localisation.


8.5.4 Which results should we use?
There is no single correct answer. Probabilities are attractive because they are on the same scale for every compartment, are easy to interpret, and allow us to identify outliers. However, as we have seen, the probabilities from TAGM-MAP in this dataset are overconfident, and a fixed threshold discriminates poorly between confident and uncertain assignments. There are several ways to address this:

use a stricter or organelle-specific threshold on the TAGM-MAP probabilities (see the challenge below)
compare the predictions of different classifiers and focus on proteins on which they agree
use TAGM-MCMC, which accounts for uncertainty in the model parameters and generally produces more informative probabilities, at a greater computational cost (see Crook et al. 2019)

As with marker curation, the choice depends on the data and the question. Whichever approach is used, predictions should always be checked against the data, using spatial maps and protein profiles, and against prior knowledge.






ExerciseExercise 2 - Challenge: Organelle-specific thresholds for TAGM-MAP






Level: 
For the SVM, we used orgQuants to set a different score threshold for each compartment. For TAGM-MAP, we instead used a single threshold of 0.999 on the overall probability.
Task 1 Use orgQuants to calculate organelle-specific thresholds on the overall_prob column, using a quantile of t = 0.75, as we did for the SVM. Look at the thresholds. Are they similar across compartments?
Task 2 Use these thresholds with getPredictions. Store the result in a new object called msn_q, so that the results from the 0.999 threshold in msn are not overwritten.
Task 3 Compare the number of proteins assigned to each compartment using the fixed 0.999 threshold (in msn), the quantile thresholds (in msn_q) and the SVM. Plot the new results on a PCA plot next to the SVM results. Are the results from the quantile thresholds closer to the SVM?
Task 4 Discuss with your neighbour: SVM scores are not probabilities, but the TAGM output is. Is it appropriate to use quantile-based thresholds on probabilities? What does a threshold of t = 0.75 mean in each case?






AnswerAnswer






Task 1

## Organelle-specific 75% quantile of the overall TAGM-MAP probability
tagm_thresholds <- orgQuants(object = msn,
                             fcol = "tagm.map.allocation",
                             scol = "overall_prob",
                             mcol = "markers",
                             t = 0.75)

Most thresholds are very close to 1, reflecting how extreme the TAGM-MAP probabilities are.
Task 2

## Apply the organelle-specific thresholds, saving to a new object
msn_q <- getPredictions(object = msn,
                        fcol = "tagm.map.allocation",
                        scol = "overall_prob",
                        mcol = "markers",
                        t = tagm_thresholds)

ans

          195           749            72           549            49 
     Lysosome Mitochondrion       Nucleus    Peroxisome            PM 
           37           675          1050            18           210

           38            15            37          5042 


Task 3

## Compare the number of proteins per compartment
table(compartment = c(fData(msn)$svm.pred, 
                      fData(msn)$tagm.map.allocation.pred, 
                      fData(msn_q)$tagm.map.allocation.pred),
      classifier  = rep(c("SVM", "TAGM-MAP fixed", "TAGM-MAP quantile"),
                        each = nrow(fData(msn)))) |>
  as.data.frame.matrix()

               SVM TAGM-MAP fixed TAGM-MAP quantile
Chromatin      168            417               195
Cytosol        860            642               749
Endosome       112             47                72
ER             435           1252               549
Golgi           61             54                49
Lysosome        49             36                37
Mitochondrion  452            717               675
Nucleus        955            806              1050
Peroxisome      23             17                18
PM             202            158               210
Proteasome      57             32                38
Ribosome 40S    20             14                15
Ribosome 60S    65             34                37
unknown       5277           4510              5042



par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
msn |>
  plot2D(fcol = "svm.pred", main = "SVM")
msn_q |>
  plot2D(fcol = "tagm.map.allocation.pred",
         main = "TAGM-MAP, organelle-specific thresholds")








Task 4
orgQuants works on any score, so the code runs without error. However, the threshold means something different in each case:

SVM scores are not probabilities and are not comparable between compartments, so setting a threshold relative to each compartment’s own score distribution is a sensible way to choose cutoffs.
TAGM probabilities are on the same scale for every compartment, so in principle a single threshold such as 0.999 should be enough. A quantile threshold ignores this: it keeps the top 25% of proteins in each compartment, regardless of their actual probability.

In practice, however, the TAGM-MAP probabilities in our data are very close to 0 or 1, so a fixed threshold of 0.999 removes very few proteins. Organelle-specific quantiles bring back some discrimination within each compartment and give results closer to those of the SVM. So, although quantiles do not use the probabilities as probabilities, they can be a useful practical tool when the probabilities are poorly spread. Whichever approach you choose, check the results on a PCA plot and against prior knowledge.














TipKey Points




Supervised classifiers predict the localisation of unknown proteins by comparing their correlation profiles with those of the markers. Proteins can only be assigned to compartments represented in the marker list.
SVM parameters (sigma and cost) are optimised by repeated cross-validation on the markers with svmOptimisation. Class weights stop the classifier favouring compartments with many markers.
getF1Scores shows the best parameters in each iteration and levelPlot shows how every combination performed. Consistent best parameters and high F1 scores indicate a stable, well-performing classifier.
svmClassification assigns every protein to a compartment, so predictions must be thresholded. SVM scores differ between compartments, so compartment-specific thresholds (orgQuants, getPredictions) are more appropriate than a single global threshold.
TAGM-MAP gives a localisation probability and an outlier probability for each protein. Probabilities are on the same scale for every compartment and are easier to interpret than SVM scores, but they are only as reliable as the model behind them.
In our data, TAGM-MAP probabilities are overconfident, so a fixed threshold assigns more proteins than the SVM, particularly in regions between compartments. Visualising predictions on spatial maps, comparing classifiers and choosing thresholds carefully all help to identify confident predictions.
Proteins that remain "unknown" after thresholding are not necessarily a problem. They may belong to compartments not in the marker list, reside in more than one location, or vary in localisation across the cell population.

text:
9.1 Introduction
In the previous lesson we classified the proteins in our U-2 OS data and generated our first spatial maps. Our msn object now contains the curated markers (markers), the thresholded SVM predictions (svm.pred), and the quality columns we added to the joined set at the end of part 1 with addProfileQC(): the number of precursors per protein in each replicate (n_rep1, n_rep2, n_rep3) with their minimum (n_min), and the proportion of values missing before imputation in each replicate (missing_rep1, missing_rep2, missing_rep3) with their maximum (missing_max).

title: 9  Visualisation and exploration
section: 9.2 Spatial maps with different dimensionality reduction methods
text:
9.2 Spatial maps with different dimensionality reduction methods
The result of classification is a list of proteins and their predicted subcellular localisations. These can be visualised as a “subcellular spatial map” using plot2D, by passing the column containing the predictions to fcol. In the previous lessons we mostly used PCA, the default. However, plot2D supports several other methods, listed in plot2Dmethods (see ?plot2D for details).

plot2Dmethods

 [1] "PCA"    "MDS"    "kpca"   "lda"    "t-SNE"  "UMAP"   "nipals" "hexbin"
 [9] "none"   "scree" 


Each method summarises the data in a different way, and no single method shows everything. As discussed in the lesson on assessing resolution, PCA preserves distances but only shows two components at a time, whereas non-linear methods such as t-SNE and UMAP often separate clusters more clearly but distort distances. It is therefore good practice to look at more than one.

9.2.1 Pre-computing coordinates
Non-linear methods such as t-SNE and UMAP can take from a minute to tens of minutes to compute on a dataset of this size. They are also stochastic, so each run gives a slightly different picture unless we set a seed. Rather than recomputing the coordinates every time we make a plot, it is good practice to compute them once, with a seed, and reuse them.
To do this, we pass plot = FALSE to plot2D. Instead of drawing a plot, plot2D then returns a matrix of the two-dimensional coordinates of each protein. Below we pre-compute coordinates for PCA, UMAP, t-SNE and linear discriminant analysis (LDA). LDA is a supervised method: it uses the markers to find the projection that best separates the compartments.

## PCA is deterministic, so we do not need to set a seed
pcas <- msn |>
  plot2D(method = "PCA", plot = FALSE)

## UMAP
set.seed(399)
umap <- msn |>
  plot2D(method = "UMAP", plot = FALSE)

## t-SNE
set.seed(399)
tsne <- msn |>
  plot2D(method = "t-SNE", plot = FALSE)

## Linear discriminant analysis (uses the markers column)
set.seed(399)
lda <- msn |>
  plot2D(method = "lda", plot = FALSE)

Each object is a matrix with one row per protein and two columns.

head(pcas)

           PC1 (35.15%) PC2 (25.23%)
A0A096LP01    -2.811345   -5.2274624
A0A0B4J2F0    -2.377583   -5.4941955
A0A3B3IRV3     2.425945    1.4670772
A0A3B3IS91     5.156840   -0.3892221
A0AV96         4.093129    0.5750826
A0AVF1         4.644023   -0.2817537




9.2.2 Plotting pre-computed coordinates
We can now pass these coordinates back to plot2D with method = "none", which tells plot2D not to compute anything. Because a matrix of coordinates does not contain the feature data, we also pass our MSnSet to methargs so that plot2D knows where to find the fcol annotation.

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot2D(pcas, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", main = "PCA")
plot2D(umap, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", main = "UMAP")
plot2D(tsne, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", main = "t-SNE")
plot2D(lda, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", main = "LDA")
addLegend(msn, fcol = "svm.pred", where = "topright", ncol = 2, cex = .7)








The same compartments are found in all four maps, but each method shows them differently. Compartments that overlap in the PCA plot may be clearly separated in the t-SNE or UMAP plots, and vice versa. Remember that distances between clusters in t-SNE and UMAP plots cannot be interpreted directly.

title: 9  Visualisation and exploration
text:
9.3 Compartment fingerprints with plotConsProfiles
Spatial maps show where proteins lie relative to each other, but they hide the profiles themselves. A compact way to summarise the profiles of a whole class is to calculate its consensus profile, the average profile of the proteins in that class, and display all of these together as a heatmap. Each row is a compartment, each column a fraction, and the colour shows the consensus profile. This gives a “fingerprint” of each compartment across the fractionation gradient.
This takes three steps in pRoloc:

mrkConsProfiles calculates the consensus profile of each compartment and returns a matrix with one row per compartment and one column per fraction.
mrkHClust clusters the compartments by their consensus profiles. We use the resulting dendrogram to order the rows of the heatmap, so that compartments with similar profiles are next to each other.
plotConsProfiles plots the matrix as a heatmap, in the given order.


## 1. Consensus profile of each marker class
fmat <- mrkConsProfiles(msn, fcol = "markers")
dim(fmat)

[1] 13 27

## 2. Order the classes by hierarchical clustering of their profiles
hc <- mrkHClust(msn, fcol = "markers", plot = FALSE)
mm <- getMarkerClasses(msn, fcol = "markers")
ord <- levels(factor(mm))[order.dendrogram(hc)]
ord

 [1] "Chromatin"     "Mitochondrion" "Golgi"         "Lysosome"     
 [5] "ER"            "PM"            "Endosome"      "Peroxisome"   
 [9] "Cytosol"       "Proteasome"    "Nucleus"       "Ribosome 40S" 
[13] "Ribosome 60S" 



## 3. Plot the consensus profiles of the markers
plotConsProfiles(fmat, order = ord)








Each compartment has a distinct fingerprint, with its abundance peaking in different fractions, and the pattern is repeated in each of the three replicates. Compartments next to each other in this plot have similar fingerprints and are harder to separate, which is consistent with what we saw with QSep in the data annotation lesson.
We can make the same plot for the SVM predictions by passing fcol = "svm.pred" to mrkConsProfiles. Proteins left as "unknown" are not included. We reuse the order from the markers so that the two plots can be compared row by row. If the classification is sensible, the newly classified proteins should keep the fingerprint of their compartment.

## Consensus profiles of the SVM predictions, in the same order as the markers
fmat_svm <- mrkConsProfiles(msn, fcol = "svm.pred")
plotConsProfiles(fmat_svm, order = ord)








The fingerprints of the predictions are usually a little less sharp than those of the markers, because the classified proteins include proteins that lie further from the centre of each compartment. A compartment whose fingerprint changes markedly would be worth investigating further.
