title: 9  Visualisation and exploration
text:
9.4 Peptide support and missing values
All of the maps we have made so far treat each protein equally. However, some proteins are quantified from many precursors, whilst others rely on only one or two. Similarly, some profiles are complete, whereas others were partly filled in by imputation. Proteins with little peptide support or many missing values tend to have noisier profiles, which can place them between clusters on a map or prevent them from being classified confidently. Overlaying this information on our maps helps us to interpret them.

9.4.1 Peptide support across the combined data
At the end of part 1 we added the number of precursors supporting each protein in each replicate (n_rep1, n_rep2, n_rep3), together with their minimum (n_min). We use the minimum because a protein is only as well supported as its weakest replicate: a protein with 12, 10 and 1 precursors has a reasonable mean, but its profile in the third replicate rests on a single precursor.

## Summary of the minimum number of precursors per protein
msn |>
  fData() |>
  pull(n_min) |>
  summary()

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   1.00    4.00    9.50   14.74   19.00  474.00 


We can show peptide support on a spatial map by scaling the size of each point. The plot2D function accepts a vector of point sizes through its cex argument. We use a log scale, so that the few proteins with very many precursors do not dominate the plot.

## Point size based on the (log) minimum number of precursors
ptsze <- 0.3 + log2(fData(msn)$n_min) / 3

plot2D(pcas, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", cex = ptsze,
       main = "PCA: SVM predictions, sized by peptide support")
addLegend(msn, fcol = "svm.pred", where = "topright", cex = .6)








Large points are well supported proteins, and small points are proteins supported by few precursors in at least one replicate. Look at where the small points lie: are they spread evenly across the map, or concentrated in particular regions, such as between clusters?


9.4.2 Missing values across the combined data
We can do the same for missing values. The missing_max column gives, for each protein, the largest proportion of values that were missing before imputation in any one replicate. Again, a profile is only as reliable as its weakest replicate.

## Summary of the maximum proportion of missing values per protein
msn |>
  fData() |>
  pull(missing_max) |>
  summary()

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
 0.0000  0.3194  0.4444  0.4598  0.5926  0.7778 


This time we make points smaller as the proportion of missing values increases, so that large points are still the most reliable proteins.

## Point size decreases with the proportion of missing values
ptsze_na <- 1.5 * (1 - fData(msn)$missing_max)

plot2D(pcas, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", cex = ptsze_na,
       main = "PCA: SVM predictions, sized by completeness")
addLegend(msn, fcol = "svm.pred", where = "topright", cex = .6)










9.4.3 Comparing compartments
We can now ask directly whether peptide support and missing values differ between compartments, and in particular whether the proteins left as "unknown" tend to be less reliable. We put both columns in long format and plot them side by side.

## Colours for each compartment, with unknown in grey
classes <- getMarkerClasses(msn)
pred_cols <- c(setNames(getStockcol()[seq_along(classes)], classes),
               unknown = getUnknowncol())

## Peptide support and missing values per predicted compartment
msn |>
  fData() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  pivot_longer(c(n_min, missing_max), names_to = "measure", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = svm.pred, y = value, fill = svm.pred)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.size = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ measure, scales = "free_y",
             labeller = as_labeller(c(n_min = "Minimum number of precursors",
                                      missing_max = "Maximum proportion missing"))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pred_cols) +
  labs(x = "SVM prediction", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        legend.position = "none")








The two measures are related: proteins with few precursors often have more missing values, because there are fewer precursors to fill in the gaps. Look at whether any compartment, or the "unknown" proteins, stand out on either measure. Do you think this is biological or technical?


9.4.4 Peptide support and missing values in each replicate
The minimum and maximum hide which replicate is responsible for a poorly supported or incomplete profile. To see this, we return to the data of each replicate in our QFeatures object, before the replicates were joined, as we did in the lesson on assessing resolution. Let’s store the names of these sets (from our QFeatures object) so that we can coerce them into individual MSnSets for plotting.

## Save names of normalised protein-level sets for each replicate, before joining
rep_sets <- c(rep1 = "proteins_norm_R1",
              rep2 = "proteins_norm_R2",
              rep3 = "proteins_norm_R3")

## Create normalised protein-level MSnSets for individual replicates
for (i in 1:length(rep_sets)) {
  
  se <- qf[[rep_sets[i]]] # Extract protein-level set
  msnset <- as(se, "MSnSet") # Convert to MSnSet
  assign(names(rep_sets[i]), msnset) # Assign name to MSnSet
}

The normalised protein-level replicate sets already contain the .n column that was generated when summarising precursor to protein level data using the aggregateFeatures function.

rep1 |>
  fData() |>
  names()

 [1] "Channel"            "Decoy"              "Proteotypic"       
 [4] "Protein.Ids"        "Protein.Group"      "Protein.Names"     
 [7] "Genes"              "PG.TopN"            "Genes.TopN"        
[10] "Translated.Q.Value" "Channel.Q.Value"    "Lib.PG.Q.Value"    
[13] "is_contaminant"     ".n"                


However, since we imputed before normalising, the normalised data does not contain information about missing values. Instead, we had added this to the pre-normalised protein-level replicate sets (named "proteins_R1", "proteins_R2" and "proteins_R3") by creating the prop_missing column. Therefore, we copy this column to our normalised protein MSnSets for each replicate, so that we can use it for plotting.

## Store names of individual replicate MSnSets
msnset_reps <- c(rep1, rep2, rep3)

## Store names of pre-normalisation protein sets that contain prop_missing
agg_sets <- c(rep1 = "proteins_R1",
              rep2 = "proteins_R2",
              rep3 = "proteins_R3")

## Add prop_missing to the individual replicate MSnSets with normalised protein data
for (i in 1:length(rep_sets)) {
  
  msnset <- msnset_reps[[i]]
  protein_set <- qf[[agg_sets[i]]]
  
  fData(msnset)$prop_missing <- rowData(protein_set)$prop_missing
  
  assign(names(rep_sets)[i], msnset)
  
}

Now we have both columns of interest, .n for the number of precursors and prop_missing for missingness, annotated on each individual replicate’s normalised protein-level MSnSet. Let’s take a look at a summary of these data per replicate.

## Store replicate MSnSets as list
msn_reps <- c(rep1, rep2, rep3)

## Number of precursors and proportion missing per protein in each replicate
sapply(msn_reps, function(x) summary(fData(x)$.n))

             [,1]      [,2]      [,3]
Min.      1.00000   1.00000   1.00000
1st Qu.   5.00000   5.00000   4.00000
Median   10.00000  10.00000  10.00000
Mean     15.65868  15.86315  15.27169
3rd Qu.  20.00000  21.00000  20.00000
Max.    474.00000 629.00000 636.00000

sapply(msn_reps, function(x) summary(fData(x)$prop_missing))

             [,1]      [,2]      [,3]
Min.    0.0000000 0.0000000 0.0000000
1st Qu. 0.2037037 0.3055556 0.2802676
Median  0.3111111 0.4333333 0.4027778
Mean    0.3488944 0.4472738 0.4247754
3rd Qu. 0.4814815 0.5833333 0.5555556
Max.    0.7777778 0.7777778 0.7777778


Our classification was carried out on the combined data. To colour the replicate maps, we copy the SVM predictions across by matching protein accessions. Proteins that were not part of the combined data (for example, because they were missing from another replicate) are labelled "unknown".

## Copy the SVM predictions from the combined data to each replicate
for (i in names(msn_reps)) {
  
  ids <- featureNames(msn_reps[[i]]) # Extract featureNames from each MSnSet
  pred <- fData(msn)[ids, "svm.pred"] # Extract classifications from each MSnSet
  pred[is.na(pred)] <- "unknown" # Set remaining proteins as unknown
  
  fData(msn_reps[[i]])$svm.pred <- pred # Add classifications from concatenated data to individual reps
}

We can now plot each replicate, with points sized by that replicate’s peptide support. To size the points by completeness instead, replace the cex argument with 1.5 * (1 - fData(msn_reps[[r]])$prop_missing).

par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
for (i in names(msn_reps)) {
  
  plot2D(msn_reps[[i]], fcol = "svm.pred",
         cex = 0.3 + log2(fData(msn_reps[[i]])$n) / 3,
         main = paste("PCA:", i))
}

Each replicate has its own PCA, so the plots may be rotated or mirrored relative to each other. What matters is that the same structure appears in each. Plotting replicates separately in this way is also a useful check that the replicates agree, and that no single replicate has noticeably lower peptide support, more missing values or poorer resolution than the others.






ExerciseExercise 1 - Challenge: Which proteins are least reliable?






Level: 

How many proteins are supported by only one precursor in at least one replicate (n_min == 1)?
What proportion of these are classified to a compartment by the SVM, and what proportion remain "unknown"? How does this compare with all proteins?
Highlight these proteins on the t-SNE map using highlightOnPlot. Where do they lie?
Repeat steps 1 and 2 for proteins with more than half of their values missing in at least one replicate (missing_max > 0.5). How much do the two groups of proteins overlap?







AnswerAnswer







## 1. Proteins with a single precursor in at least one replicate

msn |>
  fData() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  filter(n_min == 1) |>
  nrow()

[1] 616



## 2. Relative classification frequency of proteins with 1 precursor vs. all data

## Proportion of unknown in entire dataset
is_unknown <- fData(msn)$svm.pred == "unknown" 
prop.table(table(is_unknown))

is_unknown
    FALSE      TRUE 
0.3959478 0.6040522 

## Recalculate for proteins supported by n_min == 1
low_support <- fData(msn)$n_min == 1
prop.table(table(is_unknown[low_support]))


     FALSE       TRUE 
0.04383117 0.95616883 


The first table gives the proportion of all proteins that are classified (FALSE) or remain unknown (TRUE). The second table gives the same for only low-support proteins.

## 3. Highlight on the t-SNE map

## Extract featureNames for FOI (n_min == 1)
low_support_prots <- featureNames(msn[low_support])

## Annotate FOI on plot
plot2D(tsne, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", main = "t-SNE: single-precursor proteins")
highlightOnPlot(tsne, foi = low_support_prots, col = "black", pch = 1, cex = .8)









## 4. Proteins with more than half of their values missing in a replicate
msn |>
  fData() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  filter(missing_max > 0.5) |>
  nrow()

[1] 3418

## Proportion classified vs unknown
high_missing <- fData(msn)$missing_max > 0.5
prop.table(table(is_unknown[high_missing]))


    FALSE      TRUE 
0.2691633 0.7308367 

## Overlap with the low-support proteins
high_missing_prots <- featureNames(msn[high_missing])
length(intersect(low_support_prots, high_missing_prots))

[1] 491


The 0.5 cut-off is arbitrary. Try other values and see how the numbers change.

title: 9  Visualisation and exploration
text:
9.5 Overlaying protein complexes
Users may wish to add further information to their maps, for example protein complexes, pathways of interest, or compartments that were not used as training data because they lacked resolution or had too few marker proteins. Protein complexes are a particularly nice example, because their members are expected to be found together, and related complexes can reveal how finely our data resolves the cell.

9.5.1 Finding complex members by gene name
To find the members of a complex, it is convenient to search the feature data by gene name. Our data contains a column of gene names from DIA-NN (here Genes; check fvarLabels(msn) for the name in your data). Where several genes map to the same protein group, they are separated by a semicolon, so we write a small helper function that splits these and searches each gene name against a pattern.

## Return the proteins whose gene name(s) match a regular expression
find_genes <- function(object, pattern, gcol = "Genes") {
  genes <- strsplit(as.character(fData(object)[[gcol]]), ";")
  hit <- vapply(genes, function(g) any(grepl(pattern, g)), logical(1))
  featureNames(object)[hit]
}

The pattern is a regular expression. For example, "^ATP6V1" matches all gene names starting with ATP6V1, and "^(TCP1|CCT[2-8][AB]?)$" matches TCP1 and CCT2 to CCT8 (including CCT6A and CCT6B) exactly. You can also use the pRolocVis app (pRolocVis(msn, fcol = "svm.pred")) to search the feature data interactively.


9.5.2 A well-behaved complex: the TRiC chaperonin
The TRiC (or CCT) chaperonin is a large cytosolic complex of eight different subunits that helps newly made proteins to fold. We expect its subunits to be found together, making it a good first example.

## Return featureNames for members of the TRiC chaperonin
tric <- find_genes(msn, "^(TCP1|CCT[2-8][AB]?)$")

## Print the fData Genes and svm.pred for members of the TRiC chaperonin
fData(msn)[tric, c("Genes", "svm.pred")]

       Genes     svm.pred
P17987  TCP1      unknown
P40227 CCT6A      unknown
P48643  CCT5      unknown
P49368  CCT3      unknown
P50990  CCT8      unknown
P50991  CCT4      unknown
P78371  CCT2      unknown
Q99832  CCT7 Ribosome 40S


We can highlight these proteins on any map using highlightOnPlot. We first draw the map with plot2D, and then pass the same coordinates and our proteins of interest (foi, features of interest) to highlightOnPlot.

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot2D(pcas, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", main = "PCA: TRiC chaperonin")
highlightOnPlot(pcas, foi = tric, col = "black", bg = "yellow",
                pch = 21, cex = 2, lwd = 1.5)

plot2D(tsne, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", main = "t-SNE: TRiC chaperonin")
highlightOnPlot(tsne, foi = tric, col = "black", bg = "yellow",
                pch = 21, cex = 2, lwd = 1.5)








The map shows where the complex lies. To see why, we can compare the profiles of its members with those of the cytosolic markers using plotDist. The markers argument tells plotDist which proteins to highlight, here the TRiC subunits in black, while the cytosolic markers are plotted in grey.

## Cytosol markers
cyto_markers <- featureNames(msn)[fData(msn)$markers == "Cytosol"]

## TRiC subunits (black) on top of the cytosol markers (grey)
plotDist(msn[c(cyto_markers, tric), ],
         markers = tric, type = "l",
         mcol = "black", pcol = "grey",
         las = 2)
title("TRiC subunits (black) and cytosol markers (grey)")










9.5.3 Related complexes in different places: the adaptor complexes
The adaptor protein (AP) complexes select cargo for vesicle transport. They are closely related, but act in different places: AP-2 at the plasma membrane, AP-1 at the Golgi and endosomes, and AP-3 at endosomes. Can our data distinguish them?

## Members of the AP-1, AP-2 and AP-3 complexes
ap1 <- find_genes(msn, "^AP1[BGMS]")
ap2 <- find_genes(msn, "^AP2[ABMS]")
ap3 <- find_genes(msn, "^AP3[BDMS]")

lengths(list(AP1 = ap1, AP2 = ap2, AP3 = ap3))

AP1 AP2 AP3 
  6   5   5 



plot2D(pcas, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", main = "PCA: adaptor protein complexes")
highlightOnPlot(pcas, foi = ap1, col = "black", bg = "yellow",
                pch = 21, cex = 2, lwd = 1.5)
highlightOnPlot(pcas, foi = ap2, col = "black", bg = "red",
                pch = 22, cex = 2, lwd = 1.5)
highlightOnPlot(pcas, foi = ap3, col = "black", bg = "blue",
                pch = 24, cex = 2, lwd = 1.5)
legend("topleft", legend = c("AP-1", "AP-2", "AP-3"),
       pt.bg = c("yellow", "red", "blue"), pch = c(21, 22, 24),
       col = "black", bty = "n", cex = .8)










9.5.4 Adding complexes as a new fData column
Alternatively, we can store our annotations in a new column of the feature data, just as we did for markers. This keeps the annotation with the data and allows us to use all the usual plotting functions. The easiest way is to create a named vector, with the annotation as values and the protein accessions as names, and add it with addMarkers. All proteins not in the vector are labelled "unknown".
As an example, we look at the vacuolar ATPase (V-ATPase), the proton pump that acidifies lysosomes and endosomes. It has two parts: V0, which sits in the membrane, and V1, which assembles onto V0 from the cytosol and can come off again. Do the two parts sit in the same place on our map?

## V-ATPase V1 and V0 subunits
v1 <- find_genes(msn, "^ATP6V1")
v0 <- find_genes(msn, "^ATP6V0")

## Named vector of annotations
vatpase <- c(rep("V-ATPase V1", length(v1)),
             rep("V-ATPase V0", length(v0)))
names(vatpase) <- c(v1, v0)

## Add as a new fData column called "vatpase"
msn <- addMarkers(msn, markers = vatpase, mcol = "vatpase")

Markers in data: 13 out of 8736


organelleMarkers
    unknown V-ATPase V0 V-ATPase V1 
       8723           5           8 


We can now pass this column to fcol to plot a map in which only the V-ATPase subunits are coloured.

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot2D(pcas, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "vatpase", cex = 1.5, main = "PCA: V-ATPase")
addLegend(msn, fcol = "vatpase", where = "topleft", cex = .8)
plot2D(tsne, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "vatpase", cex = 1.5, main = "t-SNE: V-ATPase")








The same approach can be used for any annotation, for example proteins from a pathway of interest, proteins identified in another experiment, or a compartment that was not included in the training data.






ExerciseExercise 2 - Challenge: Map a complex of your choice






Level: 
Choose a protein complex you are interested in. Some suggestions:

COPII vesicle coat: SEC23A, SEC23B, SEC24A–SEC24D, SEC13, SEC31A
COPI vesicle coat: COPA, COPB1, COPB2, COPG1, COPE, COPZ1, ARCN1
Retromer: VPS26A, VPS29, VPS35
Ragulator: LAMTOR1–LAMTOR5
TOM complex (mitochondrial outer membrane): TOMM20, TOMM22, TOMM40, TOMM70
Nuclear pore complex: genes starting with NUP


Use find_genes to find the members of your complex in msn.
Look up their SVM predictions. Are they all predicted to the same compartment?
Highlight them on two different maps.
Plot their profiles with plotDist, together with the markers of the compartment they are predicted to.







AnswerAnswer






Here we use retromer as an example.

## 1. Find the members
retromer <- find_genes(msn, "^(VPS26A|VPS29|VPS35)$")

## 2. SVM predictions
fData(msn)[retromer, c("Genes", "svm.pred")]

        Genes svm.pred
O75436 VPS26A Endosome
Q96QK1  VPS35 Endosome
Q9UBQ0  VPS29 Endosome



## 3. Highlight on two maps
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot2D(pcas, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", main = "PCA: retromer")
highlightOnPlot(pcas, foi = retromer, col = "black", bg = "yellow",
                pch = 21, cex = 2, lwd = 1.5)
plot2D(umap, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", main = "UMAP: retromer")
highlightOnPlot(umap, foi = retromer, col = "black", bg = "yellow",
                pch = 21, cex = 2, lwd = 1.5)









## 4. Profiles with the markers of the compartment they are predicted to
## Most common prediction, ignoring "unknown"
pred <- fData(msn)[retromer, "svm.pred"]
cl <- names(which.max(table(pred[pred != "unknown"])))
cl

[1] "Endosome"

## Markers of that compartment
cl_markers <- featureNames(msn)[fData(msn)$markers == cl]

plotDist(msn[union(cl_markers, retromer), ],
         markers = retromer, type = "l",
         mcol = "black", pcol = "grey",
         las = 2)
title(paste("Retromer (black) and", cl, "markers (grey)"))








If the members of the complex are mostly "unknown", the most common prediction will be "unknown" and there will be no markers to compare with. In that case, choose the compartment by looking at the map instead.














TipKey Points




Spatial maps of classification results are made with plot2D by passing the prediction column to fcol. Different dimensionality reduction methods show the data in different ways, so it is good practice to look at more than one.
Pre-computing coordinates with plot = FALSE, using a seed for stochastic methods, and reusing them with method = "none" makes figures faster and reproducible.
mrkConsProfiles calculates the consensus profile, or fingerprint, of each compartment, and plotConsProfiles displays them as a heatmap, ordered by similarity using mrkHClust.
Peptide support and missing values can be shown on spatial maps by scaling point size. Proteins supported by few precursors, or with many values imputed, tend to have noisier profiles, so these measures help to interpret their position on the map and their classification. Plotting replicates separately shows which replicate is responsible.
Members of protein complexes can be found by gene name, highlighted on any map with highlightOnPlot, and stored as new fData columns with addMarkers. Comparing their profiles with those of their compartment using plotDist shows why they lie where they do.

title: 10  Differential localisation analyses
text:
10.1 From static maps to dynamic experiments
In the previous lessons we generated a static spatial map: for a single condition we used marker proteins and machine learning to predict where each protein resides in the cell. Whilst the steady-state localisation of proteins can provide vital information about function, these localisations are specific to the system of interest under the study conditions. Given the functional importance of protein localisation, the question naturally extends from profiling the spatial proteome of a single condition to comparing the spatial proteome between conditions. Correlation profiling methods have been widely applied to study protein dynamics in response to drugs, stress, signalling and differentiation (Itzhak et al. 2016; Orre et al. 2019; Mulvey et al. 2021; Christopher et al. 2025).
We say a protein is differentially localised (DL) if it is assigned to a different primary subcellular location (or niche) in one condition compared with another. Discovering these proteins is the main goal of a dynamic spatial proteomics experiment.
crumbs: {{< iconify fa6-brands github size=lg title='CRIT GitHub' >}}

title: 10  Differential localisation analyses
text:
NoteWhat does “differentially localised” mean in practice?



A correlation profiling experiment measures the distribution of each protein across a set of biochemical fractions. If a protein relocates, its distribution across the fractions (its profile) changes shape so that it now looks like the profile of a different organelle. A change in the amount of a protein (expression) without a change in profile shape is not differential localisation. Such differences in abundance would not be discovered in a correlation profiling experiment since differences in abundance are removed during the row sum normalisation step.
We use the term differential localisation instead of translocation since changes in the distribution of a protein can be due to changes in localised protein turnover (synthesis and degradation) as well as active movement of proteins.
crumbs: {{< iconify fa6-brands github size=lg title='CRIT GitHub' >}}

title: 10  Differential localisation analyses
text:
10.2 The use-case data: insulin-stimulated adipocytes
In this lesson we will use a dynamic LOPIT dataset of 3T3-L1 adipocytes (Conway et al. 2026). Cells were analysed under two conditions:

basal (unstimulated)
insulin-stimulated

Each condition was profiled in three biological replicates, and each replicate was fractionated into 10 fractions which were quantified with TMT 10-plex labelling. Replicate 1 of the basal condition was processed alongside replicate 1 of the insulin condition, and so on, which means the replicates are paired.
Insulin signalling in adipocytes is a classic example of regulated protein trafficking. The best-known example is the glucose transporter GLUT4 (Slc2a4), which is held in intracellular storage vesicles under basal conditions and is rapidly delivered to the plasma membrane in response to insulin, allowing the cell to take up glucose. We should therefore expect to see some proteins moving in this dataset.








Figure 10.1: LOPIT-DC maps the spatial proteome of 3T3-L1 adipocytes under basal and insulin-stimulated conditions. a) Schematic of the experimental workflow used. b) Venn diagrams of overlap in proteins identified across three replicates of LOPIT-DC in basal and insulin-stimulated conditions. Data for each condition was concatenated to give 4005 proteins in common across both conditions. c) Profile of organelle marker proteins across all 10 fractions (basal replicate 1 data shown, all replicates in Extended Data Fig. 1b). d) Principal component analysis (PCA) projection of concatenated basal data (n = 3 biological replicates) showing distinct clustering of organelle marker proteins. Each point represents an individual protein. e) PCA projection of proteins allocated to each organelle under basal and insulin-stimulated conditions. One point is one protein and points are coloured according to localisation.

title: 10  Differential localisation analyses
text:
10.3 BANDLE and SANDLE
In the workflow paper accompanying this course (Hutchings et al. 2025) we used BANDLE (Bayesian ANalysis of Differential Localisation Experiments) (Crook et al. 2022) to find differentially localised proteins. BANDLE is a fully Bayesian model, it uses Markov-chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to sample from the posterior distribution of its parameters, and it outputs a differential localisation probability for each protein. It is powerful, but it requires the user to set priors, run several long MCMC chains (typically on a high-performance computing cluster), and check that the chains have converged before the results can be used.
SANDLE (Statistical ANalysis of Differential Localisation Experiments) (Crook et al. 2026) was designed to answer the same question quickly and robustly, and to handle more complex experimental designs.









BANDLE
SANDLE




Model
Fully Bayesian (Gaussian processes + MCMC)
Robust mixture model + regression test


Run time
Minutes to hours; HPC often needed
Seconds on a laptop


Priors to set
Yes
No


Convergence checks
Yes
No


Needs markers
Yes
Marker-based test yes, marker-free test no


Paired / multi-condition designs
Supported (two conditions)
Supported (two or more conditions)


Output
DL probability + localisation predictions
DL probability + p-value / FDR (need to merge with localisation predictions from elsewhere)





SANDLE combines two complementary tests:

Marker-based test. Using the markers, SANDLE models each subcellular niche in each replicate with a robust multivariate t-distribution. The centre and spread of each niche are estimated with the minimum covariance determinant (MCD), which is insensitive to outlying markers, and graphical lasso regularisation keeps the estimates stable when a niche has few markers. Every protein then gets a probability of belonging to each niche, in each condition. The differential localisation (DL) probability compares these probabilities between the conditions: it is the probability that the niche a protein belongs to in the basal condition differs from the niche it belongs to in the insulin condition. In other words, it reflects our confidence that a protein changes compartmental identity (Crook et al. 2026). The test is called marker-based because it uses the markers to build its model of the niches.
Marker-free test. This test ignores markers and organelles altogether. It asks whether the shape of a protein’s profile changes between the conditions by more than we would expect from replicate-to-replicate noise. The result is a classical p-value, corrected for multiple testing to give a false discovery rate (FDR). Whilst removing the requirement for marker proteins has benefits, a shift in correlation profile shape can only be interpreted as differential localisation when we don’t expect major changes in cell morphology. For example, if a stimulation results in nuclear swelling, the entire nucleus (and all proteins within this organelle) could have a differential profile.

The two tests capture different kinds of evidence: “is the protein assigned to a different organelle?” and “has its profile changed?”. Together they give each protein a DL probability and an FDR, which you can use to rank and explore candidates. There is no single correct way to decide which proteins are differentially localised, you might threshold on the DL probability, on the FDR, on both, or on either, and the thresholds themselves are a choice. Requiring both tests to pass gives a short, conservative list with few false positives (Crook et al. 2026), while thresholding on either test, or using looser thresholds, gives a longer list for exploration. The right choice depends on your biological question and on what you plan to do with the candidates next.


10.3.1 Our approach: localisation and movement as two separate steps
A dynamic experiment asks two different questions about each protein:

Where is it? In which compartment does the protein reside in each condition?
Does it move? Is there evidence that its localisation differs between the conditions?

We answer these separately. For the first, we use the localisations published in the original study of this dataset (Conway et al. 2026), which are provided with the data. For the second, we use the two SANDLE tests. We then combine the two: for each protein that SANDLE flags as a candidate mover, we look up where it is localised in each condition.
You could equally produce the localisations yourself with a classifier, such as the SVM we used in Part 2, applied to each condition in turn. Using the published localisations lets us focus this lesson on differential localisation, and lets us compare our results with the original study.

10.4 SANDLE setup
SANDLE has not yet been released as an R package (but will shortly become part of the bandle package). For this course, all the functions you need are in one script, sandle_functions.R, which we load with source(). You will also need the MSnbase and pRoloc packages from Bioconductor, which we used in previous lessons.

source("code/sandle_functions.R")

The script provides the following functions:







Function
What it does

Splits an MSnSet into a list of MSnSets, one per replicate


sandle_markers()

Joins the two result tables by protein

title: 10  Differential localisation analyses
text:
10.5 Importing the data

10.5.1 Why readMSnSet2()?
In the previous lessons we started from precursor-level output, processed it in a QFeatures object, aggregated it to protein-level and then coerced the protein-level sets into MSnSets with as(..., "MSnSet"), so that we could use pRoloc.
In practice, you may have been given data that has already been processed to protein level: a table exported from Proteome Discoverer or MaxQuant, the output of a collaborator’s pipeline, or a supplementary table from a paper. This data here was taken directly from supporting material of the Conway et al. (2026) paper. We can read the table straight into an MSnSet with the readMSnSet2() function from MSnbase. The end result is the same kind of object (an MSnSet) that we created by coercion at the start of part II, and everything we learnt about pRoloc applies to it.






NoteReminder: the three parts of an MSnSet



An MSnSet stores three linked tables:

exprs(): the quantitative data, with proteins in rows and samples (here, fractions) in columns
fData(): the feature data, with one row per protein and any information about it, such as marker annotation
pData(): the sample data, with one row per column of exprs(), such as the TMT tag, condition and replicate

readMSnSet2() builds the first two from a single spreadsheet. We add the third ourselves.




10.5.2 Look at the file first
Before importing, it is good practice to look at the column names of our data file so that we know which hold the quantitation and which hold the protein information. We read just the header row of the basal file using the getEcols() function.

10.5.3 Read the data into an MSnSet

## Split each condition by replicate - generates a list of MSnSet objects

The marker-free test compares each insulin replicate with its matching basal replicate, so it relies on this. If replicates were not processed in a paired manner, the order does not matter.


The marker proteins are stored in the markers column of the feature data. As in BANDLE, the same marker list must be used for all replicates of all conditions. The markers are assumed not to move between conditions.

title: 10  Differential localisation analyses
text:
10.6 Exploring the data
Differential localisation analysis relies on the same thing as static localisation: well-resolved subcellular niches. Before we run any test we should therefore look at each replicate. Here we use plot2D() to plot the first two principal components (the default) of each replicate, coloured by marker.

## Set plot dimensions
par(mfrow = c(3, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))

## Loop over reps 1-3 of basal
for (i in 1:3) {
  plot2D(control[[i]], fcol = "markers",
         main = paste("Basal, rep", i))
}

## Loop over reps 1-3 of insulin stimulated
for (i in 1:3) {
  plot2D(treated[[i]], fcol = "markers",
         main = paste("Insulin, rep", i))
}

addLegend(control[[1]], fcol = "markers", where = "other",
          ncol = 2, cex = 1.5)








We see clear, separated clusters for most organelles and a similar overall picture in every replicate of both conditions. Note that each PCA is computed separately, so the plots may be rotated or mirrored relative to each other. What matters is the relative position of the clusters.






ExerciseExercise 1 - Challenge 1: Assessing resolution






Level: 
In a previous lesson we used QSep() to quantify how well the subcellular niches were separated. Calculate the QSep scores for replicate 1 of the basal and insulin data and plot them. Are the compartments equally well resolved in both conditions? Which niches are least well separated?






AnswerAnswer







## Carry out QSep
qs_basal   <- QSep(control[[1]], fcol = "markers")
qs_insulin <- QSep(treated[[1]], fcol = "markers")

## Plot QSep results
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(qs_basal, main = "Basal, rep 1")
plot(qs_insulin, main = "Insulin, rep 1")








Overall resolution is similar in both conditions, which suggests that the data are of comparable quality i.e., resolution. This matters because if one condition were much less well resolved, we might see more apparent ‘movement’ simply because proteins are assigned less confidently. For example, if the ER and plasma membrane are well resolved from each other in one condition but not the other, there may be a large number of apparent movers between these compartments. However, resolution can also change for biological reasons. If treatment alters the size or density of an organelle, its sedimentation profile and separation from neighbouring compartments, will change. It is therefore worth comparing resolution per organelle as well as overall. If resolution for a specific organelle differs between conditions, this may reflect either technical variation (e.g. gradient quality) or a real change in that organelle. Comparing replicates within each condition and checking whether that organelle’s marker profiles shift between conditions can help distinguish these. Where resolution is reduced, protein assignments in that region are less certain, so apparent movements involving that organelle or its neighbours should be interpreted with caution.

title: 10  Differential localisation analyses
section: 10.7 Step 1: Where are the proteins localised?
text:
10.7 Step 1: Where are the proteins localised?
The localisation of each protein in each condition, as published in the original study (Conway et al. 2026), is already in the feature data of our MSnSets, in a column called final.localisation. These localisations were predicted with BANDLE and then thresholded on the allocation and outlier probabilities so that only confident assignments were kept. All other proteins are labelled "unknown", in the same way as after thresholding the SVM predictions in Part 2.

## Check protein localisations per condition
basal |>
  fData() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  pull(final.localisation) |>
  table()


              Cytosol Endoplasmic reticulum       Golgi apparatus 
                  331                   408                   138 
             Lysosome         Mitochondrion               Nucleus 
                   80                   600                   129 
           Peroxisome       Plasma membrane            Proteasome 
                   39                   238                    87 
             Ribosome               unknown 
                  236                  1719 

insulin |>
  fData() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  pull(final.localisation) |>
  table()


              Cytosol Endoplasmic reticulum       Golgi apparatus 
                  302                   415                    95 
             Lysosome         Mitochondrion               Nucleus 
                   77                   586                   147 
           Peroxisome       Plasma membrane            Proteasome 
                   37                   205                    79 
             Ribosome               unknown 
                  202                  1860 


Let’s look at the spatial maps of both conditions side by side. As in Part II of the subcellular mapping section, we use the combined data from all three replicates, so we plot the full basal and insulin objects rather than the per-replicate lists.

## Define plot dimensions
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

## Plot subcellular maps of combined data per condition
plot2D(basal, fcol = "final.localisation", main = "Basal")
plot2D(insulin, fcol = "final.localisation", main = "Insulin")
addLegend(basal, fcol = "final.localisation", where = "bottomleft", cex = 0.6)








A large proportion of proteins are "unknown". This is expected: many proteins reside in more than one location, or in compartments not represented by the markers, as discussed earlier in the course.






NoteWhy not take the localisations from SANDLE?



The marker-based SANDLE test also calculates the probability that each protein belongs to each niche, and sandle_markers() reports the most probable niche in each condition. However, these probabilities are a step towards the DL probability, not a classification. There is no outlier or "unknown" class, so every protein is assigned to one of the marker niches however poorly it fits, and the model is not tuned or thresholded in the way a classifier is. We therefore take localisations from a dedicated classification, and use SANDLE for differential localisation.
crumbs: {{< iconify fa6-brands github size=lg title='CRIT GitHub' >}}

title: 10  Differential localisation analyses
text:
10.8 Step 2: Which proteins move?
We now run the two SANDLE tests on the per-replicate data. Neither test uses the final localisations: they give each protein a score for whether it moves, which we will combine with the predicted localisations in Step 3 below.

10.8.1 Marker-based SANDLE
The marker-based test is a single function call. sandle_markers() fits a robust t-distribution to every niche in every replicate, computes the niche probabilities for every protein, and combines them into a DL probability. We pass the two lists of replicates and the name of the marker column.
The robust fitting step uses random subsampling, so we set a seed to make the result reproducible.

## Run marker-based SANDLE
set.seed(1)
marker_res <- sandle_markers(control, treated, fcol = "markers")

## Check results
head(marker_res)

  protein    dl_prob is_marker         niche_control         niche_treated
1  A2A432 0.57586757     FALSE            Proteasome            Proteasome
2  A2A5R2 0.71444320     FALSE               Cytosol            Proteasome
3  A2A6A1 0.84145198     FALSE              Ribosome               Nucleus
4  A2A6Q5 0.90375951     FALSE              Ribosome               Nucleus
5  A2A8Z1 0.07412112     FALSE Endoplasmic reticulum Endoplasmic reticulum
6  A2A9C3 0.99182236     FALSE              Lysosome            Peroxisome
  prob_control prob_treated
1    0.5038873    0.5288237
2    0.5802071    0.5863211
3    0.3415311    0.4787456
4    0.6635241    0.3328648
5    0.9712861    0.9532214
6    0.5286807    0.3331390


The output is a data.frame with one row per protein. The columns we use are:

dl_prob: the differential localisation probability
is_marker: whether the protein is a marker. Markers are given a DL probability of 0 because they are assumed not to move

The remaining columns give the most probable niche in each condition and its probability. As explained above, we do not use these as localisations.
Since the results of marker-based SANDLE are intrinsically related to the quality of the markers provided, it is good practice to visualise the markers that we used as input data. We look at the fitted profile (mean ± 1 standard deviation) of each niche in one replicate. Each organelle should have a distinct and reasonably tight profile.

## QC check - plot fitted profile of markers for each niche
plot_marker_profiles(marker_res, replicate = 1)








These marker profiles look good. In practice, we would recommend doing this for each replicate of each condition.






NoteHow the DL probability is computed



For each protein, SANDLE averages the niche probabilities over the replicates of each condition. The DL probability is then the probability that a niche drawn for the basal condition differs from a niche drawn for the insulin condition, \(1 - \sum_k p_k^{\text{basal}}\, p_k^{\text{insulin}}\). A protein confidently assigned to the same niche in both conditions scores close to 0; a protein confidently assigned to different niches scores close to 1.
Because the DL probability uses the full set of niche probabilities, and not just the single most probable niche, it responds to any change in how a protein’s probability is spread across the niches. This includes a protein that leaves an organelle and ends up between several, or one that becomes partly associated with a second niche. What it does not see are changes in profile that leave the niche probabilities unchanged, for example a shift within a single niche. Note also that a protein that is uncertain in both conditions gets a non-zero DL probability even if it does not move, because two uncertain niche draws can differ by chance.




10.8.2 Marker-free SANDLE
The marker-free test is also a single call. It needs no markers and no model fitting, so it takes well under a second.

## Run marker-free SANDLE
free_res <- sandle_marker_free(control, treated)

## Check results
head(free_res)

  protein      p_value        fdr neg_log10_fdr    F_stat    RSS_diff
1  A2A432 0.5594732005 0.75571338     0.1216429 0.8882892 0.005704546
2  A2A5R2 0.0411199251 0.16354052     0.7863746 2.4662294 0.009056281
3  A2A6A1 0.1223651790 0.30139763     0.5208602 1.8186480 0.046431178
4  A2A6Q5 0.0480435196 0.17540045     0.7559693 2.3719371 0.037212747
5  A2A8Z1 0.0963270550 0.26333779     0.5794868 1.9586834 0.006347953
6  A2A9C3 0.0009028486 0.01708049     1.7674996 5.1593952 0.035569636


For each protein we get:

p_value and fdr: the p-value from the F-test and the Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted FDR
neg_log10_fdr: \(-\log_{10}(\text{FDR})\), convenient for plotting
F_stat: the F statistic
RSS_diff: the difference in residual sum of squares between the two models, an effect size describing how much the profile changes



10.8.3 Combining the two tests
We now join the result tables output from each test by protein. We also add the localisation of each protein in each condition from Step 1.

## Formulate final results
results <- combine_results(marker_res, free_res) |>
  mutate(loc_basal   = fData(basal)[protein, "final.localisation"],
         loc_insulin = fData(insulin)[protein, "final.localisation"])

To see how the two tests relate, we plot the DL probability on the x-axis against \(-\log_{10}(\text{FDR})\) on the y-axis. The dashed lines show the thresholds we will use: DL probability > 0.9 and FDR < 0.1. Proteins in the top-right corner are supported by both tests. Point size shows the effect size (RSS_diff).
We also highlight in red some proteins that were reported as high-confidence movers after insulin stimulation in the original study (Conway et al. 2026). These include the glucose transporters GLUT1 (Slc2a1) and GLUT4 (Slc2a4), the insulin-responsive aminopeptidase IRAP (Lnpep), which travels with GLUT4, TXNIP, which regulates glucose transporter trafficking, the Akt substrate ZNRF2, and the uncharacterised protein C3orf18.

## Store featureNames of POI
known_movers <- c("P17809",  # GLUT1 (Slc2a1)
                  "P14142",  # GLUT4 (Slc2a4)
                  "Q8C129",  # IRAP (Lnpep)
                  "Q8BG60",  # TXNIP
                  "Q71FD5",  # ZNRF2
                  "Q8BGK9",  # C3orf18
                  "Q9WTP2",  # SPRY4
                  "Q05512",  # Mark2
                  "Q9JLN9",  # Mtor
                  "Q80TM9")  # NISCH


## Plot tests against each other
plot_dl_results(results, prob_cut = 0.9, fdr_cut = 0.1, highlight = known_movers)














NoteRecap: what each measure tells us












Measure
Column
Question it answers
Comes from




DL probability
dl_prob
How confident are we that the protein changes compartment?
Marker-based test


FDR
fdr
Is the change in profile bigger than replicate-to-replicate noise?
Marker-free test


Effect size
RSS_diff
How large is the change in profile?
Marker-free test


Localisation
loc_basal, loc_insulin
Where is the protein in each condition?
Published classification (Step 1)




A high DL probability means the protein’s niche probabilities differ between conditions, so it has probably changed compartment. It says nothing about how large the change in profile is.
A low FDR means the profile change is consistent across replicates and unlikely to be noise. A very small but reproducible change can still have a low FDR.
A large effect size means a large share of the protein has shifted to different fractions. On its own it says nothing about noise, so a large but inconsistent change can have a large effect size and a high FDR. We use it to rank candidates and to prioritise them for follow-up.
The localisations tell us where a protein moves from and to. They do not tell us whether it moves: that is what the DL probability and FDR are for.

A convincing mover typically has a high DL probability, a low FDR and a reasonably large effect size. In a differential expression analysis, the FDR and effect size play the same roles as the adjusted p-value and fold change.


How many candidates do we get with each criterion?

## Count number of differentially localised proteins per approach
c(marker_based = sum(results$dl_prob > 0.9),
  marker_free  = sum(results$fdr < 0.1),
  both         = sum(results$dl_prob > 0.9 & results$fdr < 0.1),
  either       = sum(results$dl_prob > 0.9 | results$fdr < 0.1))

marker_based  marker_free         both       either 
         322          718           77          963 


The marker-free test flags many more proteins than the marker-based test. This is expected, because the two tests ask different questions. The marker-free test detects any consistent change in profile shape, including small shifts within the same organelle. The marker-based test asks whether the protein’s membership of the niches defined by the markers has changed, so a change in profile only counts if it changes which niches the protein is likely to belong to. How you combine them is up to you. Here we take the conservative option and require both, which gives a short list to start exploring. For comparison, Crook et al. (2026) required a DL probability of at least 0.8 and an FDR below 0.05 for this dataset. Challenge 2 looks at what happens with other choices.
Our candidate list, ordered by effect size:

## Filter candidates and then order by effect size (largest first)
hits <- results |>
  filter(dl_prob > 0.9, fdr < 0.1) |>
  arrange(desc(RSS_diff)) |>
  dplyr::select(protein, dl_prob, fdr, loc_basal, loc_insulin)

## Look at the top 10 hits
head(hits, 10)

9   Q9EQH3 0.9055122 2.950607e-03   unknown         unknown
10  Q8BJF9 0.9691362 6.864604e-02   unknown         unknown


And how do the previously reported movers score?

results |>
  filter(protein %in% known_movers) |>
  dplyr::select(protein, dl_prob, fdr, loc_basal, loc_insulin)

   protein   dl_prob          fdr       loc_basal     loc_insulin
1   P14142 0.6897125 1.526390e-03         unknown         unknown
2   P17809 0.9379280 3.427718e-04         unknown Plasma membrane

5   Q80TM9 0.5473357 1.010438e-02         unknown         unknown
6   Q8BG60 0.9721408 2.759772e-05         unknown         unknown
7   Q8BGK9 0.8914838 2.229997e-04         unknown         unknown
8   Q8C129 0.6619904 1.194070e-05         unknown         unknown
9   Q9JLN9 0.3728184 3.779413e-01         unknown         unknown
10  Q9WTP2 0.9245449 9.242064e-05         unknown         unknown


Most of these proteins are supported by both SANDLE tests, so SANDLE and BANDLE agree on them. All of them have a low FDR, but GLUT4 and IRAP have a lower DL probability. We look at why in the profile plots below.






ExerciseExercise 2 - Challenge 2: Choosing thresholds






Level: 
Thresholds are a choice, not a law of nature. Find how many candidates you get if you use a more stringent threshold (DL probability > 0.95 and FDR < 0.01) and a more exploratory one (DL probability > 0.8 and FDR < 0.2). How many of the known_movers pass in each case?






AnswerAnswer







## Apply filters / thresholds
stringent <- results |> filter(dl_prob > 0.95, fdr < 0.01)
explore   <- results |> filter(dl_prob > 0.8,  fdr < 0.2)

## Number of DL proteins using these thresholds
nrow(stringent)

[1] 18

nrow(explore)

[1] 183

## Check how many of the previously reported DL proteins meet each threshold
sum(known_movers %in% stringent$protein)

[1] 2

sum(known_movers %in% explore$protein)

[1] 5


Loosening the thresholds recovers more of the known movers, at the cost of a longer list that will contain more false positives. Which you choose depends on what you will do next: a short list for expensive validation, or a longer list for exploration and enrichment analysis.

title: 10  Differential localisation analyses
section: 10.9 Step 3: Where do the movers go?
text:
10.9 Step 3: Where do the movers go?
We now bring the two steps together. For each candidate mover we look up its localisation in each condition, and summarise the movements as a table of from and to compartments, similar to the plotTable() output of BANDLE.

hits |>
  dplyr::count(loc_basal, loc_insulin, sort = TRUE)

               loc_basal     loc_insulin  n
1                unknown         unknown 53
2        Plasma membrane Plasma membrane  6
3        Plasma membrane         unknown  4
4                Nucleus         Nucleus  3
5                Nucleus         unknown  2
6  Endoplasmic reticulum Plasma membrane  1
7  Endoplasmic reticulum         unknown  1
8        Golgi apparatus Golgi apparatus  1
9        Golgi apparatus         unknown  1
10         Mitochondrion         unknown  1
11               unknown Golgi apparatus  1
12               unknown         Nucleus  1
13               unknown Plasma membrane  1
14               unknown        Ribosome  1


You will probably find that many candidates are "unknown" in one or both conditions. This is not a problem with the analysis. A protein that moves is, almost by definition, often a protein that does not sit neatly within one compartment: it may be distributed between several, be in transit, or be in a compartment that is not represented by the markers. Conway et al. (2026) found the same in this dataset, where most high-confidence movers were “undefined” in at least one condition.

10.9.1 Types of movement
To see this more clearly, we take all proteins that pass either test and classify each by what happens to its localisation.

candidates <- results |>
  filter(dl_prob > 0.9 | fdr < 0.1) |>
  mutate(
    test = case_when(dl_prob > 0.9 & fdr < 0.1 ~ "both",
                     dl_prob > 0.9             ~ "marker-based only",
                     TRUE                      ~ "marker-free only"),
    move = case_when(
      loc_basal == "unknown" & loc_insulin == "unknown" ~ "unknown -> unknown",
      loc_basal == "unknown"                            ~ "unknown -> compartment",
      loc_insulin == "unknown"                          ~ "compartment -> unknown",
      loc_basal == loc_insulin                          ~ "same compartment",
      TRUE                                              ~ "compartment -> compartment"))

table(candidates$move, candidates$test)

                            
                             both marker-based only marker-free only
  compartment -> compartment    1                 0                7
  compartment -> unknown        9                25               65
  same compartment             10                11              381
  unknown -> compartment        4                 6               31
  unknown -> unknown           53               203              157


Each type of movement tells us something different:

compartment → compartment: the protein is confidently classified to one compartment in each condition, and they differ. These are the clearest candidates.
compartment → unknown and unknown → compartment: the protein leaves, or arrives at, a confidently classified compartment, but its other location is uncertain. It may move to a compartment that is not represented in the markers, become distributed across several compartments, or sit between clusters.
unknown → unknown: the profile changes, but the protein cannot be confidently classified in either condition. These are often proteins that sit between compartments or are in more than one location (i.e., multi-localised).
same compartment: the profile changes, but the protein is classified to the same compartment in both conditions. These may reflect partial relocation, where only a fraction of the protein moves, a shift within a compartment, or a change that the markers cannot resolve. Crook et al. (2026) interpret proteins with strong marker-free support but a low DL probability in the same way, as “more complex or heterogeneous spatial reorganisation rather than simple compartmental shifts”.

We can now make the from/to table for all candidates.

candidates |>

Using candidates, find all proteins that are classified to the plasma membrane in the basal condition. Where are they classified after insulin stimulation? Which of the two SANDLE tests supports each of them?

Proteins classified to the plasma membrane in both conditions are not necessarily false positives. Their profile has changed, but not by enough to move them out of the plasma membrane cluster, which could reflect a partial change, for example a fraction of the protein being internalised. Proteins that become "unknown" after insulin have moved away from the plasma membrane cluster without being confidently classified elsewhere. Look at their profiles with plot_protein_profiles() (below) before drawing conclusions.

title: 10  Differential localisation analyses
text:
10.10 Visualising the candidates

10.10.1 Protein profiles
Always look at the data. plot_protein_profiles() plots the profiles of chosen proteins in both conditions: thin lines are individual replicates, thick lines the mean, and the shaded band ± 1 standard deviation.
We pass our two lists containing MSnSets for each replicate. We then pass a vector containing the names of our proteins of interest (which must match the featureNames of our MSnSets). Finally, we give labels for our two conditions.

plot_protein_profiles(control, treated, proteins = hits$protein[1:12],
                      labels = c("basal", "insulin"))








A convincing mover shows a consistent change in profile shape across all three replicates, with little overlap between the two conditions.
Now let’s look at two of the known movers. GLUT4 (P14142) is the classic insulin-responsive protein, and IRAP (Q8C129) travels with GLUT4 in the same storage vesicles.

plot_protein_profiles(control, treated, proteins = c("P14142", "Q8C129"),
                      labels = c("basal", "insulin"))








Both profiles change clearly and consistently, which is why both proteins have a very low FDR. Their DL probabilities are lower because GLUT4 and IRAP are stored in specialised vesicles that are not represented by any of the marker niches, and both are "unknown" in both conditions. Their profiles change, but not in a way that clearly moves them from one marker niche to another. This is a good example of a protein giving a clear signal in one test and a weaker one in the other, and of why it helps to look at both.
We can also look at the strongest candidates, by effect size, from each type of movement.

## Select the top 2 candidates from each movement type
top_by_type <- candidates |>
  group_by(move) |>
  slice_max(RSS_diff, n = 2) |>
  ungroup()

## Check the data
top_by_type |>
  dplyr::select(protein, move, loc_basal, loc_insulin, dl_prob, fdr)

# A tibble: 10 × 6
   protein move                       loc_basal      loc_insulin dl_prob     fdr
   <chr>   <chr>                      <chr>          <chr>         <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Q9CQE7  compartment -> compartment Endoplasmic r… Plasma mem… 0.915   5.70e-4
 2 Q9CRA5  compartment -> compartment Plasma membra… Golgi appa… 0.709   6.01e-2
 3 Q99M28  compartment -> unknown     Nucleus        unknown     0.346   5.44e-2
 4 Q62422  compartment -> unknown     Cytosol        unknown     0.00421 1.70e-2
 5 P27661  same compartment           Nucleus        Nucleus     0       1.29e-7
 6 Q9JIX8  same compartment           Nucleus        Nucleus     0       1.15e-5
 7 P17809  unknown -> compartment     unknown        Plasma mem… 0.938   3.43e-4
 8 P48428  unknown -> compartment     unknown        Cytosol     0.00277 3.77e-6
 9 Q9WV86  unknown -> unknown         unknown        unknown     0.751   8.86e-2
10 Q9QXM1  unknown -> unknown         unknown        unknown     0.964   3.06e-2

## Plot these proteins
plot_protein_profiles(control, treated, proteins = top_by_type$protein,
                      labels = c("basal", "insulin"))










10.10.2 Movers on the spatial map
Next, let’s put a few movers back onto the spatial maps. We plot the PCA of the combined data for each condition, coloured by localisation, and add the movers on top using highlightOnPlot. We use the top four candidates from both methods, plus GLUT4 and Q8C129.

## Save featureNames of protein of interest to annotate
movers <- c(hits$protein[1:4], "P14142", "Q8C129")

## Define plotting dimensions
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 6
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

plot2D(basal, fcol = "final.localisation", main = "Basal")
highlightOnPlot(basal, foi = movers, col = "black", bg = "yellow", pch = 21, cex = 1.5)
highlightOnPlot(basal, foi = movers, labels = TRUE, col = "black", cex = 0.5, pos = 3)

plot2D(insulin, fcol = "final.localisation", main = "Insulin")
highlightOnPlot(basal, foi = movers, col = "black", bg = "yellow", pch = 21, cex = 1.5)
highlightOnPlot(basal, foi = movers, labels = TRUE, col = "black", cex = 0.5, pos = 3)








Here we see all movers in yellow, labelled with their accession number since the default for labels = TRUE is to use the featureNames. In some cases, it might be easier to compare the movers if each individual protein has its own colour and symbol.The bg and pch arguments of highlightOnPlot can be a single value (all movers look the same) or one value per feature of interest provided in a vector.

mover_col <- c("black", "red", "blue", "darkorange", "green3", "magenta")
mover_pch <- c(21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 21)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

plot2D(basal, fcol = "final.localisation", main = "Basal")
highlightOnPlot(basal, foi = movers, col = "black", bg = mover_col, pch = mover_pch, cex = 1.5)

plot2D(insulin, fcol = "final.localisation", main = "Insulin")
highlightOnPlot(basal, foi = movers, col = "black", bg = mover_col, pch = mover_pch, cex = 1.5)








We can also plot a legend rather than cluttering our plot with labels.

par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
plot.new()
legend("center", legend = movers, pch = mover_pch, pt.bg = mover_col,
       col = "black", pt.cex = 1.6, ncol = 3, bty = "n")








The PCA of each condition is computed separately, so the two maps may be rotated or mirrored relative to each other. A mover should sit in, or closer to, a different cluster after insulin stimulation. A protein that moves to "unknown" will often move into the space between clusters.






ExerciseExercise 4 - Challenge 5: Follow your own proteins






Level: 
Choose three proteins from Challenge 3, or from the different types of movement above. Plot their profiles with plot_protein_profiles() and show them on the spatial maps using highlightOnPlot.






AnswerAnswer







## Here we take the top protein of three movement types
movers <- top_by_type |>
  group_by(move) |>
  slice_max(RSS_diff, n = 1) |>
  ungroup() |>
  slice_head(n = 3) |>
  pull(protein)

## Check that we have 3 accessions
movers

[1] "Q9CQE7" "Q99M28" "P27661"

## Plot profiles of movers
plot_protein_profiles(control, treated, proteins = movers,
                      labels = c("basal", "insulin"))







## Plot maps of movers
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot2D(basal, fcol = "final.localisation", main = "Basal")
highlightOnPlot(basal, foi = movers, col = "black", bg = c("black", "brown", "yellow"), 
                pch = 21:23, cex = 1.5)

plot2D(insulin, fcol = "final.localisation", main = "Insulin")
highlightOnPlot(basal, foi = movers, col = "black", bg = c("black", "brown", "yellow"),
                pch = 21:23, cex = 1.5)







## Add legend 
par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
plot.new()
legend("center", legend = movers, pch = 21:23, pt.bg = c("black", "brown", "yellow"),
       col = "black", pt.cex = 1.6, ncol = 3, bty = "n")


















10.10.3 Visualising overall trends
There are several different ways we can visualise the overall movement trend of these proteins. The bandle package has functions to generate alluvial (also known as Sankey) and chord (also known as circos) plots to capture the flow of proteins between conditions.
Let’s load the bandle package.

library("bandle")

The plotTranslocations function takes a list of two MSnSets, one per condition, and a feature data column giving the localisation of each protein in each condition. Our basal and insulin objects already contain the localisations in their final.localisation column, so we simply subset them to our candidates (here all proteins passing either test).

## Extract candidates from both conditions
msnset_cands <- list(basal[candidates$protein, ],
                     insulin[candidates$protein, ])

## Check the number of proteins in each object
lapply(msnset_cands, nrow)

[[1]]
[1] 963

[[2]]
[1] 963


Next, we set a colour scheme for the subcellular classes, with "unknown" in grey, and pass msnset_cands to plotTranslocations, specifying the fcol containing the localisations. The default plot generated by plotTranslocations is an alluvial plot, which uses code from the ggalluvial R package.

## Set the colours of the plot to match the organelles
mrkCl <- getMarkerClasses(basal, fcol = "markers")
cols <- c(getStockcol()[seq(mrkCl)], "grey")
names(cols) <- c(mrkCl, "unknown")

## Plot the flow of proteins
alluvial <- plotTranslocations(params = msnset_cands,
                               fcol = "final.localisation",
                               col = cols)
alluvial + ggtitle("Differential localisation: basal to insulin")








The same information can be shown as a chord diagram by setting type = "chord".

plotTranslocations(params = msnset_cands,
                   fcol = "final.localisation",
                   col = cols,
                   type = "chord")








Proteins that stay in the same compartment, including those that are "unknown" in both conditions, appear as flows from a compartment to itself. To focus on proteins whose localisation changes, subset candidates with filter(loc_basal != loc_insulin) before building msnset_cands.

title: 10  Differential localisation analyses
text:
10.11 Interpreting the results
Computational prediction of differential localisation is largely exploratory. LOPIT data contains noise between fractions and replicates, and some proteins naturally sit between organelles or in several at once. The results should be used as a starting point for further investigation (for example, searching the literature for evidence of movement, imaging, or biochemical follow-up), rather than as validation in themselves.
Some things to keep in mind:

Localisation and movement are separate questions. A classification tells us where a protein is in each condition; SANDLE tells us whether it moves. A protein can move without changing its localisation, and a change in localisation near a threshold is not, on its own, evidence of movement.
Markers are assumed not to move. If a marker protein does relocate, the marker-based test cannot detect it, and it may distort both the classification and the niche model. The marker-free test does not have this limitation, but it also flags consistent shifts of whole compartments between conditions, as we saw in Challenge 4.
Many movers are "unknown". Proteins that move often do not sit neatly within one compartment. Movements to and from "unknown" are real results, not failures, but they need careful checking of the profiles.
Results depend on data quality. Poorly resolved compartments lead to uncertain assignments, which in turn inflate DL probabilities. Always check resolution first.
The marker-based test has a random component. The robust fitting step uses random subsampling, particularly for niches with few markers. Set a seed for reproducibility, and treat proteins close to a threshold with caution.
Thresholds are your choice. This applies to the localisations, the DL probability and the FDR. Requiring both a high DL probability and a low FDR gives a short list supported by two kinds of evidence. Using either test, or looser thresholds, gives a longer list for exploration. Choose based on your question and how you will follow up the candidates.







TipKey Points




A protein is differentially localised if it changes subcellular niche between conditions, seen as a change in the shape of its profile across fractions.
We answer two separate questions: where each protein is in each condition, from a classification such as the published localisations or an SVM, and whether it moves, using SANDLE.
SANDLE detects differential localisation in seconds, with no priors, MCMC or HPC, making it a fast and robust alternative to BANDLE.
The marker-based test models each niche with a robust t-distribution and gives a DL probability. The marker-free test compares profiles between conditions and gives a p-value and FDR without needing any markers.
Combining the SANDLE scores with the localisations shows where the movers go. Many move to or from "unknown", reflecting proteins that sit between compartments or in more than one location.
How to threshold, and on which test, is up to you: stringent for a short list, looser for exploration. Candidates should always be checked by plotting profiles and spatial maps, and followed up experimentally.

title: 11  Glossary
text:
11.1.1 Mass spectrometry basics

Precursor ion = the intact, charged peptide ion that is selected for fragmentation. In analysis, a precursor is a unique combination of peptide sequence, modifications and charge state.
Fragment ion = an ion produced by fragmentation of the precursor ion, thus only representing a fraction of the original peptide sequence (e.g. b and y ions).
MS1 spectrum = a survey scan of all intact ions eluting at a given time, separated by mass-to-charge ratio (m/z). Each peptide typically appears as an isotopic envelope of peaks, with intensities that can be used for quantification.
MS2 (MS/MS) spectrum = a mass spectrum of fragment ions produced by fragmenting selected precursor ions, separated by m/z. In DDA, a spectrum usually comes from a single precursor; in DIA, it contains fragments from all precursors in an isolation window (a chimeric spectrum).
Isolation window = the m/z range of precursor ions that is passed to the collision cell and fragmented together. In DIA, windows are typically several to tens of m/z wide and step across the full m/z range.
Chimeric spectrum = an MS2 spectrum containing fragment ions from more than one precursor. DIA spectra are chimeric by design, which is why identification relies on specialised software rather than PSMs.



11.1.2 Acquisition methods

Data-dependent acquisition (DDA) = an acquisition mode in which the instrument selects the most abundant precursor ions from each MS1 scan and isolates and fragments them individually. Each MS2 spectrum therefore usually originates from a single precursor.
Data-independent acquisition (DIA) = an acquisition mode in which all precursor ions within predefined m/z windows are fragmented together, without selecting individual precursors. This gives more complete and reproducible coverage across samples than DDA.



11.1.3 Chromatography

Liquid chromatography (LC) = the separation of peptides over time before they enter the mass spectrometer, which reduces the number of peptides being analysed at once.
Retention time = the time at which a peptide elutes from the LC column. Peptides with the same sequence elute at reproducible times, which helps to identify them.
Extracted ion chromatogram (XIC) = a plot of the intensity of a specific ion (precursor or fragment) against retention time. In DIA, precursors are identified partly because their fragment ion XICs peak together (co-elute).



11.1.4 Identification and data levels

Peptide spectrum match (PSM) = an assignment of an observed MS2 spectrum to a peptide sequence, based on how well it matches the theoretical spectrum of that sequence. PSMs arise from DDA data; DIA has no PSMs.
Spectral library = a collection of reference spectra and retention times for peptides, used to search DIA data. Libraries can be built from DDA experiments or predicted in silico from sequence.
Peptide-centric search = an identification strategy that asks whether the expected fragments of a given peptide are present in the data, as used in DIA. It contrasts with the spectrum-centric approach of DDA, where each spectrum is matched to a peptide.
Modified peptide = a peptide sequence together with its post-translational or chemical modifications (e.g. oxidised methionine), regardless of charge state. One modified peptide can give rise to several precursors.
Protein group = a set of proteins that cannot be distinguished from one another based on the identified peptides, which are reported together as a single entry.
False discovery rate (FDR) = the expected proportion of incorrect identifications among those accepted. It is usually estimated with decoy sequences and controlled at a threshold such as 1%.



11.1.5 Quantification and data processing

Label-free quantification (LFQ) = quantification based on the measured signal of each peptide in each sample, without chemical labels. Each sample is acquired in a separate MS run.
Tandem mass tag (TMT) = an isobaric peptide label used for relative quantification of peptides across samples. Labelled peptides from different samples have the same mass at MS1, and quantification is based on reporter ions released on fragmentation at the MS2 or MS3 level.
Isobaric labels = tags with the same total mass that are indistinguishable at MS1 but release different reporter ions on fragmentation, which allows quantification across samples in the same run.
Reporter ion = a low-mass fragment released from an isobaric tag whose intensity reports the relative abundance of a peptide in a given sample.
Missing value = a peptide or protein that is not quantified in a sample. Missing values are common in proteomics, especially for low-abundance peptides, and are less frequent in DIA than in DDA.
Normalisation = adjusting intensities to remove technical differences between samples or runs (e.g. loading amount), so that samples can be compared.
Aggregation (summarisation) = combining lower-level measurements (e.g. precursors) into a higher level (e.g. proteins) using a method such as the median or a model-based approach.



11.1.6 Spatial proteomics

Subcellular fractionation = the partial separation of a lysate into fractions enriched in different organelles, usually by centrifugation.
Localisation of organelle proteins by isotope tagging (LOPIT) = a spatial proteomics method that measures protein abundance across subcellular fractions, traditionally using TMT labels and DDA.
DIA-LOP = the label-free DIA version of the same approach, in which fractions are acquired by DIA rather than labelled with TMT.
Abundance profile = the pattern of a protein’s abundance across fractions. Proteins in the same compartment tend to have similar profiles.
Marker protein = a protein with a well-established subcellular location, used to define the expected profile of each compartment for classification.
Relocalisation = a change in a protein’s subcellular location between conditions (e.g. treated vs untreated), detected as a change in its abundance profile.
